title: browsertrix: import a user's WACZ files from Browsertrix
description:
Add a 'rustyweb browsertrix' subcommand that authenticates to a Browsertrix instance (Webrecorder's hosted crawling service, which produces the WACZ files rustyweb serves), lists a user's archived items, downloads each WACZ into the home directory's archive folder, and indexes it as a local (File) source.

Grounded in the Browsertrix REST API (from its OpenAPI):
- Auth: POST /api/auth/jwt/login (form username/password) -> JWT bearer token.
- Whoami/orgs: GET /api/users/me, GET /api/orgs (paginated).
- List items: GET /api/orgs/{oid}/all-crawls (crawls + uploads), paginated.
- WACZ: GET /api/orgs/{oid}/all-crawls/{id}/download (authenticated stream) for downloading; GET /api/orgs/{oid}/crawls/{id}/replay.json for presigned resource URLs. Collections: /api/orgs/{oid}/collections/{id}/download.

DESIGN
- Command: rustyweb browsertrix [--host URL] [--org SLUG] [--home DIR] [filters].
- Uses --home like the other subcommands (default '.'); WACZs are written under <home>/archive and the index under <home>/index.
- Host default https://app.browsertrix.com; --host for self-hosted.
- Credentials from env (BROWSERTRIX_USER / BROWSERTRIX_PASSWORD) rather than flags, so passwords do not appear in the process list. (Optionally a token.)
- Flow: login -> resolve org (--org or the sole org) -> list all-crawls (paginated) -> for each item, download its WACZ into <home>/archive/<name>.wacz, then index that local file.
- ALWAYS DOWNLOAD (no --no-download for now): stream the authenticated /download endpoint straight into <home>/archive and index as a File source, so it is durable and replayable long-term. This matches rustyweb's rule that local WACZs live under <home>/archive (index stores them home-relative and portable). Browsertrix presigned/replay.json URLs are short-lived, so indexing them as remote URL sources would break replay after expiry - hence we download. (A remote/no-download mode was considered and deferred: rustyweb-15z.4, closed.)
- Provenance + incremental: record the Browsertrix item id on the collection so re-runs skip already-indexed items unless --force.
- Reuse ureq + serde_json; no new heavy deps. Test against a mock HTTP server serving canned JSON, not the live service.

This is a way to close the loop with Webrecorder, whose Browsertrix creates the WACZ files and whose ReplayWeb.page does the replay.
notes: When implemented, imported WACZs should be assigned to a Collection per the two-level model in rustyweb-collections-model-5co, and downloaded into <home>/archive (already reflected in this epics design).
close_reason: Importer complete and merged to main (PRs #48/#50/#53/#58/#59/#60): API client, import subcommand (auth + public), download & stream ingest, incremental sync/provenance, finding-aid seeding, nested WACZ, concurrency, docs + tests. Remaining follow-up split out: rustyweb-browsertrix-verify-download-hash-tmrn (verify download vs replay.json hash).

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Priority/framing (maintainer): the Browsertrix importer is strategically key -- it's the "index your own crawls" on-ramp for adoption, and promoting Webrecorder / Browsertrix tooling is an explicit goal. Treat it as a first-class track once the hosted SUCHO demo path is up (ingest + deploy), not a side project.

Streaming decision to make before building 15z.1-.3: revisit 15z.3 ("always download"). The maintainer prefers indexing WACZs where they are (streaming, no download) -- it keeps the on-disk footprint index-only, which is ideal for a self-hoster. Streaming is now proven (rustyweb-streaming-index-r0n). So a Browsertrix importer that resolves an org's WACZ resource URLs (per the browsertrix public API) and STREAMS them when range + CORS allow is more coherent than always-download. Keep download as the fallback (private or non-range-capable hosts). Decide streaming-first vs always-download up front, since it shapes 15z.1/.2/.3.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Resolved the streaming-vs-download question flagged in the 2026-07-18 comment (maintainer): the importer targets the AUTHENTICATED API (JWT -> a user's own crawls; the 'index your own crawls' on-ramp), and supports BOTH ingest modes, with STREAMING-FIRST as the priority (it's the path that handles the signed/presigned WACZ URLs).

15z.1 (API client) landed on branch browsertrix-api-client: crates/rustyweb-lib/src/browsertrix.rs. A Transport-trait-abstracted client (mirrors http_range::RangeFetch) with: login (JWT), me(), orgs(), items() (paginated all-crawls), resources() (replay.json -> presigned range-capable paths = the streaming target), and download()/download_url() (authenticated /download stream = the durable fallback). 8 unit tests against canned JSON via a FakeTransport (no live server / no mock-HTTP dep); the mock-server end-to-end test stays with 15z.7. Deferred for a follow-up/.3: wiring the client's GET/POST through http_range's retry/backoff (transient 429/503 politeness) for long paginated ingests.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: Import controls added to .2/.3 (branch browsertrix-api-client): (a) selection — --collection <id> / --crawl <id> to import a specific Browsertrix collection or item (server-side all-crawls filters), with --into <name> as the rustyweb target collection (renamed from --collection); (b) QA filtering. Decision (maintainer): default to REVIEWED-ONLY — only import crawls a reviewer has QA'd in Browsertrix (reviewStatus set). --include-unreviewed imports everything; --min-review <1-5> sets a rating threshold; a single named --crawl is always included. Rationale: for a published/shared instance you want vetted content by default; the skipped-unreviewed count is logged with a hint so an all-unreviewed account isn't a silent no-op.

title: Verify downloaded WACZ against the Browsertrix replay.json hash
description:
The Browsertrix importer (rustyweb-15z.3) downloads each WACZ from its presigned replay.json URL but does not verify the bytes against the resource hash the API provides (replay.json resources[].hash, e.g. sha256:...). The .part→rename dance guards against a partial/truncated write, and indexing records its own SHA-256 (so `rustyweb verify` can detect later corruption) — but we do not catch a silently-wrong/corrupt download AT import time, against the source-of-truth hash.

Add: after download_wacz, compute the SHA-256 of the downloaded file and compare to res.hash (strip the "sha256:" prefix); on mismatch, delete the file and error out for that item (do not index). Reuse collections::file_sha256. Cheap (one pass over the just-written file) and turns a bad download into an immediate, clear failure instead of a subtly broken crawl.

Files: main.rs (download_wacz / run_browsertrix). Small; add a unit or e2e assertion (serve wrong bytes → import errors).
close_reason: Split out of the epic into standalone issue rustyweb-browsertrix-verify-download-hash-tmrn.

title: Import public Browsertrix collections (no login required)
description:
Let a curator import a PUBLIC Browsertrix collection — one Webrecorder (or a self-hosted instance) has published openly — WITHOUT any BROWSERTRIX_USER/PASSWORD/TOKEN. Today `import browsertrix` always logs in (JWT bearer), so public content held by an org you don't have an account on is unreachable, even though Browsertrix exposes it through an unauthenticated API.

## Public API (base https://app.browsertrix.com, verified v1.23.0)
1. `GET /api/public/orgs/{orgSlug}/collections` → `{org, collections[]}`; each collection has `id`, `oid`, `slug`, `name`, `totalSize`, `crawlCount`, `pageCount`, `allowPublicDownload`. (`resources` is empty here.)
2. `GET /api/orgs/{oid}/collections/{collId}/public/replay.json` → `resources[]`, one per WACZ: `path` (presigned S3, range-capable HTTP 206, expires ~48h), `hash` (sha256), `size`, `name`, `crawlId`.
3. `GET /api/public/orgs/{orgSlug}/collections/{collSlug}/download` → stable, token-free WACZ. GET-only, ignores Range (whole-file stream). For a multi-crawl collection this is a MULTI-WACZ (nested .wacz) — nested-WACZ indexing landed in rustyweb-15z.8 (#51), so this path now works.

Two ways in, both viable:
- per-crawl `resources[].path` — flat single WACZs, index cleanly, but presigned URLs expire ~48h (fine once downloaded to <home>/archive).
- collection `/download` — one nested multi-WACZ, token-free/stable, needs the nested-WACZ support we now have.

## Proposed shape
- Public-mode flag, e.g. `import browsertrix --public --org <orgSlug> [--collection <collSlug>]`, that skips login and hits the `/api/public/...` endpoints. No credentials read; error clearly if credentials are supplied alongside --public (they're ignored).
- Reuse the existing download-and-index flow (durable copy under <home>/archive, whole-file fixity) and the metadata seeding from rustyweb-15z.6 (org name → creator, collection description/tags/dates → finding aid). The public collections payload carries name/slug and counts; confirm it also exposes description/caption/tags/date range for seeding (may be a thinner object than the authenticated one — degrade gracefully).
- Respect `allowPublicDownload`: if false, skip/refuse with a clear message.
- Add the two/three public endpoints to the `browsertrix.rs` client behind the existing `Transport` trait; keep auth optional (public transport sends no Authorization header).
- Provenance/incremental (rustyweb-15z.5) should work the same via the Browsertrix item/crawl ids.

## Tests / verification
- Extend the mock Browsertrix server in tests with the `/api/public/...` routes; assert a `--public` import needs no env credentials, seeds the finding aid, and skips already-imported crawls on re-run.
- Manual smoke against a real public org (e.g. `usgov-archive`, Webrecorder's US Gov Web Archive — 15 public collections).

Relates to rustyweb-15z.6 (metadata seeding) and rustyweb-15z.8 (nested multi-WACZ, prerequisite for the collection `/download` path, now landed).
close_reason: Done: merged to main in #60 (import browsertrix --public, incl. --stream).

title: Index nested (multi-)WACZ files
description:
WACZ files can nest: a multi-WACZ is a ZIP whose datapackage.json lists other .wacz files (conventionally under data/) as resources, with no top-level archive/ WARCs. This is exactly what Browsertrix's public collection /download endpoint returns for any collection with >1 crawl.

rustyweb's indexer currently assumes a flat single-level WACZ and would SILENTLY index a multi-WACZ as empty (no error):
- wacz.rs iter_warc_paths (~L257) only yields entries under archive/ ending in .warc.gz/.warc; a multi-WACZ has none.
- find_cdx_entry/search_cdx read the single top-level CDX; read_datapackage reads the single top-level datapackage.json.
Replay is unaffected: wabac.js/ReplayWeb.page already resolves nested WACZs via range reads. The gap is indexing-only.

Scope:
- Detect the multi-WACZ case in wacz.rs (datapackage resources are .wacz, or no archive/ WARCs but .wacz entries exist).
- Recurse into each nested .wacz entry (extract to temp) to pull its WARCs, CDX, and pages for full-text + CDX indexing.
- Recommended approach A (recurse and flatten): keep one Wacz manifest entry per outer file; index all nested content. Alternative B (explode nested WACZs into Collection members) deferred; member file-resolution is trickier since members are ZIP entries, not files.
- Add a multi-WACZ fixture + test. Real fixture available: Browsertrix public /download for a multi-crawl collection, e.g. climate-economic-justice-screening-tool (3 crawls).
- Note in code/docs that replay already handles nesting.

Prerequisite for the simpler Browsertrix import path (one combined /download per collection instead of enumerating + downloading each crawl WACZ).
close_reason: Landed in PR #51: detect nested multi-WACZ (structural), stream each Stored inner in place via SubRangeFetch (no extraction), flatten into one crawl entry, show bundled-crawl count. Verified on the real usgov-archive climate collection.

title: Streaming import + refreshable-remote replay for Browsertrix (index-only footprint)
description:
Optional alternative to the always-download flow (15z.3), for self-hosters who want an INDEX-ONLY footprint: stream-index a Browsertrix WACZ from its presigned replay.json URL WITHOUT downloading, and keep replay working despite ~48h presigned-URL expiry.

Supersedes the naive closed 15z.4 (which indexed the presigned URL as a plain Url source): that is not durable because a baked-in signed URL dies in ~48h and replay breaks. The fix is a REFRESHABLE-REMOTE source that re-signs on demand.

Design:
- New Source variant storing the STABLE identity (host + org id + item/crawl id + resource name/hash), not a fixed signed URL.
- Index: resolve a fresh presigned URL, stream-index in place (download=false) — reuses the existing Url/streaming path + http_range range GETs.
- Replay: make viewer_source point at /files/{id} for this source (as for local files); serve_file re-resolves a fresh presigned URL and 302-redirects to it (fits the existing remote-redirect pattern at server.rs ~706). Cache the signed URL until near expiry so we do not re-auth per range request.
- serve needs Browsertrix credentials/config to re-sign (env or a config file under <home>). This is the real operational cost: fine for a self-hoster indexing their own org; a bigger decision for a public/shared instance. Strictly opt-in; download-for-durability (15z.3) stays the default.
- Handle refresh failures gracefully (creds rotated / item deleted / Browsertrix down) with a clear replay-time error.

Contrast with stable remote URLs (e.g. SUCHO on S3): those already stream-index AND remote-replay today via a plain Url source with no refresh needed — this task is only about the EXPIRING-URL case. Depends conceptually on 15z.1 (client resolves resources). Files: collections.rs (Source), index.rs, server.rs (serve_file/viewer_source), main.rs/config, DESIGN.md.
close_reason: Landed in PR #53: Source::Browsertrix + SourceResolver; import --stream (index-only); on-demand re-resolution for replay (24h cache + stale-token self-heal); local/remote source pills. Verified live against real Browsertrix.

title: Delete a crawl or a collection (remove files + update the index)
description:
Add commands to remove content, keeping the archive folder, the manifest, and the Tantivy index consistent:
- `rustyweb crawl delete <id> [--home] [--yes]`
- `rustyweb collection delete <id|name> [--with-crawls] [--home] [--yes]`
(mirrors the existing `crawl set` / `collection set|list`).

CRAWL DELETE must remove, as one consistent operation:
1. The Tantivy documents for that crawl — delete by term on the crawl_id field, then commit. (Verify crawl_id is a term-indexed field usable with delete_term; add a delete path to SearchIndex if missing.)
2. The manifest Wacz entry (collections.rs / Manifest).
3. The local WACZ file under <home>/archive — ONLY for a File source (a Url source has no local file); guard against deleting a file still referenced by another entry.
4. The cached thumbnail (<home>/index/thumbs/<crawl_id>.jpg and .pinned) — overlaps with rustyweb-thumb-gc-2x5c.
Then, if the crawl was the last member of its collection, decide: drop the now-empty collection or keep it.

COLLECTION DELETE — decide/settle the semantics (flag it for the maintainer):
- default: delete the collection GROUPING only, leaving its crawls (reassign each to its own singleton collection, id==crawl id); OR
- `--with-crawls`: also delete every member crawl (files + index docs) as above.

TRICKY PARTS (why this needs care):
- Tantivy deletes are term-based and only take effect on commit; disk space is reclaimed only on segment merge, so the index wont shrink immediately (document this; a follow-up could force a merge).
- Consistency/atomicity: a crash mid-delete can orphan a file or leave stale index docs. Pick an order (delete index docs+commit → save manifest → delete file/thumb last) and tolerate a re-run cleaning up leftovers. Relates to rustyweb-atomic-reindex-7x3j.
- Destructive: require confirmation unless --yes; print exactly what will be removed (file paths, doc counts).
- Idempotence: deleting an unknown id is a clear error; a partially-deleted crawl can be re-deleted to finish cleanup.

Files: search.rs (delete-by-term + commit), collections.rs (Manifest removal helpers), index.rs (orchestration: delete_crawl/delete_collection), main.rs (CLI + confirmation), thumbnail.rs (remove thumb), DESIGN.md/README. Tests: index a fixture, delete it, assert it is gone from search + manifest + disk, and that a reindex does not resurrect it.

title: Admin / management mode: create collections & add crawls from the browser
description:
Give indice a write surface so a non-CLI user can create/edit collections and add crawls from a browser, WITHOUT the Tauri desktop shell.

WHY NOW (decision, edsu 2026-08-03): the desktop-app epic (rustyweb-desktop-app-i91t) is a packaging concern — it wraps an experience that today has no front door for creating collections or adding crawls. Those admin workflows are the actual unlock and are what a desktop app would eventually sit on top of. So we PAUSE the Tauri track and build the admin backend + a browser admin UI first.

KEY ARCHITECTURAL FINDING (backend survey 2026-08-03): the write surface is INDEPENDENT of Tauri. Today all mutation is CLI-only; the HTTP server is deliberately read-only (opens Tantivy read-only at server.rs:63 so the CLI can hold the write lock). But the library-level write primitives already exist and are clean (home, ...) fns: index::index_location (add crawl, auto-creates collection), index::set_collection (create/edit finding aid), seed_collection, set_crawl_note, thumbnails. The gap is purely the HTTP/transport + writer-locking + auth layer. The existing 'management mode' design (serve --manage, opt-in, default read-only) was already meant to be shared by CLI and app — so it runs fine in a plain browser. Tauri only adds a native file-picker (index-in-place by path vs byte-upload) + double-click packaging.

SCOPE
- Management-mode server endpoints (add crawl) — rustyweb-desktop-app-i91t.3 (re-homed here, decoupled from the app shell).
- Collection write endpoints (create/edit finding aid) — NEW, was unticketed.
- Browser admin UI (forms/pages served under --manage) — NEW; generalizes the desktop-flavored empty-state (i91t.4).
- Delete over HTTP — layered on rustyweb-71im (CLI delete primitive) once that lands.

AUTH DECISION (open): default serve --manage is fine unauthenticated for localhost/single-user. The moment the management surface is reachable off-localhost it needs auth. Decide the model before exposing writes on a bound address (see the auth-decision task).
close_reason:
DONE. The epic as written is delivered: a non-CLI user can create and edit collections, add crawls, write finding aids and import from Browsertrix, all from a browser under 'serve --manage'.

Shipped: .1 collection write endpoints, .2 auth model (loopback-trust + forward-auth), .3 browser admin UI, .5 Browsertrix import UI, plus i91t.3 add-archive endpoints and i91t.4 empty first-run state, both re-homed here from the desktop epic. Landed mainly in PRs #74/#75 (2026-08-05) and after.

The 2026-08-03 call this epic rested on turned out right, and is worth keeping: the desktop app was packaging around an experience with no front door, and the write surface proved INDEPENDENT of Tauri. The library primitives were already clean (home, ...) fns; the only gap was HTTP transport, writer locking and auth. The desktop epic has since been abandoned outright (rustyweb-desktop-app-i91t, 2026-09-27) and nothing was lost by it, because this track carried the actual unlock.

WHAT IT DID NOT COVER, and where it went. Writer locking turned out to be much more than this epic assumed: the in-process mutex it shipped with was not enough once the CLI and server could both write, which led to the cross-process index and manifest locks (PRs #136/#138/#140) and then to 'indice reconcile' for the store-spanning gap no lock can close (rustyweb-9lxf).

THREE CHILDREN OUTLIVED IT and are now standalone rather than closed, since they are separate ideas that happened to be filed underneath:
- r67p.4 MCP write surface (P3). Keeps its 'related' link to rustyweb-mcp-endpoint-bobk, which is the better pairing. Note its stated blockers (HTTP management endpoints + auth model) have BOTH since settled, so it is no longer waiting on anything.
- r67p.6 crawler Accept header on the crawl page (P3, parked in its own title).
- r67p.7 backroom storage view: what is consuming local disk (P3).

title: Collection write endpoints: create/edit a collection finding aid over HTTP
description:
Expose collection create/edit over HTTP, mounted ONLY under serve --manage (same opt-in gate as the add-crawl endpoints in rustyweb-desktop-app-i91t.3; default serve stays read-only per server.rs:63).

Thin handlers wrapping the EXISTING library primitives — no new persistence logic:
- index::set_collection (index.rs:365 -> Manifest::apply_fields) — create/update finding-aid fields: name, description (EAD abstract), curator, creator (origination), dates, rights, subjects[], narrative (Markdown body). Source of truth is the git-committable collections/<slug>/README.md.
- index::set_collection_thumbnail (index.rs:404) — pinned collection thumbnail.
- (optional) seed_collection (index.rs:385) for import-seeded metadata.

Suggested shape: POST /api/collections (create), PUT/PATCH /api/collections/{id} (edit). Return the resulting collection JSON. After write, reload the read-only searcher / re-read the manifest so the change shows immediately (mirror the reload i91t.3 does after indexing).

Requires the write-capable manifest handle + management gate introduced by i91t.3, hence blocked-by it. Files: server.rs (routes+handlers), reuse index.rs/collections.rs primitives.

title: Decide auth model for the management write surface
description:
Decision task (settle before serve --manage is ever reachable off-localhost).

Today the server has NO auth — it's a public read-only site. serve --manage adds mutating endpoints. For the desktop/localhost single-user case that's acceptable unauthenticated (bound to 127.0.0.1). But the moment --manage is exposed on a non-loopback bind, unauthenticated writes are a hole.

Decide: (a) restrict --manage to loopback binds only + refuse to start --manage on a non-loopback address without an explicit auth config; and/or (b) a real auth model (shared token? basic auth? reverse-proxy-trusted header?) for networked admin. Document the chosen guardrail and enforce it at serve startup. Blocks nothing yet but MUST be resolved before any packaged/networked management deployment.
close_reason: Merged in PR #74: forward-auth (proxy identity header + shared secret) + loopback-trust; loopback guard on non-loopback bind.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
DECIDED + IMPLEMENTED on branch management-mode (commit 5bd746e). Model: forward-auth for institutional service deploys + loopback-trust for local.

- Local mode (default --manage): trusts every request; server now HARD-REFUSES to start if bound non-loopback without an auth proxy (was a soft warning).
- Forward-auth mode (--auth-proxy-header <H> --auth-proxy-secret <S>, secret also via INDICE_AUTH_PROXY_SECRET): behind an authenticating reverse proxy that does SSO and injects the user in <H>; indice honors it only when the request also carries the shared secret in X-Indice-Auth-Secret (constant-time compare). Forged/absent identity or a request that skipped the proxy -> 403. who-is-admin delegated upstream (anyone the proxy authenticates); signed-in user shown on /manage; public read-only site not gated.

This was the merge blocker: the management surface can no longer be exposed unauthenticated. Tested (forward_auth_gates_management_routes). Leaving open to close on merge to main.

Follow-up ideas (not needed now): optional --manage-allow allowlist to narrow admin below 'anyone the proxy authenticated'; configurable secret header name.

title: MCP write surface: let agents add crawls & create collections (management over MCP)
description:
Idea (edsu, 2026-08-03): expose the management/write functionality to agents over MCP, so an agent can build and curate an archive — not just search it.

This is the WRITE counterpart to rustyweb-mcp-endpoint-bobk (which is read-only: agents search & retrieve). Candidate MCP tools, each a thin wrapper over the SAME library primitives the HTTP management endpoints use:
- add_archive(path|url, collection, name?) -> index::index_location (the add-crawl path landed in rustyweb-desktop-app-i91t.3 on branch management-mode).
- create/edit collection finding aid -> index::set_collection (rustyweb-admin-mode-r67p.1).
- (later) delete -> rustyweb-71im once the delete primitive exists.

Design notes to carry forward:
- Same opt-in gate as HTTP management mode (default off); a write-capable MCP surface is even more sensitive than the browser one because it's automated, so the auth decision (rustyweb-admin-mode-r67p.2) applies with extra force.
- Progress: MCP is request/response, so long ingests need either a job-id + poll tool or a synchronous call with a sane timeout (the HTTP side streams SSE; MCP can't, so reuse the job registry with a get_job_status tool).
- Consider whether the read MCP (bobk) and this write MCP are one server with a capability flag, or two — likely one server, tools gated by the management flag.

Not scheduled; depends on the HTTP management endpoints + auth model settling first. Parked here so it isn't lost.

title: Import from Browsertrix in the management UI (connect → browse → select → import)
description:
A separate management-UI flow (distinct from the generic add-archive path/URL/upload form) for importing from Browsertrix. Authenticated discovery + batch selection, not a single location string.

WHY SEPARATE: (1) authenticated (host/org + creds or token), (2) discovery+selection wizard (list orgs -> collections/items -> filter by QA review status -> select many), (3) carries Browsertrix provenance + refreshable presigned URLs (re-resolved at replay via the resolver).

BACKEND ALREADY EXISTS as the closed CLI importer (epic rustyweb-15z, merged): browsertrix.rs client (auth, list orgs/collections/items, --public), run_browsertrix/run_browsertrix_public in main.rs (download & --stream ingest, incremental sync, finding-aid seeding), index_location_with_resolver, BrowsertrixResolver at replay. What's MISSING for the UI = HTTP endpoints (mounted under serve --manage) wrapping the LISTING step (GET browsertrix orgs/collections/items for a given host+creds) and the IMPORT step (POST selected items -> reuse the same ingest path, streamed as an add-archive-style job with SSE progress + searcher reload). Auth/creds handling for a browser context (not just env vars) needs design; ties to the auth decision rustyweb-admin-mode-r67p.2.

SHARES SHAPE WITH Archive-It (epic rustyweb-kx53): connect-to-source -> browse -> select -> import. Consider a common 'import from a remote account' wizard/scaffold that both Browsertrix and Archive-It plug into, rather than two bespoke flows.

Depends on the management-mode foundation (i91t.3) and the generic admin UI (r67p.3) landing first.

title: Show crawler Accept header on the crawl page (parked)
description:
The crawler **User-Agent is already displayed** on the crawl page: parsed from the WARC `warcinfo` record (`http-header-user-agent`) into `Wacz.user_agent` (collections.rs:207), populated in `upsert_wacz` (index.rs:1323), rendered as a mono provenance row (server.rs:2066). Populated for Browsertrix WACZs. Nothing to do there.

This issue is only the **Accept header**, which is PARKED because it needs the read path we want to avoid:
- Accept lives ONLY in WARC `request` records. The indexer never reads them: `record_to_raw` gates on `response` (index.rs:2194) and the CDX-guided path pre-filters to HTML/PDF/urn:text MIME (index.rs:2037), so request records (`application/http; msgtype=request`) are never fetched.
- No cheap source: `warcinfo`, `datapackage.json`, and CDX carry no Accept.
- Per-request Accept varies across a crawl, so there's no single clean value — you'd show a set.

To do it anyway (deferred): add a CDX filter branch + a request-record parser (warc.rs only parses HTTP responses today), relax the response-only gate, add `accept: Vec<String>` to `Wacz`, populate in `upsert_wacz`, push a MetaRow next to the UA row. Larger, corpus-linear read change — not worth it now.

title: Backroom storage view: what's consuming local disk (archive + index)
description:
A management-mode (backroom) view that shows what is consuming local storage, so an operator can see where disk is going as an archive grows.

Two things to surface:
1. **Archived data** — the WACZ files under `<home>/archive/<slug>/`. Total, and ideally broken down by collection (and per crawl), since that's the dominant cost.
2. **Search index** — the Tantivy index footprint under `<home>/index/full_text`, by file type (store/pos/term/idx/fast/fieldnorm), with bytes/doc. This already exists as `index::index_stats` / `IndexStats` (the CLI `indice stats` command); reuse it rather than recomputing.

Presentation: a page in the backroom (behind `serve --manage`) with the archive-vs-index split, a per-collection breakdown of archived bytes, the total on-disk footprint, and doc count / bytes-per-doc. Could reuse the size/scale projections from `stats` (1M / 100M docs) as a 'what this scales to' hint. Consider a small bar/treemap, but a sorted table is enough to start.

Notes:
- Archive sizes: sum file sizes under each collection's archive subdir; a streamed (not downloaded) crawl has no local WACZ, so it contributes 0 archived bytes but still has index cost — worth distinguishing local vs streamed.
- Read-only/cheap: walk the dirs + call index_stats; no writer/lock needed, so it's safe to render live in `serve`.
- Ties to the scale epic (qw5) footprint model and the `stats` CLI; this is the UI surface of the same numbers.

Motivation: operator asked to be able to see, in the backroom, what local storage (archived data and the index) is being consumed by.

title: annotations.js: replace 1s replay-doc poll with an observer
description:
watchReplayDoc() (static/replay/annotations.js) sets a 1000ms setInterval that
never stops; each tick calls findReplayDoc, which walks all iframes and, for
shadow-root discovery, does root.querySelectorAll('*') recursively (depth up to
8). On a large replayed page this is continuous CPU/battery cost for the life of
the tab, even after the replay doc is found and stable.

Fix: stop polling once the doc is found + stable (or use a MutationObserver on
the replay container to detect the frame appearing), and rely on the existing
rwp-url-change listener for subsequent navigations. From /code-review of PR #111
(finding #6, efficiency). Not a correctness bug.

title: annotations: capture selection prefix/suffix across node boundaries
description:
currentSelection()'s textBefore/textAfter (static/replay/annotations.js) slice
only node.data of the selection's start/end text node. A selection starting at
offset 0 of a node (start of an element — common) yields an empty prefix even
though visible preceding text exists in a sibling/parent; same for suffix at a
node end. The stored TextQuoteSelector then loses disambiguating context, so
rangeForQuote falls back to plain indexOf(exact) and can highlight the wrong
occurrence when the quoted text repeats on the page.

Fix: gather prefix/suffix by walking neighboring text nodes (e.g. a TreeWalker
over the doc) to collect ~32 chars of real surrounding context, not just the
boundary node. From /code-review of PR #111 (finding #7, robustness). There is
already an indexOf fallback, so this is an enhancement, not a break.

title: Warn in the UI that annotations are public
description:
Annotations are public to read and stored in the clear as Markdown in
collections/<slug>/annotations.jsonl (committable to version control), but the
authoring UI doesn't say so. A user could reasonably assume a "note" is private
and put something sensitive in it.

Add a clear, unobtrusive warning in the annotation composer (the replay-side
Notes panel, static/replay/annotations.js) — e.g. a short line under the
textarea like "Notes are public — anyone who can read this archive can read
them." Keep it quiet (muted text), not a modal. Consider also noting it near the
per-collection annotations index and in the management docs.

The docs already say this (guides/annotations.md has a :::note about public,
in-the-clear storage), so this is about surfacing it at the point of authoring,
not just in the manual. Context: annotations shipped in PR #111; visibility is
intentionally public-for-now (Ed's call), so the fix is a warning, not a
permission change. See rustyweb-page-annotations-gnqf.
notes: Fixed in PR #116 (branch annotation-public-warning off main): muted 'Notes are public…' line in the composer() builder (shows on new + edit) + .anno-public-note CSS. Static assets only; node --check clean. Close when #116 merges.
close_reason: Merged via PR #116 (muted public-notes warning in the composer; Ed reworded to 'Notes are public, so anyone who can read this archive can read them.').

title: Atomic reindex: build into temp dir and swap, so a failed rebuild never touches the working index
description:
reindex currently rebuilds the full-text index destructively and in place: it deletes index/full_text up front, then recreates it from the manifest sources. If the rebuild fails partway (a remote source down, a crash, disk full, process killed), you are left with a partial index — worse than before you started. The resilient-reindex work (rustyweb-reindex-resilient-aev) softened this: a source that fails after retries is now skipped with a warning and reindex still commits a usable-but-incomplete index and exits non-zero. But the working index is still mutated in place, so a hard failure (crash/kill mid-rebuild, not a per-source error) can still leave it degraded.

Make reindex atomic: build the new index into a sibling temp dir (e.g. index/full_text.new) and swap it in with an atomic rename only once the rebuild fully succeeds. On any failure, the existing index/full_text is left untouched — you are never worse off than before the reindex.

Notes / considerations:
- No copy of the old index is needed. reindex already builds the new full-text index from scratch from the sources, so "build into temp" just means writing that fresh build to a sibling path instead of overwriting in place. Cost is transient extra disk: old + new full_text coexist until the swap (~2x full-text index size for the duration).
- Swap: build into <index>/full_text.new, then rename old -> full_text.old (or remove), rename new -> full_text. rename on the same filesystem is atomic. Clean up any stale .new/.old dirs from a previous interrupted run at start.
- Interaction with skip-on-failure: decide the policy when some sources were skipped. Options: still swap in the partial index (current behavior: usable but incomplete) but from the temp dir, OR only swap when 0 sources were skipped and otherwise keep the old index + exit non-zero. Leaning toward: swap in the partial rebuild (so a mostly-good rebuild still lands) but keep exiting non-zero — preserves today's semantics while removing the mid-rebuild-crash risk. Confirm with maintainer.
- Manifest (collections.json / waczs.json) is separate and tiny; keep its save ordered so it stays consistent with whichever index is live after the swap.
- Tests: simulate a failure after the temp index is partly built and assert the original index is still intact and searchable; assert a successful reindex swaps cleanly and leaves no .new/.old dirs.

Follow-up to rustyweb-reindex-resilient-aev (now closed). Ties to the shareable/self-serve goal (a reindex on someone else's box shouldn't be able to destroy their working index).
close_reason: Shipped in PR #83: reindex builds into full_text.new and rename-swaps atomically; a crash/kill/disk-full mid-rebuild leaves the live index intact (mid-swap crash recovers from full_text.old on next run). Partial-rebuild-still-swapped policy preserved. Unit + e2e tests, docs updated.

title: Audit log: append-only <home>/events/<YYYY-MM>.jsonl
description:
Companion to rustyweb-manifest-provenance: the manifest records current custody, an event log records what happened. Together they answer "who deleted this collection", which indice currently cannot answer at all.

DESIGN:
- Event { time, actor: SubjectId, action, target, detail, outcome, message }.
- Action enum covering MUTATIONS ONLY: collection create/update/delete, crawl add/upload/delete, import browsertrix/archiveit, annotation create/update/delete. No reads. No auth failures (those stay tracing::warn from the middlewares -- valuable but far noisier, and they would bloat a committed file).
- Annotation events record the id + collection, NOT the note text: the text already lives in annotations.jsonl with full git history.
- Monthly files give rotation for three lines of code; retrofitting rotation onto one growing file is the kind of thing you only do once painfully. ~200 bytes/event.
- CRITICAL: use O_APPEND + a single line write. Do NOT reuse annotations.rs read-whole-file-then-write_atomic pattern -- that exists because annotations are edited in place. An audit record must not be rewritable, and a truncated rewrite would destroy history.
- Best-effort at the call site: a failed audit write logs tracing::error and does NOT fail the users operation, or a full disk becomes a management outage.
- Plus tracing::info with the actor at each mutation, for operators whose logs go to a pipeline.

DOCS: this file holds login identifiers and is NEVER served over HTTP (no route, ever). reference/home-directory.md must tell operators who publish their home dir to accept that or gitignore events/. Unlike annotations.jsonl, it is not meant to be published.

Tests: append twice -> two lines, second append does not rewrite the first; month rollover picks a new path; an audit write failure does not fail the operation (point home at a read-only dir).
close_reason: Done, stale-open. crates/indice-lib/src/events.rs implements the spec: Event { time, actor: SubjectId, action, target, detail }, the mutations-only Action enum, monthly <home>/events/<YYYY-MM>.jsonl files, O_APPEND + single-line write (events.rs:153, explicitly NOT the annotations read-modify-write pattern), fsio::ensure_within as a backstop plus month_file built from parsed integers so a hostile Event::time cannot escape the directory, and best-effort call sites (auth.rs:391 logs tracing::error and lets the operation stand). Tests at events.rs:200. The docs requirement is met too: reference/home-directory.md documents events/ (line 46) and flags that it holds login identities when deciding what to commit (line 81). The outcome/message fields were deliberately deferred with the reason recorded in the Event doc comment ('an outcome field can be added later without breaking existing logs'), which is a design decision rather than an unmet requirement.

title: Audit the rust/path-injection CodeQL alerts (28 open)
description:
28 open rust/path-injection alerts sit permanently unaddressed, so the CodeQL
gate is red on most PRs and everyone has learned to ignore it. They are NOT all
the same, which is why blanket-dismissing would be wrong:

- CLI-sourced (safe): e.g. index/metadata.rs -- the path derives from the
  operator's own --home flag (clap arg), never from a request. CodeQL's threat
  model counts argv/env as untrusted, hence the flag. Not attacker-controllable.
- HTTP-sourced (needs real review): server/assets.rs x7 -- serve_file and the
  thumbnail handlers build filesystem paths from URL path params
  (crawl id / collection slug). These look safe because ids are resolved
  THROUGH the manifest (col.source.resolve(..); an unregistered id 404s) rather
  than concatenated, and the file must exist -- but each of the 7 should be
  traced individually rather than assumed.
- collections.rs x~15 -- collection-slug -> path joins; slugify/
  ensure_safe_collection restrict to [a-z0-9-], but confirm every path actually
  goes through that guard.

Task: walk the 28, classify each (CLI-sourced / guarded-by-allowlist /
genuinely-needs-a-fix), fix anything real, then dismiss the rest individually
with an accurate per-alert justification so the gate goes green and future
alerts mean something again. Do NOT dismiss as a batch with one boilerplate
reason.

Also worth noting: relocated code re-registers as a NEW alert at the new path
(seen in #117 and #119), so the gate fails on pure code motion until these are
resolved. Context 2026-09-07/08.
notes:
EXPERIMENT RESULT (2026-09-08): fixing the shape did NOT clear the alerts.

Ed's call was to un-dismiss all 28 and instead fix the underlying pattern
(rustyweb-validated-id-newtypes-4upp -> CollectionId newtype, implemented in
PR #119). After the fix, a fresh CodeQL scan still reports exactly 28
rust/path-injection alerts -- same distribution (collections.rs 20,
server/assets.rs 7, annotations.rs 1), only the line numbers moved.

Conclusion: CodeQL's Rust dataflow does not model `CollectionId::parse` (or the
earlier inline `chars().all(is_ascii_alphanumeric)` allowlist) as a sanitizer.
It traces String -> parse -> as_str() -> path and flags the sink regardless. No
reasonable code change clears this rule for this codebase, because every path
ultimately derives from argv (--home) or a request. The only route to a green
gate would be a custom CodeQL sanitizer model, which needs advanced setup + a
custom query pack -- disproportionate for one rule.

So the decision is unchanged in shape but the justification is much stronger
now: dismissing can cite "an unvalidated collection id is unrepresentable --
collection_dir takes &CollectionId, whose only constructors validate", which is
compiler-enforced (verified: passing &str is E0308).

DO NOT re-run this experiment. Remaining choice is dismiss-with-strong-reason
vs. accept a permanently red gate. Ed to decide.
close_reason: All 28 rust/path-injection alerts dismissed individually (2026-09-09), post-merge at their final paths, with per-group justifications: CLI/manifest-I/O (11), on-disk directory scans (6), type-enforced CollectionId (4), serve_file manifest indirection (2), thumbnail handlers (5). Zero path-injection alerts open. Gotcha for next time: GitHub caps dismissed_comment at 280 chars, so the full reasoning lives in this bead.

title: Web archive authenticity (WACZ signatures)
description: Future work on verifiable authenticity, distinct from provenance. A signed WACZ carries a datapackage-digest.json with a hash + cryptographic signature of datapackage.json (webrecorder WACZ auth spec). Two stages: (a) detect and display presence of a signature (no crypto deps); (b) verify the signature against the datapackage (public-key or certificate-signed; needs crypto). Complements the existing sha256 fixity (verify command). Moved out of the provenance epic (was rustyweb-provenance-imd.4) so provenance can wrap up.

title: Detect and display WACZ signature
description: Detect datapackage-digest.json in the WACZ and show a signed/verified status on the collection page alongside the sha256 fixity. Stage (a): detect + display presence (no crypto). Full cryptographic verification is a follow-on stage (b).

title: Permission layer: Reader / Curator / Admin with typed extractors
description:
Authentication and authorization are currently one boolean. `admin_ctx() -> (bool, Option<String>)` answers "is there an identity?" and "may they do this?" with the same value, and NO mutating handler checks it -- add_archive, upload_archive, create_collection, both delete handlers and all seven import handlers do not even take a HeaderMap. The only gate is which router block a route was mounted in. So any authenticated user can delete any collection (with_crawls=on -> remove_dir_all, taking other users annotations.jsonl with it) and spend the servers Browsertrix/Archive-It credentials.

This was fine while the only population was administrators (the model decided in r67p.2). Page annotations introduced a second population -- contributors who sign in to leave a note -- without a second privilege level.

DECIDED MODEL (with Ed, 2026-09-11), three ordered roles:
  Reader     anonymous, or authenticated but not on the roster: public read only
  Curator    create collections, add/upload crawls, edit finding aids, run imports,
             annotate; delete a crawl THEY added and their own notes
  Admin      all of the above, plus delete any crawl, delete a collection, and
             moderate anyone notes
One-line summary: "Curators add and can undo their own additions; only admins remove a collection."

Why not plain "curators delete what they create" (Eds first instinct): ownership is clean for leaves and breaks for containers. If Alice creates a collection and Bob adds 40 crawls, "Alice deletes what she created" destroys Bobs work -- so the rule needs an exception, and exceptions are what make a model hard to communicate. Restricting curator-delete to crawls keeps the real motivation (self-service undo after a mis-upload) while the one irreversible shared act stays privileged. Matches archival practice: accession is a role, deaccession is privileged.

DESIGN:
- Role as an ordered fieldless enum (derive Ord) so a check is `role >= Role::Curator`.
- Principal { id: SubjectId, display_name, role } replacing the tuple. SubjectId already exists (identity.rs).
- Evidence enum { Loopback, Proxy, Cookie } making "the display cookie is rendering-only" a compiler-checked rule rather than a comment. Key regression test: a valid cookie alone resolves to a Principal but is refused on a write.
- Enforcement via axum FromRequestParts extractors Curator(Principal) / Admin(Principal) with PRIVATE fields, so holding one is proof the check ran and no code outside auth.rs can fabricate one. A handler signature then declares its privilege, and privileged helpers (start_index_job, the delete wrappers) take &Curator / &Admin as a witness parameter -- so adding a route and forgetting the check is a TYPE ERROR, not a silent exposure. Same "make illegal states unrepresentable" move as CollectionId.
- Roles from an optional <home>/users.yaml roster (id, name, role, aliases). Absent file => every authenticated user is Admin, i.e. byte-identical to today, so no existing deployment changes behavior.
- Keep ONE manage_routes block, re-documented as authentication-only. Do NOT add per-block role middleware: two mechanisms that can disagree is worse than one the compiler checks.
- GET /api/browsertrix/* and /api/archiveit/* are reads that spend the servers credentials -- they need Admin/Curator, not Contributor. Non-obvious.
- No annotate-only tier yet; the ordered enum leaves room to slot Contributor between Reader and Curator later.

Depends on the provenance fields bead for curator-delete-own-crawl.
close_reason: done

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
STAGING (corrected 2026-09-11). The dependency on manifest-provenance was filed backwards and is now reversed: added_by can only be POPULATED once handlers know who is acting, and getting an identity into handlers IS this bead (add_archive currently takes no HeaderMap at all).

So this bead ships first, with the simpler half of the agreed rule:
  Curator = create collections, add/upload crawls, edit finding aids, run imports, annotate; edit/delete own notes
  Admin   = the above, plus delete any crawl, delete a collection, moderate any note
i.e. curators temporarily cannot delete crawls either.

Then rustyweb-manifest-provenance-sfu7 adds Wacz.added_by using the Principal this bead introduces, and a small follow-up relaxes crawl-delete from Admin to 'Curator who added it', completing Ed's model.

title: Browsertrix import UI — v2 follow-ups (download, creds, tests)
description:
Follow-ups deferred from the v1 Browsertrix import UI (PR #77):

- **Durable download option.** v1 streams selected crawls in place (index-only; replay re-resolves via the server's creds). Add a download-vs-stream toggle for a durable local copy (matches the CLI's default). Needs the download helper (currently download_wacz in the bin) extracted to the lib so the server can reuse it, plus per-item archive subdir handling.
- **Per-crawl write-lock scoping.** bx_import holds AppState.write_lock across the whole item loop (incl. network fetches), so a concurrent add-archive waits for the entire import. Scope the lock per index call.
- **Provider client caching.** Each browse call (orgs/collections/items) builds a fresh Client; on the user/pass path that's a login per step. Cache/reuse a client per host (the replay resolver already caches one).
- **In-browser credentials / multiple accounts** (the earlier 'Option B'). v1 uses server-side env creds + a fixed BROWSERTRIX_HOST. Let an operator enter host + token/user-pass in the UI per session, and/or pick among multiple configured accounts. Needs careful credential handling (no logging/persistence) and interacts with the auth model.
- **End-to-end tests.** v1 tests cover only unconfigured (503) + gated (404); the browse/import glue can't be driven by the browsertrix FakeTransport because BrowsertrixProvider::client returns a concrete Client<UreqTransport>. Make the provider return a boxed/generic client (or accept a transport) so a fake Browsertrix can exercise orgs/collections/items + the import loop.
- **Review filter surfacing.** v1 shows a 'reviewed' hint and pre-checks reviewed crawls; consider a min-review / include-unreviewed control mirroring the CLI.

title: Verify downloaded WACZ against the Browsertrix replay.json hash
description:
Split out of the (now closed) Browsertrix importer epic rustyweb-15z as standalone follow-up.

The Browsertrix importer downloads each WACZ from its presigned replay.json URL but does not verify the bytes against the resource hash the API provides (replay.json resources[].hash, e.g. sha256:...). The .part->rename dance guards against a partial/truncated write, and indexing records its own SHA-256 (so `rustyweb verify` can detect later corruption) -- but we do not catch a silently-wrong/corrupt download AT import time, against the source-of-truth hash.

Confirmed on main (2026-07): res.hash is parsed from replay.json and stored for provenance / incremental-sync keys (set_browsertrix_provenance_by_id, seen keys), but the downloaded bytes are never compared to it. run_verify only re-hashes against the manifest's own computed sha256, not against Browsertrix's advertised hash.

Add: after download_wacz, compute the SHA-256 of the downloaded file and compare to res.hash (strip the 'sha256:' prefix); on mismatch, delete the file and error out for that item (do not index). Reuse collections::file_sha256. Cheap (one pass over the just-written file) and turns a bad download into an immediate, clear failure instead of a subtly broken crawl.

Files: main.rs (download_wacz / run_browsertrix). Small; add a unit or e2e assertion (serve wrong bytes -> import errors).

title: Facet on hostname in addition to site (registrable domain)
description:
Search currently facets on the SITE — the registrable domain computed via site_of() (psl crate), e.g. stanford.edu. Add a facet on the full HOSTNAME too, so meaningful subdomains are distinguishable: library.stanford.edu, exhibits.stanford.edu, sul.stanford.edu all collapse to "stanford.edu" today, which hides useful structure for large multi-subdomain institutions.

Implementation:
- Add a `host` field to the Tantivy schema (string/facet, fast/columnar like the existing site field), populated at index time from each page URL’s host (already available where site_of() runs in search.rs). SCHEMA CHANGE → requires a reindex (SearchIndex::open detects the mismatch and tells the user to reindex).
- Surface it: add host to the facet overview (facet_overview_scoped) and the facet UI (views.rs/server.rs), alongside site.
- Design choice to settle: two independent facets (site AND host), or a single HIERARCHICAL facet path (site → host, e.g. /stanford.edu/exhibits.stanford.edu) that gives both levels in one collapsible tree. Hierarchy reads better for the stanford.edu case; note host cardinality can be high, so consider top-N + counts.
- Keep site faceting as-is; host is additive.

Files: search.rs (schema field + extraction + facet aggregation), views.rs + server.rs (facet UI + query filter, e.g. host: alias like the existing crawl: alias), DESIGN.md/README (note the new facet + that it needs a reindex). Relates to the crawl/site faceting already present.

title: Ingest: warn when a CDX record names an unknown WARC
description:
In collect_page_records_via_cdx (crates/indice-lib/src/index/ingest/pages.rs),
each CDX record is located via starts.get(base) where base is the CDX entry's
filename. On a miss the record is silently dropped (`None => Vec::new()`), while
the fetch/parse failure immediately next to it logs
`tracing::warn!(url, "skipping unreadable CDX record: ...")`.

So a WACZ whose CDX references a WARC name that isn't in the ZIP (or whose name
normalization differs) produces a quietly under-indexed crawl with no signal --
pages just go missing. Add a warn! on that arm too (ideally naming the CDX
filename, deduped or counted so a systematically-mismatched WACZ doesn't emit
thousands of lines -- e.g. tally misses and warn once with the count at the end).

Pre-existing; predates the WaczAccess refactor (PR #118). Found by /code-review
of #118, 2026-09-07.

title: Spike: declare fsio::ensure_within as a CodeQL barrier instead of re-dismissing path-injection alerts
description:
SPIKE, may come back "not supported". Ed asked (2026-09-12) whether the new
containment check means we can stop ignoring the path-injection warnings. It
does not, and this is the thing that would actually help.

THE PROBLEM IS NOT THE DISMISSALS, IT IS RE-DISMISSING

CodeQL keys an alert to a source LOCATION, so moving code re-mints the same
finding as a brand-new alert and the old dismissal does not carry. We have now
paid this three times:

  - the original 27 path-injection alerts, dismissed individually (38 total
    across that sweep, comments capped at 280 chars, which made it tedious)
  - #57, re-minted in collections.rs purely because #126 moved
    write_finding_aid a few lines
  - #58-#61 in events.rs / fsio.rs, each new module getting its own pair

Every future refactor of a write path will do it again.

WHY THE CONTAINMENT CHECK DOES NOT FIX IT

Verified empirically: after adding fsio::ensure_within, alerts #60/#61 moved
with the code (to fsio.rs:93 and :107) and are still state=dismissed, NOT
state=fixed. CodeQL did not recognize the guard as a barrier.

It also could not, even in principle, for the remaining flow. The alert says
"this path depends on a user-provided value" and that value is `home`, from
--home. `home` is the root we validate AGAINST, not a component we validate;
there is nothing to check it for, because pointing it anywhere is the
operators prerogative. So the alert text stays literally true forever, and
"wont fix" is the correct disposition for that class.

What ensure_within actually guards is a DIFFERENT risk: a bad component (a
collection id, a crawl id, a month) escaping the home. CodeQL was not tracking
that as a separate flow.

WHAT TO TRY

Declare the barrier once instead of dismissing N times. CodeQL models-as-data
lets a model pack mark a function as a sanitizer/barrier; we already run
advanced setup (.github/codeql/codeql-config.yml), so there is a place to put
one. fsio::ensure_within being a single chokepoint is what makes this possible
now and was not possible before -- there was no one function to point at.

Steps:
  1. Check whether CodeQL models-as-data supports Rust sinks/barriers at all.
     Rust support is young; a query-pack change is what produced the original
     27 alerts, so this may simply not exist yet. If not, stop here and record
     the finding -- that is a useful answer.
  2. If it does: add a model pack declaring fsio::ensure_within as a barrier
     for rust/path-injection, wire it into codeql-config.yml.
  3. Confirm a fresh scan reports the write sites as fixed rather than needing
     dismissal, and that it does NOT suppress a genuine finding -- test by
     temporarily adding a write that bypasses ensure_within and checking it is
     still flagged. A barrier that hides real problems is worse than the
     dismissals.

EXPLICITLY NOT THE ANSWER

paths-ignore for these files. That is what we did for the vendored
ReplayWeb.page bundles (ui.js/sw.js), and it was deliberately scoped to those
and never the directory, because our own annotations.js had to stay scanned.
Excluding our own write paths from scanning is the opposite of what we want.

FALLBACK if the spike fails: carry on dismissing, and keep the 280-char
reason handy. The status quo is tolerable, just irritating.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: Fourth occurrence (PR #129): adding carry_permissions shifted the lines in fsio.rs, so the dismissals on #60/#61 stopped applying and CodeQL minted #62/#63 at fsio.rs:122 and :151. Nothing about the code's safety changed; only its line numbers did. Running tally of the re-dismissal tax: the original 27, then #57 (collections.rs, moved by #126), then #58-61 (new modules), now #62-63 (same file, lines moved). Every write-path edit will keep doing this.

title: Group collection members by site on the collection detail page
description:
On the collection detail page, group member crawls by site instead of showing every crawl as its own tile.

Context: the collection detail page now shows a grid of member crawls, each with its representative image (rustyweb-crawl-thumbnail-s1ff). A collection often contains repeat crawls of the SAME site over time, which share the same og:image, so the grid can look repetitive (e.g. 10 near-identical tiles for one site crawled 10 times).

Idea: collapse members by site (registrable domain, the same `site` value the Site facet uses) into one tile per site, with:
- a representative image (any member's thumbnail for that site),
- a "crawled N times" badge / capture date range,
- expand to the individual crawls (or link to a site-scoped view / search).

Considerations:
- Grouping key: registrable domain (site) vs exact host (domain) vs seed URL. Site (eTLD+1) is probably right, matching the Site facet.
- A collection can legitimately mix many one-off sites (no repeats) — in that case grouping is a no-op and the flat grid is fine, so only group where it reduces clutter.
- Ordering: by most-recent capture, or by crawl count.
- Interaction: clicking a site tile could go to a search scoped to collection + site (collection:<slug> site:<host>), which already works, or to an expanded member list.
- Ties into the two-level collection model and could inform a future "site" as a first-class grouping level.

v1 (flat per-crawl grid) shipped in s1ff; this is the refinement. Lower priority — do if the repetition is noticeable in practice.

title: Two-level collections (Collection groups WACZs)
description: Introduce a first-class curated Collection that groups many WACZ/crawl members, replacing the current one-WACZ-is-one-collection model. A Collection carries curatorial provenance (name, description, intent/scope) and becomes the primary browse and facet unit; each member WACZ keeps its technical provenance (see the provenance epic). This scales rustyweb from an individual archive to an institutional one (e.g. reorganizing TBs of WARC) and is the structural fix for the long collection list. See the Discovery, Provenance and Collections section of DESIGN.md.
close_reason: Two-level collections complete: data model + migration (.1), collection facet in search (.2), grouping + metadata CLI (.3), browse UI (.4).

title: Collection group data model + migration
