Also landed the wget WARC-Target-URI angle-bracket fix and `indice crawl list`. Replay verified end-to-end on a wget crawl of ducklake.select.

title: Durable writes: one atomic-write helper, and make the manifest critical section the API
description:
Came out of a design question from Ed (2026-09-12) about whether the filesystem handling wants an abstraction. Survey says: not a missing layer, but two specific problems.

── PROBLEM 1: the write discipline is assigned backwards ──────────────────
Two disciplines coexist in the tree.

ATOMIC (temp file + rename):
  - annotations.rs:352 `write_atomic` -> collections/<slug>/annotations.jsonl
  - index/swap.rs -> the whole index directory swap
  - archiveit.rs:360-373 -> WARC download via .part + rename
  - index/ingest/acquire.rs:248 -> download_to_temp

PLAIN std::fs::write, which TRUNCATES then writes:
  - collections.rs:609 `Manifest::save` -> index/waczs.json  <-- the authoritative
    record of every crawl in the archive, including provenance set out-of-band
    (browsertrix/archive_it refs, added_by) that a reindex CANNOT rebuild
  - collections.rs:1018 `write_finding_aid` -> collections/<slug>/README.md
    <-- every curator hand-written narrative
  - collections.rs:1147 `write_crawl_note` -> collections/<slug>/crawls/<id>.md
  - thumbnail.rs:51

So the newest and least critical committable file is the ONLY state file
written safely, and the most important one is not. annotations.rs already
argues the case correctly in its own docstring ("a crash mid-write can never
truncate the store"); that reasoning never propagated backwards.

Not hypothetical: this is the mechanism behind the "fails open" finding on
rustyweb-manifest-provenance-sfu7. `Manifest::open` erroring on a
partially-written waczs.json is exactly what made an empty before-snapshot
dangerous.

Also NOTHING fsyncs anywhere in the crate. So even the atomic paths survive a
process crash but not a power loss: rename is atomic w.r.t. other processes,
but neither the data blocks nor the parent directory entry are durable.

FIX (small, ~30-50 lines): hoist `write_atomic` out of annotations.rs into a
shared home (a small `fsio` module, or `collections`), and use it for
Manifest::save, write_finding_aid, write_crawl_note. Add opt-in fsync of the
file AND the parent directory for the manifest at least. Keep the error context
strings — they are good.

── PROBLEM 2: open/mutate/save is three calls with an invisible invariant ──
There are TEN `Manifest::open` -> mutate -> `save()` sites (index/metadata.rs
x2, index/ingest/mod.rs, index/delete.rs x2, index/provenance.rs x3,
index/reindex.rs). `save()` rewrites the whole file from an in-memory vec, so
every one of those is a read-modify-write whose atomicity is the CALLER
discipline. Nothing in the API says so.

The lock that enforces it lives in a different layer entirely:
server/mod.rs:135 `write_lock: std::sync::Mutex<()>` — advisory, guarding
nothing structurally. The library is deliberately `(home, ...)` free functions
and should stay that way, but that means the caller is sometimes the CLI
(single process, fine) and sometimes a server job (needs the lock).

This is exactly how a lost-update race shipped in manifest-provenance: A opens,
B ingests and saves, A saves its stale copy and erases B entry while B
documents stay in Tantivy. Caught in review, fixed by holding the lock — but
the fix was discipline again, not structure.

FIX: make the critical section the API rather than the caller problem, e.g.

    Manifest::update(&index_dir, |m| { ... })?   // open + apply + atomic save

so there is no way to express the unlocked version. Same move as CollectionId
(private field + parse) and the Curator witness type. Consider whether the
server write_lock should become the thing that hands out the writer, rather
than a Mutex<()> next to it.

── EXPLICITLY NOT WANTED ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
A Filesystem/VFS trait for testability. Tests already use tempfile::TempDir and
exercise the real filesystem, which is strictly MORE faithful — the bugs here
(truncation, partial reads, rename semantics, fsync) are precisely the ones a
mock cannot reproduce, so a mock would test the mock. Path CONSTRUCTION is also
already in decent shape: CollectionId makes an unvalidated path component a
compile error, and collection_dir/annotations_path/crawl_note_path centralize
the joins. (A CrawlId newtype is separately bead rustyweb-4upp.)

── WHY THIS NEVER SURFACED ────────────────────────────────────────────────
Worth recording, because it is a process observation rather than a code one.
`fs::write` for the manifest was FINE while the server was strictly read-only
and the CLI was the single writer — one process, no concurrency, and a torn
write needed a crash at an exact moment. Management mode (Aug 2026) introduced
concurrent writers and answered it with `write_lock`, which handles CONCURRENCY
but not TORN WRITES; the write discipline was never revisited under the new
risk profile. And Manifest::save has not changed since, so it never appears in
a diff — which is the class of issue diff-based review systematically misses.

PRIORITY: P1 because phase 1 is cheap and the failure mode is real data loss of
unrecoverable provenance. Exposure today is low (single user), so rescope
freely — but the fix is smaller than the analysis.
close_reason:
Landed across three PRs, all merged: #136 (index tier), #138 (request-path writers + the 503 policy), #140 (the manifest's critical section).

WHAT THE BEAD ASKED FOR, AND WHAT HAPPENED

"One atomic-write helper" was #129 (fsio). "Make the manifest critical section the API" is index::manifest::manifest_write — open, hand to the caller, save, all inside one hold of a manifest lock. That is Manifest::update from #129, withdrawn then because the signatures could not carry the guard; #132 removed that obstacle.

The decisive point, which the original plan had right and is worth keeping: locking Manifest::save alone would not have worked, because by then the stale read has already happened. The lock has to span the read, which is why the API is a closure rather than a guarded save.

THREE TIERS, NOT ONE
- INDEX (.index.lock): everything that writes Tantivy documents — ingest, rebuild, optimize, delete, annotation sync. Held for the operation.
- MANIFEST (.manifest.lock): one read-modify-write of waczs.json. Ordered inside the index lock. Separate so a description can be saved during a multi-hour rebuild, which was Ed's explicit call.
- Request path: bounded acquire, 10s then 503 + Retry-After naming the holder. Background jobs and the CLI still block.

BUGS FOUND ALONG THE WAY THAT THE BEAD DID NOT PREDICT
- The plan's table said ingest-vs-ingest was covered by Tantivy's writer lock (true) and implied that was the worst case. REBUILD vs ingest was not covered at all — reindex writes the sibling full_text.new, and Tantivy names its lock relative to the index dir — and the loss was total: the swap deletes the old index AND the rebuild saved a stale manifest. Live on main at the time.
- A rebuild could resurrect a deleted crawl (snapshot re-indexes an entry whose file is gone, preserves it, saves it back).
- A note saved mid-rebuild had its document discarded by the swap.
- Provenance written after index_location released the lock could be erased by a concurrent rebuild, which also made the next import re-download every WARC.
- The finding-aid save still took AppState.write_lock, so describing queued behind an in-process ingest anyway — the headline property was not delivered until #140's last commits.

WHAT REMAINS (filed separately, none of it data loss)
- rustyweb-9lxf: the store-spanning gap. No transaction exists over Tantivy plus the manifest, so a crash between the commit and the manifest save orphans documents. Permanent by construction now that the files-on-disk model is settled; repair rather than prevention.
- Lock plumbing consolidation and busy-before-authorization: see the beads filed alongside this closure.

The storage question was settled while closing this out: markdown and JSON stay on disk rather than moving to a database, so the locking is the accepted price.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
PHASE 1 DONE + PHASE 2 PARTIAL (PR in flight).

Done: fsio::write_atomic (temp + fsync + rename + dir fsync), used by Manifest::save, write_finding_aid, write_crawl_note, and the two annotation writers, which now delegate instead of keeping a second copy. Manifest::update packages the read-modify-write at the seven short sites; reindex and ingest stay open-across-the-operation with comments saying why.

STILL OPEN, and it needs a decision rather than a patch: making the LOCK unforgettable. Manifest::update is packaging, not serialization. Two concurrent callers still each read, mutate their own copy, and atomically install it; the later save wins. That is the class of bug that shipped in #126.

Two ways to close it, both with real costs:

(a) A process-wide lock inside the library (static Mutex, or a ManifestWriter guard type). Cheap and covers the server. But reindex and ingest hold the manifest across long operations, so the lock would be held for minutes, and any nested Manifest::update inside a closure deadlocks. Needs an audit that no path nests, and a loud doc.

(b) Thread a capability from the server: AppState.write_lock stops being a Mutex<()> and becomes the thing that hands out a writer, which library mutators then require (like the Curator witness). Structurally the right answer and it makes the requirement visible in signatures. But it widens the ingest signatures, which already carry ten parameters, and that was the reason crawl custody went out-of-band in the first place.

Leaning (b) for correctness and (a) for effort. Worth Ed's call before doing either.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: Phase 2 option (b) -- thread a write-lock capability from the server -- is blocked on rustyweb-ingest-params-mqls, now linked. The reason (b) looked expensive is precisely that the ingest signatures already carry 9-10 parameters and cannot take another; fixing that first makes (b) cheap, and makes the choice between (a) and (b) much less close.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Manifest::update was WITHDRAWN from PR #129 at Ed's call (2026-09-12), because the lock stayed external and an abstraction named 'update' that does not serialize reads safer than it is. The implementation is not lost: commit fd60bc6 on the pre-rewrite durable-writes branch has it, along with the seven converted call sites and the save-on-success/leave-alone-on-error test. Recover with 'git show fd60bc6' when the locking design is settled.

PR #129 is now fsio only (atomic write + containment), which is independent of the lock question.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Finding that reframes the design (2026-09-14, verified in the source).

THE PLAN'S TABLE WAS WRONG ABOUT ONE PAIR. It recorded 'ingest vs ingest' as already excluded by Tantivy's INDEX_WRITER_LOCK, which is true (both open index/full_text). But REINDEX vs INGEST is NOT excluded, and the loss is total rather than partial:

- reindex opens its writer on the SIBLING dir: reindex.rs:105 open_with_heap(new_dir) where new_dir = index/full_text.new. An ingest opens index/full_text (ingest/mod.rs:279).
- Tantivy's lock file is '.tantivy-writer.lock' RELATIVE TO THE INDEX DIRECTORY (tantivy-0.26.1 directory_lock.rs:46), so those are two different locks. Neither sees the other.
- reindex reads the manifest ONCE at the start (reindex.rs:46) and saves ONCE at the very end (reindex.rs:205), after swap_in_new_index.
- swap_in_new_index (swap.rs:52) renames full_text -> full_text.old, full_text.new -> full_text, then REMOVE_DIR_ALL(full_text.old).

So: `indice reindex` starts at T0. A curator adds a crawl through the workroom at T1 — it indexes into full_text and saves the manifest with the new entry. At T2 reindex swaps and DELETES full_text.old, destroying that crawl's documents, then saves its T0 manifest copy, erasing the entry. Both halves gone, silently, no error on either side. There is no server reindex endpoint, so this is CLI-reindex vs server-add, i.e. exactly the cross-process case that server/mod.rs:210 documents as a supported workflow.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE DESIGN: reindex must exclude INGESTS for its whole duration — its output is stale with respect to any ingest that commits during the build, so no amount of narrowing the manifest critical section fixes it.

But reindex does NOT need to exclude MANIFEST-ONLY writes (write_finding_aid, set_collection, set_collection_thumbnail, the provenance setters). Those add no documents, so the rebuilt index is not stale with respect to them; only the manifest would be clobbered, and that is fixable by having reindex re-read the manifest just before saving and re-apply only the entries it rebuilt. That distinction is what decides whether a multi-hour rebuild makes the workroom's describe-work unusable or merely stops new crawls being added.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Review findings on PR #136 that are NOT fixed there, so the next slice has them written down.

INDEX-TIER WRITERS STILL UNLOCKED (both write documents, so both belong to the tier #136 established):

1. delete_crawl / delete_collection (index/delete.rs:87, :201). A rebuild can RESURRECT A DELETED CRAWL. Sequence: reindex acquires the lock and snapshots the manifest with crawl X; a curator deletes X in the workroom (server/manage.rs takes only the in-process write_lock, so this proceeds); delete drops X's docs, removes archive/<slug>/X.wacz and the manifest entry; the rebuild re-indexes from its snapshot, finds X's file missing, warns 'skipping missing local WACZ' but PRESERVES the entry, and saves the snapshot. X is back in waczs.json pointing at a file that no longer exists, the deletion is half-undone, and reindex exits non-zero.

2. index_annotation_upsert / the annotation sync (index/search_sync.rs:27, :50). A note saved between the rebuild's annotation pass and its swap has its document deleted by remove_dir_all. Recoverable (annotations.jsonl survives) but silently unsearchable until someone runs another rebuild, and nothing reports it.

Both were left out of #136 because they run on the REQUEST PATH, where the blocking acquire is the wrong answer: taking the flock inside a handler that already holds AppState.write_lock is exactly the wedge #136 had to fix in the ingest job (park a blocking thread on an external lock while holding the mutex that gates every workroom write). So they need the poll-then-deadline-then-503 policy first. That is the decided wait policy (agreed 2026-09-14): background jobs and the CLI block after announcing the holder; request-path writes poll to ~10s then 503 with Retry-After.

MANIFEST TIER (the original subject of this bead) — the constraint #136 surfaced: NOBODY MAY HOLD THE MANIFEST ACROSS A LONG OPERATION. Both index_location (ingest/mod.rs, read once before the loop, saved per WACZ) and reindex (read at the start, saved at the end) currently do, so a finding-aid save mid-ingest is erased by the next per-WACZ save. The uniform rule has to be: re-read, apply, save, release, under a brief hold, at every save point. For reindex that means re-reading just before saving and re-applying only the entries it rebuilt.

ALSO WORTH DOING (review suggestion, not a defect): a single chokepoint inside index/ — something like index::writer(home, what) -> (IndexLock, SearchIndex) — would cover all seven production writable-open sites at once instead of each one remembering the convention, without touching the ~50 test sites that open a bare temp index. The two gaps above are what forgetting the convention already costs. Good shape for the slice that brings delete and the annotation sync in.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
LOCK ORDERING IS NOW A RULE, NOT AN OBSERVATION — constraint for the next slice (found 2026-09-18 while explaining the lock to Ed).

PR #136 made the server take the cross-process index lock BEFORE AppState.write_lock, at all six sites that need both (manage.rs:206/222, imports.rs:312/317, 348/353, 408/413, 673/678, 704/709). That was required: acquiring it inside write_lock parks a blocking thread on an flock while holding the mutex that gates every workroom write.

The consequence, which the module doc originally got wrong: the order is now genuinely INVERTIBLE, so it must be stated as a rule. A handler that holds write_lock and then calls a library function taking the index lock deadlocks against a job that took them in the documented order — AB-BA, and it HANGS rather than failing.

The three handlers holding write_lock today are safe only because the library functions they call do not take the index lock yet:
  manage.rs:557 (set_collection), :584 (delete_crawl), :654 (delete_collection), plus the annotation writes in api.rs:275/312/358.

So when delete_crawl / delete_collection / index_annotation_upsert come under the index lock, the acquisition must be HOISTED TO THE TOP OF EACH HANDLER, above write_lock — NOT simply added inside the library function. Adding it to the library function is the obvious move and it is the deadlocking one.

Also measured while answering the thundering-herd question:
- flock wake-all is benign: the kernel wakes waiters, one wins, the rest block again. No spinning, no errors, nothing to handle.
- But flock is NOT FIFO, so there is no queue fairness; sustained contention can overtake a waiter indefinitely. Acceptable at curator scale, worth knowing before anyone runs this multi-tenant.
- Each waiting job parks a tokio blocking-pool thread (512 default) for the whole wait, and there is no cap on queued jobs (job_counter just increments). Read paths mostly do not use that pool — page rendering and search do not — but api.rs:203 list_annotations does, so a saturated pool would stall annotation listing.
- Verified end-to-end that the accession desk already shows the wait: the message is sent as a  event before , and manage.js:18 renders any phase, so no UI change was needed. The SSE stream a browser receives starts with:
  event: phase
  data: {"type":"phase","phase":"waiting for reindex (pid 40927) (started 1s ago) to finish…"}

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: Correction to the previous comment: its last bullet should read "the message is sent as a `phase` event before `begin`". Two backticked words were eaten by shell command substitution when it was written.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Wording correction on the thundering-herd bullet above: I wrote "before anyone runs this multi-tenant", which is the wrong term. indice has no tenancy model — one home is one archive with one curatorial group, and roles come from a single users.yaml; there is nothing to isolate between tenants.

What the flock-unfairness note actually depends on is SUSTAINED WRITE CONTENTION, not the number of people. Starvation needs the lock to be essentially never free, so a waiter can be overtaken round after round. Several curators doing occasional adds does not produce that: the lock is idle almost all the time. The shape that would is an automated writer in a tight loop or on a schedule (a cron-driven Archive-It sync, a script feeding crawls in) competing with an interactive add — the human could be repeatedly overtaken while the machine keeps winning.

Worth adding that this is largely moot for the intended deployment anyway: server/mod.rs:133 says one in-flight add at a time is plenty for the single-user desktop case, and imports.rs:661 makes the same assumption for imports. So the honest status of flock unfairness is a documented property with no reachable failure today, not a risk to design around — it belongs in the "what it does not protect against" list rather than in a queue-fairness work item.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Review findings on PR #138 NOT fixed there, with rationale, so the manifest-tier slice has them.

1. UNBOUNDED WAIT ON THE IN-PROCESS MUTEX. Only the cross-process flock is deadline-bounded. All five request handlers then do a plain write_lock.lock() with no bound (api.rs create/update/delete, manage.rs crawl/collection delete), so a request can still park past its own 10s budget. Harmless today because the only write_lock holder that does NOT also hold the index lock is set_collection (the finding-aid save), which is short. It stops being harmless the moment the manifest tier adds long-lived write_lock holders — so that slice should either bound the mutex wait too (manage.rs:151 acquire_write_lock is the existing try-then-announce-then-block shape) or make every write_lock holder take the index lock first. DESIGN currently says a handler "waits ten seconds and then returns 503", which is true of the flock and not of the mutex immediately after it.

2. THE BOUNDED WAITER POLLS AND SO LOSES RACES. Wait::Forever calls file.lock() and joins the kernel wait queue; Wait::Until polls try_lock every 50ms. On release the kernel hands the lock to a queued waiter before the poller next ticks, so a request-path acquire can miss many free windows inside its budget and 503 anyway, while background jobs win every time. Inherent to mixing blocking and polling acquisition on one flock. Acceptable while contention is occasional; if it bites, the fix is a real queue rather than a shorter poll.

3. BUSY IS CHECKED BEFORE AUTHORIZATION in three handlers, so a curator who lacks permission for that object gets 503 (plus the holder name, pid and runtime) instead of 403, and is told to retry something they will never be allowed to do. Not fixed because the authoritative custody check is deliberately made INSIDE the lock (manage.rs comment: reading it outside leaves a TOCTOU window where the crawl is re-added under a different owner). Fixing it properly means a cheap advisory pre-check outside the lock purely to reject early, with the real check still inside. Worth doing if the disclosure matters; the caller is already an authenticated curator, so it is low.

4. CLEANUP, not defects: manage.rs threads a Busy(String) variant through two hand-rolled outcome enums, which is exactly what Write<T> was added to avoid, and acquire_index_for_request re-wraps Acquisition into a nested Result<Result<_, String>> saying the same thing a third time. Returning Write<IndexLock> would collapse four copies of the adapter. Also read_holder is called on every 50ms poll tick though only the last value is used, and the "waiting" WARN fires once per request-path acquire even though that caller will not wait it out.

5. THE 503 TEST COSTS 10s. REQUEST_LOCK_WAIT is a const with no test seam. Considered and declined: an env var or a ManageConfig field to save ten seconds of CI is not worth the API surface. Retry-After is now derived from the const so the two cannot drift.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Second review pass on PR #138. Fixed there: optimize_if_fragmented decided outside the lock (the fix had landed one level too low, on optimize(), which nothing calls on the post-ingest path); locking created an index dir in a wrong home just to report there is no index; the annotation update/delete audits still preceded may_edit so a 403/404 logged a change; the rejected-collection-id signal was lost when the audit moved; the annotation handlers were the only non-poison-tolerant write_lock holders; Retry-After could floor to 0; the JS showed raw bodies for every status; the contention WARN claimed bounded callers were "waiting"; read_holder ran every poll tick.

STILL OPEN, for the manifest-tier slice:

1. FIVE ENCODINGS OF "BUSY". Acquisition::{Held,Busy}, Write::{Done,Busy}, CrawlDeleteOutcome::Busy, DeleteOutcome::Busy, and the anonymous Result<IndexLock, String> that acquire_index_for_request returns — one state, four translation steps. Acquisition is already the shape callers need; returning anyhow::Result<Acquisition> and matching directly removes the wrapper, the nested Result, and the Ok/Err reversal that reads like an error when it is not.

2. THE PREAMBLE IS COPY-PASTED INTO FIVE HANDLERS, comment and all (api.rs x3 byte-identical, manage.rs x2 same shape). The ordering rule is enforced by five people remembering to paste the same block, which is exactly what lock.rs:103 warns about. A `with_request_index_lock<T>(home, what, impl FnOnce() -> Result<T>) -> Result<Write<T>>` — or a tower layer over the write routes — makes it structural: the body cannot run without the guard, and the next handler omitting it becomes a compile question rather than a silent hang. Worth doing before a sixth handler exists.

3. THE 10s TEST. REQUEST_LOCK_WAIT is still a const with no seam, so tests/manage.rs spends ~10s sleeping. Declined twice now on the grounds that an env var or a ManageConfig field is not worth the API surface for CI time — but note the second reviewer points out a real coverage cost too: nothing exercises the "acquires mid-wait" path through HTTP. That path IS now unit-tested in lock.rs (a_bounded_acquire_succeeds_when_the_lock_frees_up), which was the cheaper answer.

4. BUSY BEFORE AUTHORIZATION (raised in both passes). An unauthorized curator waits 10s, parks a blocking thread, and gets 503 plus the holder name/pid instead of 403. Not fixed because the authoritative custody read is deliberately inside the lock (TOCTOU: a crawl id is a hash of its source, so the entry can be deleted and the same WACZ re-added under a different owner). A fix means an advisory pre-check outside the lock purely to reject early, with the real check still inside — i.e. deliberately duplicated authorization logic, which is its own hazard. Decide explicitly rather than drifting into it.

5. UNBOUNDED MUTEX WAIT after the bounded flock wait (carried over from the first pass) — still the thing the manifest tier must not make worse.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
xhigh review of PR #140 (manifest tier). Fixed there: nested manifest_write silently losing the inner write (now refused — re-entrancy is right for the index lock and wrong for this one); the finding-aid save still taking AppState.write_lock so describing still queued behind an in-process ingest job (the headline property was not actually delivered on the server path); the collection delete happening outside the hold via a remove_dir_all whose error was discarded; provenance setters creating index/ in a wrong home; dead create_dir_all in metadata; plus four doc claims that overstated what the code guarantees and one test that could pass vacuously.

STILL OPEN after #140:

1. NO BOUNDED MANIFEST ACQUIRE. lock_manifest is Wait::Forever only, justified by "the hold is always brief" — which is false for one caller: a rebuild applies every crawl it rebuilt in a single closure, so that hold is O(crawls) with a linear scan per upsert plus a rewrite of every dirty finding aid. A request-path writer (delete, annotation) blocks for the whole of it, past the 10s budget it gets on the index lock, with no 503. The docs now say this honestly. Fix if it bites: a lock_manifest_within mirroring lock_index_within, and have the rebuild apply in batches rather than one closure.

2. THE REBUILD STILL WRITES STALE name AND collection. targets is snapshotted before the rebuild; index_one is handed Some(name) and (collection_id, collection_name) from it; the final upsert writes those into the freshly-opened manifest. Only browsertrix/archive_it/added_by are re-read fresh. So a manifest-only writer that renames a crawl or moves it between collections mid-rebuild is silently reverted. NOT reachable today — no rename or move endpoint exists — but it is exactly what rustyweb-y7p6 (crawl set --collection / re-home) would add, so that bead must handle it. Note the tension: the rebuild tags the *documents* with the snapshot name, so simply preferring the fresh manifest value would leave the index and the manifest disagreeing.

3. PERFORMANCE, unmeasured: index_location now does two full Manifest::open per call (planning snapshot + the one inside manifest_write), and Manifest::open re-reads waczs.json, runs migrate_flat_finding_aids and parses every collection README. archiveit::import_crawls calls index_location once per crawl and then set_archiveit_provenance_by_id, so an N-crawl import does ~3N full manifest loads and 2N full waczs.json rewrites. On an archive with hundreds of collections that is a real per-crawl cost on a hot path. Worth measuring before optimising.

4. MEMORY: a rebuild now holds three copies of the metadata at once — the targets snapshot (kept alive to the end because the annotations loop reads it), the Vec<Indexed> of everything rebuilt, and the manifest opened inside the closure. Dropping the snapshot after the annotations loop, or hoisting the annotation ids out of it, removes a third.

5. Carried over and unchanged: the five encodings of "busy" plus the copy-pasted acquire preamble across five handlers (do it before a sixth exists), busy-checked-before-authorization, and the unbounded AppState.write_lock wait after the bounded flock wait. On that last one — #140 removed write_lock from the finding-aid save, so the set of holders that do not also hold the index lock is now empty. Deleting AppState.write_lock entirely is probably the right end state and would close that item; worth checking each remaining holder first.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Storage question settled (2026-09-22): Ed prefers keeping markdown and JSON on disk over moving the manifest into a database, so the files stay and the locking is the accepted price of that choice. Do not revisit SQLite without a concrete trigger.

Two consequences recorded rather than left implicit:

1. The store-spanning gap is now PERMANENT BY CONSTRUCTION — there is no transaction available over Tantivy plus the manifest, so a crash between the commit and the manifest save will always be able to orphan documents. Repair is the answer instead of prevention: filed as rustyweb-9lxf (reconciliation pass, probably an addition to `indice verify`).

2. The question surfaced a documentation bug that was actively dangerous: DESIGN told curators `index/` was all derived and safe to gitignore, while waczs.json holds the only copy of which crawls exist, where every remote one came from, custody, and import provenance. Fixed on the manifest-lock branch.

title: Interstitial modal on replay: 'you're viewing an archived copy'
description:
When someone lands on a replayed page via a direct link, show a dismissible modal making it clear they are viewing content inside a web archive — an archived copy captured at a point in time — NOT the live site at its original location. The ReplayWeb.page toolbar/banner already conveys this, but it is easy to miss (small, top of frame), especially for a visitor who arrived from an external link straight into a memento.

Behaviour:
- On the initial load of the replay viewer for a memento, overlay a modal: e.g. "You are viewing an archived copy of <original-url>, captured <capture datetime>, from <collection / crawl name>. This is not the live web page and may look or behave differently." with a clear dismiss (and ESC/backdrop close), and optionally a "visit the live page" link (caution: it may have changed or be gone).
- Show it once per session (sessionStorage), so clicking around within a crawl does not re-nag. Show again for a genuinely new direct entry.
- Accessible: focus the dismiss, trap focus while open, ESC to close, aria-modal.

Where: the replay viewer (static/replay/viewer.html) — rustyweb owns that wrapper page around the <replay-web-page> element, so the modal is our overlay (independent of the ReplayWeb.page bar). Pull the original URL / capture datetime / collection+crawl from the values the server already injects into the viewer.

Notes / relations:
- Pairs with the persistent structured replay URLs (rustyweb-federation-shwl.1, /crawl/{id}/{ts}/{url}): those are exactly the bookmarkable/shareable direct-entry links this modal is for, and they carry (crawl, ts, url) to populate the message. Consider building this after, or design the trigger to key on top-level navigation into a memento vs in-archive clicks.
- Fits rustyweb’s provenance ethos (surface that this is an archive, and its capture context). Keep it lightweight — no heavy JS/deps; a small self-contained overlay in viewer.html.
- Files: static/replay/viewer.html (modal markup/CSS/JS), maybe server.rs/views where viewer config is injected; README/DESIGN note.

title: Faceted overview on collection (and WACZ) detail pages
description:
Idea (maintainer): show facets on the collection detail page (/collection/{id}), scoped to that collection -- and evaluate the same for the individual WACZ detail page (/wacz/{id}).

Today: the homepage shows an archive-wide facet overview (facet_overview()) and the search page has the full facet sidebar (collection, site, date, type, language). The collection page shows metadata + member WACZs; the WACZ page shows provenance + seed pages -- neither shows facets.

Proposal: compute a SCOPED facet overview on these detail pages, reusing the existing faceting (search_faceted supports filters; facet fields include site, year/month timeline, type, lang, and status). Scope by FIELD_COLLECTION (the curated collection) on the collection page, and FIELD_COLLECTION_ID (the per-WACZ id) on the WACZ page. Render the familiar breakdown (top sites, a month timeline, types, languages) with each value linking into a scoped search. This turns each collection into a faceted "reading room" entry point rather than just a member list.

Individual WACZ: same idea scoped to one WACZ. The collection facet is moot there, but site/date/type/language/status still help convey what a crawl captured. Evaluate value vs clutter (a single WACZ may be small) -- likely lower priority than the collection page.

Building blocks already exist (facet_overview / search_faceted + the facet sidebar view); this is mostly wiring a scoped facet query into the two detail handlers and reusing the sidebar rendering. Relates to the faceted-discovery work.
close_reason: Both detail pages now carry the scoped facet overview. Crawl page done via FacetScope::Crawl + collection_id as a recognized search filter (chip resolves the opaque WACZ id to the crawl's name). Collection page shipped earlier in the stack.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Collection detail page DONE (PR forthcoming): scoped facet overview on /collection/{id} via new SearchIndex::facet_overview_scoped(FacetScope::Collection). Renders Top sites / By year / Types / Languages (Collection dimension dropped as moot; empty dimensions skipped), each value linking into a search already scoped to the collection (`/search?q=collection:<id> <field>:<value>`), reusing the homepage browse-link markup/CSS. Crawl detail page (/crawl/{id}) — DEFERRED, keeping this open. FacetScope::Crawl (over collection_id) is already implemented, so the facet counts are trivial to compute. The open question is the click-through: to scope a search to a single crawl the link needs `collection_id:<id>` to be a recognized filter, which would surface an opaque WACZ-hash id in the search box / active-filter chip. Options to decide: (a) add collection_id as an EXTRA_FILTER with a "Crawl" label (removable chip, but shows the hash); (b) scope invisibly in the query text (no chip, still leaks the hash); (c) crawl-page facets as a non-linking overview only. Per the original scope note this page is lower priority ("evaluate value vs clutter; a single WACZ may be small"), so parking it for a maintainer call on the UX.

Timeline (month histogram) on detail pages also not done here — facet_overview_scoped returns the facet groups, not the SearchResponse timeline; could add if wanted.

title: Read-only API, Memento interop & federation across rustyweb instances
description:
Give rustyweb a simple read-only HTTP API, Memento (RFC 7089) interop, and federation so different rustyweb instances (and other archives) can discover each other's content. Read-only to start.

KEYSTONE -- persistent replay URLs. Today a replayable page is a query-string URL (/replay/viewer?source=/files/{id}&url=&ts=&name=&collection=&collection_id=): instance-local, not persistent, and it redundantly encodes name/collection the server could look up. The minimal identity of a memento is (crawl_id, ts, url), and crawl_id is a stable hash of the source. So the persistent URL becomes:
  /crawl/{crawl_id}/{ts}/{url}   e.g. /crawl/a926c132/20220305013545/https://uinp.gov.ua/
It nests under the existing /crawl/{id} detail page (detail vs replay), is bookmarkable/persistent, aligns with single-crawl replay coherence (no composite mementos), and IS a Memento URI-M. Name/collection breadcrumb are looked up server-side from the manifest. This same URL is what the API returns, Memento advertises, and federated peers link to -- so it is built first.

DISCOVERY SUBSTRATE -- web-archive.txt (Mahoney, Terras, Zeller & Lee, "web-archive.txt: A Well-Known Locations Descriptor for Discovery and Coordination of Web Archives", 2026, v0.1). Rather than invent a rustyweb-specific discovery format, adopt web-archive.txt: a TOML descriptor served at /.well-known/web-archive.txt (RFC 8615 well-known URI, content-type text/plain) AND advertised via a Link rel="service-desc" header on the home page. It declares, in four sections: version (version + last_updated); archive identity (id [2-6 lowercase alnum], name inline table w/ en+alt, established, website, email) + archive.organisation (name/type/location ISO-3166/website) + archive.scope (crawl modalities, legal authority + documentation, RFC-3339 temporal coverage interval, domains, and a collections list as id+name inline tables); api (documentation, rate_limit) + api.memento (timemap/timegate endpoint templates + access) + api.cdx (query template + access); and replay state templates (rewritten/no_toolbar/raw). Endpoint templates use {url} + {datetime} (YYYYMMDDhhmmss) placeholders and MAY use {collection} bound to scope.collections.id.

web-archive.txt becomes rustyweb's standard, decentralised identity + capability document: the thing peers read to discover one another (task .5) and the thing external aggregators/validators read. rustyweb PUBLISHES one (new task .9 -- maps its Manifest + collections + Memento routes + persistent replay URL onto the spec's tables) and CONSUMES peers' descriptors for federation config. Because it is a community spec (not rustyweb-specific), rustyweb can federate at the Memento level with ANY web-archive.txt-publishing archive, not just other rustyweb instances. rustyweb keeps its richer NATIVE JSON API (task .2) for rustyweb-to-rustyweb specifics (live counts, capabilities, resolve); web-archive.txt is the interop lingua franca layered over it. NB: scope.authority / scope.coverage / scope.crawl modalities overlap the finding-aid provenance epic (rustyweb-findingaid) -- the descriptor is a natural machine-readable EXPORT of that curatorial metadata, so design the two together.

THREE LAYERS on top:
1. Read-only JSON API -- beyond /api/search: a NATIVE instance descriptor (name, version, collection/crawl counts, capabilities, instance base), /api/collections, /api/collections/{id}, /api/crawls/{id}, and a URL-resolution endpoint /api/resolve?url= -> [{crawl_id, ts, collection}] (page-level, index-backed). Each API result carries its persistent memento URL + the instance base. (The standard cross-archive identity doc is web-archive.txt, task .9; this native JSON is the richer rustyweb-to-rustyweb surface.)
2. Memento (RFC 7089) -- TimeMap + TimeGate + Memento-Datetime/Link headers, built on /api/resolve. Makes rustyweb a first-class Memento server so existing aggregators (Time Travel, MemGator) federate rustyweb instances at the URL level for free; these endpoints are ALSO advertised in web-archive.txt api.memento (task .9). Honest limitation: rustyweb indexes PAGES (HTML/PDF), not every subresource, so TimeMaps are page-level.
3. Federation -- an instance is configured with peer base URLs; it discovers each peer by fetching the peer's /.well-known/web-archive.txt (identity, scope, api endpoints), then does live FAN-OUT search: query self + peers concurrently (reuse the ureq client + retry/backoff + timeouts; degrade gracefully when a peer is down), merge + dedup + ATTRIBUTE each result to its origin instance so links open the peer's persistent replay URL. (Alternative considered: harvest peer catalogs into a local aggregate index -- scalable + resilient but stale/heavier; fan-out chosen for the no-central-service, self-host ethos.)

SYNERGY with cross-WACZ replay (rustyweb-cross-wacz-replay-dk4): dk4's leading approach is exactly a GET /api/resolve?url= lookup (landed on a page not in this crawl -> which other crawl has it -> re-launch). The resolve endpoint (task .3) is that building block; dk4 depends on it. dk4's temporal-coherence caution applies to choosing which crawl/ts to fall back to.

Decisions baked in (maintainer): URL shape = /crawl/{id}/{ts}/{url}; discovery/identity = web-archive.txt at /.well-known/ (adopt the spec, do not invent our own); federation = live fan-out; Memento = included. Task priorities + deps allow deferring Memento or federation. Read-only throughout; consider CORS for cross-instance browser calls and optional rate-limiting for a public API.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Folded in the web-archive.txt spec: Mahoney, Terras, Zeller & Lee, "web-archive.txt: A Well-Known Locations Descriptor for Discovery and Coordination of Web Archives" (2026, v0.1). PDF: ~/Dropbox/Papers/Mahoney/web_archive_txt__A_Well_Known_Locations_Descriptor_for_Discovery_and_Coordination_of_Web_Archives.pdf

Decision: adopt web-archive.txt as rustyweb's discovery/identity substrate rather than inventing our own format. Concretely: new task .9 PUBLISHES /.well-known/web-archive.txt (+ Link rel=service-desc); .5 CONSUMES peers' descriptors for federation config (works for any web-archive.txt-publishing archive, not just rustyweb); .2 keeps the richer rustyweb-native JSON /api/ (dropped the invented /.well-known/rustyweb); .4 advertises its Memento endpoints via api.memento and the persistent replay URL via replay.*. Key spec facts used: TOML at /.well-known/web-archive.txt, text/plain; four sections version/archive/api/replay; {url}+{datetime}(YYYYMMDDhhmmss) placeholders, optional {collection}; RFC 8615 well-known + RFC 2119 language; a validator + IIPC registry are 'forthcoming' (bootstrap layer for archives without a descriptor). Overlap noted with the finding-aid epic (scope.authority/coverage are a curatorial-metadata export).

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: Idea (discovery/peer-finding): use a DHT to share the locations of rustyweb instances, so instances can find each other without a central registry. A node could announce itself (and perhaps the collections/URL-prefixes it holds) under a well-known DHT key (e.g. a hash of "rustyweb" or of a collection/host), and peers query the DHT to discover instances to federate with or route URL-resolution queries to. Pairs naturally with the /.well-known/web-archive.txt descriptor (shwl.9) and the resolve endpoint (shwl.3) — DHT for *finding* peers, those endpoints for *describing/querying* them. Open questions: which DHT (BitTorrent mainline/Kademlia via a Rust crate like mainline, libp2p-kad, or a purpose-built overlay); what to announce (instance URL only vs. content hints); Sybil/abuse resistance; whether this is opt-in. Keep the light-deps bar in mind.

title: Persistent structured replay URLs: /crawl/{id}/{ts}/{url}
description:
Replace the query-string replay URL (/replay/viewer?source=&url=&ts=&name=&collection=&collection_id=) with a persistent, bookmarkable path that nests under the existing crawl detail page:
  /crawl/{crawl_id}/{ts}/{*url}
Server route parses the path, looks up crawl_id -> wacz source (viewer_source), and renders the viewer configured for (source, url, ts). Name + collection breadcrumb are derived server-side from the manifest (no longer in the URL). Update every internal link builder to emit the new form: search-results rows, crawl-detail replay button + seed-page links, collection viewer_source. Adjust viewer.html to read its config from the path (or server-injected values) instead of query params.
Considerations: the archived URL keeps its scheme in the path (https://...), so handle the // wrinkle (pywb-style) via an axum wildcard capture + normalization; preserve the original URL's own query string. Optionally 302-redirect the old /replay/viewer?... form (nothing external links to it yet). This URL is the Memento URI-M and the link target for the API + federation, so it is the foundation task. Files: server.rs (router + handlers), views.rs, static/replay/viewer.html, DESIGN.md routes table.

title: Read-only JSON API: instance descriptor, collections, crawls
description:
Extend the read-only rustyweb-NATIVE JSON API beyond /api/search:
- Native instance descriptor at /api/: instance name, rustyweb + API version, collection/crawl counts, capabilities (search, resolve, memento, federation), and the instance base URL. The richer rustyweb-to-rustyweb document (live counts + capabilities).
- /api/collections -> list (id, name, description, counts, date range).
- /api/collections/{id} -> collection detail + members (crawl id/name/dates).
- /api/crawls/{id} -> crawl metadata (provenance, seed pages, capture range, source, thumbnail).
Each result/object carries its persistent replay/memento URL (from task .1) and the instance base. Consider CORS (Access-Control-Allow-Origin) for cross-instance browser calls and stable, documented JSON shapes.

NOTE: the STANDARD, cross-archive identity/capability document is web-archive.txt at /.well-known/web-archive.txt (task .9), NOT a rustyweb-specific /.well-known/rustyweb (dropped -- do not invent our own). This native JSON API is the deeper rustyweb-to-rustyweb surface layered under that standard descriptor: /api/ gives live counts + capabilities that the static TOML descriptor does not. Peers identify each other via web-archive.txt (task .5); rustyweb peers can then also read this /api/ for the richer view.

Files: server.rs (routes + handlers), reuse Manifest + search. Depends on .1.

title: URL-resolution endpoint: GET /api/resolve?url=
description: Add GET /api/resolve?url=<original-url> -> JSON list of captures across crawls: [{crawl_id, ts, collection, memento_url}] (optionally &datetime= to sort by closeness). Index-backed exact-URL lookup over the Tantivy url field (page-level; not subresources). This is the shared building block for BOTH Memento (task .4, a TimeMap is this data) AND cross-WACZ replay resolution (rustyweb-cross-wacz-replay-dk4 approach 1: on a miss, find which other crawl has the URL and re-launch). Return closest/most-recent ordering options. Files: search.rs (a resolve query), server.rs (route). Depends on .1.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: Overlap to reconcile (2026-07-25): the multi-WACZ scale valve for replay (bukh Phase 2 / dk4) needs a server-side pagesQueryUrl-shaped resolver over the Tantivy index (?url=/?search=/?page=/?pageSize=). That is the same index-backed URL->WACZ resolution as this /api/resolve?url= endpoint. Decide one shared core (two response shapes/paths) vs. siblings before building either, so we don't implement two resolvers.

title: Memento (RFC 7089): TimeMap, TimeGate, Link/Memento-Datetime headers
description:
Expose rustyweb as a Memento server, built on the resolve endpoint (.3):
- TimeMap: GET /timemap/link/{url} (application/link-format) and /timemap/json/{url} -> all captures (URI-Ms = /crawl/{id}/{ts}/{url}) of a URL with their Memento-Datetimes.
- TimeGate: GET /timegate/{url} honoring Accept-Datetime -> 302 to the closest memento URI-M.
- Add Memento-Datetime + Link (rel=original/timemap/timegate/memento) headers on replay responses.
Enables existing aggregators (Time Travel, MemGator) to federate rustyweb instances at the URL level for free.

ADVERTISE these endpoints in web-archive.txt api.memento (task .9): timemap.endpoint + timegate.endpoint as URI templates with {url}/{datetime} placeholders (e.g. timegate = { endpoint = "https://host/timegate/{url}", access = "online" }), so the spec's validator/registry and any web-archive.txt-aware aggregator can find them without prior knowledge. The persistent replay URL maps to replay.rewritten (and a no-toolbar variant to replay.no_toolbar) in the same descriptor.

Honest limitation to document: page-level coverage only (rustyweb indexes pages, not every subresource). Temporal coherence: each URI-M is single-crawl-scoped and coherent. Files: server.rs (routes + headers), search.rs. Depends on .3.

title: Peer configuration for federation
description:
Let an instance be configured with a list of peer base URLs (read-only). Mechanism options to decide: a peers.json under <home> (portable with the home dir) vs a serve --peer flag vs both.

DISCOVER + VALIDATE each peer by fetching its /.well-known/web-archive.txt descriptor (the web-archive.txt spec, task .9) and parsing the TOML: archive.id + archive.name (identity/attribution label), archive.scope (domains / temporal coverage / collections -- lets fan-out skip peers whose scope cannot match a query), and the api.* / replay templates (how to query + how to build the peer's replay/memento URLs). Handle unreachable/incompatible/no-descriptor peers gracefully. Because web-archive.txt is a community spec, a peer need NOT be a rustyweb instance -- any archive publishing a descriptor with api.memento can be federated at the Memento level (task .8); rustyweb peers additionally expose the native /api/ (task .2) for the richer view, so prefer /.well-known/web-archive.txt for identity and fall back to / enrich with /api/ when the peer is rustyweb.

A minimal parser for the four web-archive.txt sections (version/archive/api/replay) is needed here on the CONSUME side; it is the mirror of the PUBLISH side in task .9 -- share a serde struct + a toml dep between them. Peers are trusted-by-configuration; no writes. Files: a config loader (collections.rs or a new config module) + a web-archive.txt model (shared with .9), main.rs (serve). Foundation for fan-out search (.6).

title: Federated fan-out search across peers
description: Add federated search: query the local index AND fan out to each configured peer's /api/search concurrently, then merge. Reuse the ureq client (retry/backoff already present) via spawn_blocking, with a per-peer timeout and graceful degradation (a down/slow peer yields a warning, not a failure; note which peers were skipped). Merge + dedup results (same url across instances) and ATTRIBUTE each result to its origin instance, so its link opens THAT instance's persistent replay URL (from .1). Expose via /api/search?federate=true (or /api/federated-search) and the HTML search page. Latency = slowest responding peer within the timeout. Files: server.rs (federated handler), search.rs (merge), reuse http client. Depends on .2 (peer API), .5 (peer config), .1 (URLs).

title: Federated-results UI (origin-instance attribution)
description: Surface federated results in the web UI: badge/label each result with its origin instance (this instance vs a named peer), link cross-instance results to the peer's persistent replay URL, and show which peers were queried/skipped. Keep local-only search the default; federation opt-in. Files: views.rs, server.rs, app.css. Depends on .6.

title: Memento aggregation across peers (exploratory)
description: Optionally make rustyweb a Memento AGGREGATOR: a federated TimeMap/TimeGate that queries configured peers' TimeMaps (and its own) and merges them, so a single rustyweb instance can answer who-has-this-URL across the federation. This is the Memento realization of federation at the URL level (complements fan-out SEARCH which covers topical/collection discovery). Evaluate vs just letting an external aggregator (MemGator) point at the instances. Depends on .4 (Memento) and .6 (federation). Lower priority / exploratory.

title: Publish a web-archive.txt descriptor at /.well-known/web-archive.txt
description:
Implement the PUBLISH side of the web-archive.txt spec (Mahoney et al. 2026, v0.1): serve rustyweb's own machine-readable identity + capability descriptor so peers (task .5), external aggregators, and the spec's validator/registry can discover this instance.

- Serve GET /.well-known/web-archive.txt -> a TOML document, content-type text/plain (application/toml MAY be offered). RFC 8615 well-known path.
- Advertise it with a Link: <...>; rel="service-desc" header on the home page (the archive.website resource).

Map rustyweb's model onto the spec's four sections:
- version: version = "0.1" (spec version), last_updated (date the descriptor/manifest last changed).
- archive: id (short slug -- config/serve flag), name (inline table, en + optional alt), established?, website (public base URL), email?.
- archive.organisation: name/type/location(ISO-3166)/website -- from config (overlaps finding-aid curatorial metadata, rustyweb-findingaid).
- archive.scope: crawl modalities, authority {type, documentation}, coverage (RFC-3339 interval, derivable from the index min/max capture dates), domains (derivable from indexed hosts), and collections = the manifest collections as {id, name} inline tables.
- api / api.memento / api.cdx: documentation URL, rate_limit; memento timemap/timegate endpoint templates ({url}/{datetime}) from task .4; api.cdx only if/when rustyweb exposes a CDX endpoint (omit otherwise -- unsupported capabilities SHOULD be omitted).
- replay: rewritten (+ optional no_toolbar/raw) endpoint templates for the persistent replay URL (task .1), with {url}/{datetime} and optional {collection}.

Config-driven identity fields (id/name/org/authority/etc.) have no home in the WACZ data -- add a small instance-config source (serve flags or a config file under <home>) and reuse it for .5 peer model. Share the serde struct + toml dependency with the CONSUME-side parser in task .5. Emit only known-good fields; keep it valid against the spec (required fields present, URLs absolute w/ scheme). Depends on .1 (replay templates); best done with .4 (memento endpoints to advertise). Files: server.rs (well-known route + Link header), a web-archive.txt model module (shared with .5), main.rs/config, DESIGN.md + README routes table. Cross-links: rustyweb-findingaid (scope/authority/coverage are the curatorial-metadata export).

title: RSS/Atom feeds for new crawls, collections, and annotations
description:
Syndicate what is new in an archive so people can follow it without polling the site.

SCOPE: two phases, both in this bead (Ed, 2026-09-12 — not a separate PR).

── PHASE 1: a real site base URL ──────────────────────────────────────────
Prerequisite, because feeds need absolute URLs and the setting we have cannot
provide one. `--site-url` exists (added in PR #124) but:
  1. THE SCHEME IS DISCARDED — main.rs keeps only host[:port] in
     ManageConfig.site_authority, since the CSRF guard compares authorities and
     deliberately ignores scheme. Feeds need http-vs-https.
  2. IT IS GATED ON --manage (`site_url.filter(|_| manage.enabled)`) — right
     when the CSRF guard was the only consumer, backwards for feeds, since a
     public read-only deployment is the most likely thing to serve one.
  3. IT IS CLI/ENV ONLY — not committable with the rest of a home config.

Promote it from a CSRF implementation detail to a first-class site setting:
  - config.yaml gains `site: { url: "https://archive.example.org" }`
  - --site-url / INDICE_SITE_URL remain overrides; precedence flag > env > config
  - store the parsed base on AppState, populated regardless of --manage
  - the CSRF guard derives its authority FROM that base (no behaviour change;
    the existing same_site_request tests must stay green)
  - note build_router loads users.yaml today but NOT config.yaml, so add that
  - fallback when unset: derive from Host + X-Forwarded-Proto rather than
    refusing to serve, so the zero-config loopback case keeps working

── PHASE 2: the feeds ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
THREE FEEDS (public, like the rest of the read side):
  - new crawls — ordered by Wacz.date_indexed
  - new collections — ordered by Collection.created
  - new annotations — by Annotation.created/modified, across all collections
Plus per-collection variants, which are probably the common want (following ONE
collection): /collection/{id}/crawls.xml, /collection/{id}/annotations.xml.

OPEN QUESTIONS
  - Atom or RSS 2.0? Atom has proper dates (RFC 3339, what we already store) and
    required ids; RSS 2.0 has wider reader support out of habit. Leaning Atom.
  - One combined "everything" feed too? Cheap, and probably what most people
    would actually subscribe to.
  - Annotation feeds carry the note body: already public, already rendered as
    sanitized HTML by markdown::render, so yes, content type=html. Author MUST
    use Creator::public_name(), never the raw name — the feed is a new public
    surface and that sanitizer is the only thing keeping login addresses off it.

IMPLEMENTATION NOTES
  - All three sort keys are already stored: a feed is a manifest read plus a
    template, no new index work. Crawls/collections come from Manifest::open;
    annotations need annotations::load per collection, the only one with real
    cost. Cap at N most recent (50?) and document the cap.
  - Hand-roll the XML (maud or a small writer) rather than adding a feed crate —
    single-binary project, small format. MUST escape properly: a crawl name or
    note body containing & or < otherwise produces invalid XML. Worth an
    invariant test in the style of
    annotation_note_html_cannot_carry_executable_markup.
  - <link rel="alternate"> to the existing pages (/crawl/{id},
    /collection/{id}, /collection/{id}/annotations).
  - <link rel="alternate" type="application/atom+xml"> in the page <head> so
    readers autodiscover.

Relates to the federation epic (rustyweb-federation-shwl) — a lightweight
sibling of the read-only API / Memento work, and may belong under it.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
PREREQUISITE, now scoped (Ed asked whether --site-url already covers this). It exists but is unusable for feeds as-is, for three reasons:

1. THE SCHEME IS DISCARDED. main.rs parses --site-url with url::Url and keeps only host[:port] in ManageConfig.site_authority, because the CSRF guard compares authorities and deliberately ignores scheme. Feeds need an absolute URL, so http vs https matters.

2. IT IS GATED ON --manage. `site_url.filter(|_| manage.enabled)` — correct when the only consumer was the CSRF guard (and it stopped a typo in a shared env file from killing a read-only server), but exactly backwards for feeds: a public read-only deployment is the MOST likely thing to serve a feed, and it currently ignores the setting entirely.

3. IT IS CLI/ENV ONLY. Not in config.yaml, so it cannot be committed with the rest of a home's configuration.

PROPOSED FIX (do this first, own PR): promote it from a CSRF implementation detail to a first-class site setting.
- config.yaml gains `site: { url: "https://archive.example.org" }`
- --site-url / INDICE_SITE_URL stay as overrides; precedence flag > env > config
- store the parsed base URL on AppState, populated regardless of --manage
- the CSRF guard derives its authority from that base (no behaviour change; keep the existing tests green)
- feeds, and anything else needing absolute URLs, use the full base

Note build_router already loads Users::load(home); it does NOT currently load Config, so this adds that. Also decide the fallback when nothing is set: feeds could derive a base from the request (Host + X-Forwarded-Proto) rather than refusing to serve, which keeps zero-config working for the loopback case.

title: Pin that /files never gains Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
description:
GET /files/{id} serves raw WACZ bytes with `access-control-allow-origin: *` (server/assets.rs). That is fine and intentional today: the bytes are already public, and ACAO:* never pairs with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, so it grants only anonymous cross-origin reads.

It stops being fine the moment anyone adds credentialed access or private collections. Add a cheap regression test asserting the /files response carries ACAO:* and does NOT carry access-control-allow-credentials, so that combination can never be introduced silently.

Noted during the auth review; no action needed beyond the test.

title: Finding-aid-style provenance & curator context
description:
Make rustyweb surface much richer provenance and encourage curators to share the scope, rationale, and context of archival collections -- an EAD / finding-aid approach -- at the collection and crawl levels.

Motivation (audit of current state): crawl-level TECHNICAL provenance (software/operator/user-agent/robots/pages/capture-dates) is displayed but every row is conditional, so a WACZ with a thin datapackage.json/warcinfo (e.g. the SUCHO crawls) shows almost nothing. Collection-level CURATORIAL provenance is genuinely thin: the Collection struct has only description + curator. Several fields are parsed-but-dropped (warcinfo isPartOf/hostname/conformsTo; datapackage modified) or not read at all (datapackage keywords/licenses/contributors). DESIGN.md already frames curatorial vs technical provenance (Maemura et al., 'If These Crawls Could Talk') and calls for surfacing it prominently.

Decisions (with maintainer): (1) full EAD-ish field set; (2) Markdown narrative for the notes; (3) FOLD this into the Browsertrix epic rustyweb-15z -- Browsertrix brings collection description/tags/org that will populate these fields, so design and build them together. Adding optional manifest fields is backward-compatible and needs NO reindex; re-reading WACZs for the dropped/unread fields DOES need a reindex.

Sequencing: A) model + CLI + UI (no reindex, no Browsertrix dep); B) crawl-level enrichment (reindex); C) Browsertrix mapping (15z.6 maps Browsertrix metadata onto these fields). Full design recorded in the session plan.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Shared foundation with rustyweb-cross-wacz-replay-dk4 (2026-07-25 design discussion): 'replay a collection' requires a collection-level (multi-WACZ) replay primitive that doesn't exist yet — today replay is single-WACZ only (viewer?source=/files/{id}).

The primitive: a per-collection multi-WACZ JSON doc (wabac format) generated from the two-level manifest — { resources: [{ name, path, hash, crawlId }], metadata: {...} } — where each resources[].path points at a member's /files/{id} (local) or presigned/remote URL (streamed). Wire the viewer to open source=<that collection JSON>. Reuses the existing /files/{id} byte server; no new byte-serving code.

Build order: bukh's core IS this foundation (homepage one-click 'replay collection' + browse-pages entry point = wabac's Pages sidebar). dk4 (cross-WACZ link resolution) then layers on top mostly additively. So bukh naturally precedes dk4.

Shared scale valve (ties to qw5): small collection -> multi-WACZ JSON with NO pagesQueryUrl (wabac loads every member's index client-side, native resolution, fine for a few WACZs). Large collection (e.g. usgov-archive 570k pages / hundreds of WACZs) -> the browser can't hold all member indexes; set metadata.pagesQueryUrl so wabac defers URL->WACZ resolution to the server and lazily loads only needed members. See dk4 for the full sw.js trace.

comments.text:
Phase 1 (foundation) IMPLEMENTED on the working tree (2026-07-25; not yet committed/merged): collection-level multi-WACZ replay.
- New endpoint GET /collection/{id}/replay.json (server.rs collection_replay_json) emits the wabac multi-WACZ manifest {resources:[{name,path,hash,crawlId}], metadata} from Manifest::members_of(id), reusing viewer_source() for each path (/files/{id} local, remote URL for Url) and prefixing sha256:.
- viewer.html now namespaces a .json (multi-WACZ) source by collection id (was source.split('/').pop() = the shared 'replay.json'); explicit ?coll= wins.
- 'Replay collection' affordance added BOTH places (answers this issue's open question): a button on /collection/{id} and a replay link on each homepage card. Entry point (the other open question) = the collection multi-WACZ viewer.
- Tests: tests/collection_replay.rs (wabac shape, sha256: prefix, local paths, 404). Full suite green. Verified end-to-end via curl (JSON + 206 ranges); browser render of the merged collection is the one remaining MANUAL check.

Works for small/medium collections via wabac's NATIVE multi-WACZ mode (member indexes load client-side). Phase 2 (the scale valve, metadata.pagesQueryUrl backed by the Tantivy index) is still needed for large/institutional collections — tracked as a new qw5 child. Related: dk4 layers cross-WACZ discovery on this same foundation.

title: Search/facet by source kind (local vs remote)
description:
Let users filter and facet search results by whether a crawl is stored locally or hosted remotely (a remote URL, or a streamed Browsertrix source). Complements the local/remote source pills added in rustyweb-15z.9 (PR #53) — the same distinction, now as a search dimension: e.g. "show only content I have a durable local copy of," or "only streamed crawls."

Design note / the wrinkle: source kind is a property of the crawl’s manifest Source (File vs Url/Browsertrix), and it is MUTABLE without re-indexing content — `index --download` turns a remote URL into a local File, and a Browsertrix source is remote. So an index-time Tantivy field would go stale until a reindex.

Two approaches:
- (a) Index a `source_kind` (local|remote) field/facet on each doc. Simple faceting, but a SCHEMA CHANGE (reindex) and it can drift from the manifest when a source’s kind changes; must be recomputed on every (re)index.
- (b) Derive from the manifest at query time (recommended). Low cardinality (two values) + the crawl→kind map is cheap to build from the manifest. A `source:local` / `source:remote` query alias expands to `crawl_id:(…)` over the matching crawls (mirrors the existing `crawl:` alias rewrite in server.rs), and the facet counts are computed from the manifest ∩ the result set. No reindex, always fresh.

Recommend (b). Surface it as a facet in the results sidebar (like site/year/type) and a `source:` filter. Files: search.rs (facet aggregation / alias), server.rs (query rewrite + facet UI), views.rs. Relates to the crawl/site/type faceting already present and to the source pills (rustyweb-15z.9).

title: Index extracted page text from Browsertrix pages.jsonl / extraPages.jsonl (fixes JS-rendered content being unsearchable)
description:
Index the extracted page `text` from Browsertrix pages.jsonl / extraPages.jsonl.

Root cause found while debugging a SUCHO search miss: searching the homepage term "Петиція" (on https://uinp.gov.ua/) returns nothing, even though it's clearly visible in replay. The term is JS-rendered, so it is NOT in the raw HTML response body (confirmed). Browsertrix captured the rendered text, but for this 2022-vintage crawl it wrote it into the WACZ's pages files, NOT as `urn:text:` WARC records:
- CDX has 30044 records and ZERO `urn:` records (no urn:text:).
- pages/pages.jsonl (seed pages) and pages/extraPages.jsonl (4150 pages here) each have a `text` field per entry.
- The homepage pages.jsonl entry has text (2708 chars) that DOES contain "Петиція".

rustyweb currently reads pages.jsonl only for seed-page metadata (url/title/ts -> seed_pages) and ignores the `text` field; it never reads extraPages.jsonl. Body text is taken from urn:text: (absent here) or scraped HTML (missing JS-rendered content). Result: rendered content is unsearchable and recall is badly degraded for Browsertrix crawls of this shape -- including the flagship SUCHO demo.

Fix: during indexing, also read the `text` (and title) from pages/pages.jsonl AND pages/extraPages.jsonl, and merge it into the per-URL page body -- treat it like Browsertrix rendered text (same role as the urn:text: path). Prefer rendered text (urn:text OR pages-jsonl text) over scraped HTML for the body; keep HTML title/description/lang where richer.

Considerations:
- Both index paths must do it: the default CDX-guided/streaming path (collect_page_records_via_cdx) does not currently read pages.jsonl at all for text; the full-scan path (index_wacz) doesn't either. The pages files are small zip entries -- cheap to read once during setup (the streaming setup already opens the ZIP central directory).
- Merge by URL into the existing MergedPage (add a source, e.g. jsonl_text, slotted with rendered_text). Decide precedence: urn:text: vs pages.jsonl text (they're the same kind of data; either is fine -- prefer whichever is present).
- Skip the header line ({format,id,title}) in each jsonl. Handle both pages.jsonl and extraPages.jsonl; tolerate absence (py-wacz and some WACZs have no text).
- Pages that exist only in extraPages.jsonl (not surfaced as a page today) should become searchable pages, tagged to the WACZ/collection like any other page. Watch doc counts (this could add many docs -- here ~4150/WACZ).
- Titles from pages.jsonl may be better than scraped ones; consider using them as a fallback.
- Timestamps: pages.jsonl has ts; use for the page if the HTML capture ts is missing (mirror the urn:text merge which only fills an empty ts).
- Add a regression test with a fixture WACZ that has pages.jsonl text but the term absent from HTML, asserting the term is searchable after indexing.

Impact: HIGH -- fixes a large class of "I can see it in replay but can't search it" misses on the SUCHO demo and directly improves the Browsertrix importer (15z) results, since those are exactly these WACZs. P1.

Relates to the Browsertrix importer epic (rustyweb-15z) and the urn:text: rendered-text handling already in index.rs (record_to_raw / index_merged).
close_reason: Implemented: read the text field from pages/pages.jsonl + pages/extraPages.jsonl and fold it into the per-URL page body (interchangeable with urn:text:), in both the CDX-guided and full-scan paths. Unit test (read_page_texts) + end-to-end test (term present only in pages.jsonl is searchable via the default path). Confirmed root cause on the SUCHO WACZ: CDX had zero urn:text records; the rendered text (incl. the missing term) lives in pages.jsonl.
