title: Ingest signatures: group the 9-10 parameters instead of silencing clippy eight times
description:
Ed flagged this (2026-09-12) while reviewing the durable-writes work. It is a
smell that has already cost real bugs, not just aesthetics.

THE STATE OF IT

  index_location_with_resolver(location, home, name, collection, download,
      force, concurrency, resolver, progress)                        -- 9
  index_one(source, home, manifest, search, name, collection, download,
      concurrency, resolver, progress)                               -- 10
  record::upsert(manifest, id, collection, source, display_name, meta,
      stats, fixity)                                                 -- 8

There are EIGHT #[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)] in index/ingest
(mod.rs x3, pages.rs x4, record.rs x1). Clippy raised this eight times and was
silenced eight times, which is the actual finding.

WHAT IT HAS ALREADY COST (both of these are in git history, not hypothetical)

1. Crawl custody. In #126, Wacz.added_by could not be threaded through ingest
   because it would be an ELEVENTH parameter on four already-crowded
   signatures, so it was set OUT-OF-BAND after ingest instead. That required a
   before/after manifest snapshot to know which crawls were new, and that
   snapshot is where two review findings came from: a lost-update race
   (attribution ran outside the write lock and erased a concurrent job entry)
   and a fail-open bug (an unreadable snapshot became an empty one, claiming
   every unattributed crawl). Both fixed, but neither would have existed if the
   actor could simply have been a parameter.

2. Durable writes. Option (b) on rustyweb-durable-writes-f4h5 -- thread a
   write-lock capability from the server so library mutators cannot be called
   without it -- is blocked for exactly the same reason, and is why that bead
   still has an open design fork.

So the cost is not "hard to read". It is that the pipeline has stopped
accepting new parameters, and workarounds are being chosen instead, and the
workarounds have bugs.

SHAPE OF THE FIX

Group by what the parameters actually are. They fall out cleanly:

  - WHAT to ingest: location/source, name, collection
  - HOW: download, force, concurrency
  - ENVIRONMENT/WIRING: home, manifest, search, resolver, progress

So a params struct (or a small builder) per group, or one Ingest<..> value
threaded through. The test is whether the CALL SITES read better afterwards --
Ed previous steer on the ingest refactor was that a long module is fine if the
pipeline reads well, and the same standard applies here. A struct that just
renames the same ten things is not worth doing.

Two specific reductions worth taking while in there:

  - Option<&dyn IndexProgress> appears everywhere. Its absence means only "do
    not report", which is exactly what a null-object impl handles: take
    &dyn IndexProgress and give callers a no-op. That removes the Option (and
    the None::<&T> inference awkwardness) rather than moving it.
  - Option<&dyn SourceResolver> is NOT the same case: absence there is
    meaningful (no credentials configured), so it should stay an Option.

CONSTRAINTS

  - Pure refactor, no behaviour change; the existing ingest tests are the net.
  - Coordinate with rustyweb-streaming-setup-consolidate-850t, which touches
    the same region. Land one before starting the other, same warning as the
    index.rs split had.
  - index_location / index_path are the public API used by the CLI and the
    server. Either keep thin wrappers with the current shape, or accept a
    breaking change and update both callers.
close_reason:
Landed as PR #132 (merged aa0a2dd).

Eight `#[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]` in `index/ingest/` → zero, and
the acceptance criterion met: adding a collaborator to the ingest is now a
field plus a setter rather than an edit to every frame between the boundary
and its consumer.

Shape: `index::Ingest` (context, `std::process::Command` style, private
fields, `#[must_use]` setters), `pages::Docs` (the document-tagging quartet),
`record::Indexed` (what the pipeline learned about one WACZ). Progress became
unconditional via default trait bodies + `index::NoProgress`, removing 19
`Option<&dyn IndexProgress>` declarations and 25 `if let Some(p)` blocks. The
rule that came out of it, now in the `Ingest` doc comment and DESIGN.md: an
`Option` in a signature should assert something about the domain — which is
why `resolver`, `name` and `concurrency` keep theirs.

Two things found in review rather than by the compiler, both of which the
refactor itself made reachable:

1. `reindex` used to pass `download: false` positionally; once `download`
   was a field it forwarded `&Ingest` wholesale, so
   `Ingest::new(&home).download(true).reindex()` would re-fetch each
   `Source::Url`, and because the id derives from the *effective* source it
   upserted a second manifest entry under a new id while the original
   survived, dropping the by-id provenance (`browsertrix`, `archive_it`,
   `added_by`). Fixed structurally:
   `let cx = &self.download(false).name(None).force(true);`. Note `force` is
   set *true*, not neutralised to false — a rebuild re-indexes every source
   unconditionally. Guards:
   `integration.rs::a_rebuild_does_not_download_a_remote_source` (verified
   failing without the fix, 2 entries vs 1) and
   `a_rebuild_does_not_rename_crawls`.
2. `#[must_use]` on the builder, because `Ingest` is `Copy`: `ingest.force(true);`
   as a statement otherwise compiles and silently drops the setting, with no
   move for the borrow checker to catch later.

Deferred on purpose: the plan's `Run` type (the open manifest + writer as a
receiver). Its main justification was being the single place a lock witness
could be demanded, and the locking design (rustyweb-durable-writes-f4h5)
concluded the lock attaches to the resource instead. Its remaining win is real
but separate — `index_location` and `reindex` still duplicate
`Config::load` → `open_with_heap` → `set_stored_body_cap` → `Mutex::new`, and
`reindex`'s Config-before-reconcile_index_swap ordering is still enforced by
comment only.

PRIMER staleness from this PR recorded on rustyweb-primer-refresh-yd8s.

title: Refactor ingest: WaczAccess handle + short index_one pipeline
description:
Follow-on to the index.rs split (qrd1 / PR #117). After the mechanical move,
crates/indice-lib/src/index/ingest.rs is ~1616 lines of code (+~1034 tests). The
length is mostly because index_one() inlines the plumbing of each phase and
threads an awkward (Option<String> remote_url, Option<PathBuf> local,
Option<NamedTempFile> _tmp) triple that every downstream step re-matches.

This is a behavior-preserving REFACTOR (not pure code motion): introduce a
readable "how do I read this WACZ" handle and extract phase functions so
index_one reads as a short pipeline. Ed's steer: a large module is fine as long
as the pipeline is short/readable — do NOT over-fragment into tiny files.

Core abstraction:
    enum WaczAccess { Stream { url }, Local { path, _tmp } }
    impl WaczAccess { fn is_remote(); fn read_datapackage() -> WaczMetadata;
                      fn fixity(progress) -> Result<(String,u64)>; }
Phase verbs:
  - acquire::open(source, home, collection, download, resolver, progress)
        -> Result<(Source /*effective*/, WaczAccess)>   // all source resolution
  - pages::index(&access, id, name, collection, search, workers, thumbs, progress)
        -> Result<CrawlStats>   // nested-detect -> stream/scan dispatch -> thumbnail
  - manifest::record(manifest, ids, &effective, &meta, &stats, fixity)  // provenance + upsert

index_one then collapses to ~30 lines (begin -> acquire -> read meta -> delete_crawl_docs
-> pages::index -> index_collection -> fixity -> manifest::record).

DEDUP payoff (the point): WaczAccess removes three remote-vs-local matches that
currently duplicate logic — the stream+thumbnail block is written twice (remote
branch ~500-521 vs local-streamable ~522-547), plus the datapackage-read match
(~438-442) and the fixity match (~577-598). All collapse to one path over the
RangeFetch trait / access methods.

Suggested module layout (don't over-split): ingest/{mod.rs (entry points +
index_one + WaczAccess), acquire.rs, pages.rs (the engine, ~600 lines is fine),
manifest.rs, tests.rs}.

Sequencing: do as its OWN PR off main AFTER #117 merges (avoid stacking). Verify
with the existing ingest tests (behavior unchanged) + fmt/clippy. Coordinate with
rustyweb-streaming-setup-consolidate-850t (same region). Design discussed
2026-09-07.
notes: Done in PR #118 (branch ingest-waczaccess off main). WaczAccess{Stream,Local} + acquire::open / pages::index / record::upsert; index_one body ~50 lines (was ~300). ingest/mod.rs 1618->395; acquire 361, pages 918, record 115, tests 1027. Dedup: stream+thumbnail block (was written twice) -> one stream_with_thumbnail over RangeFetch; datapackage + fixity matches -> access methods. Behavior preserved (212 lib tests, 47 index-tree, unchanged names); clippy 0, fmt clean; nothing outside index/ingest/ touched. Close when #118 merges.
close_reason: Merged via PR #118: WaczAccess + acquire/pages/record phases; index_one ~50 lines.

title: Import from an Archive-It account
description:
An importer for Archive-It (the Internet Archive’s subscription web-archiving service), analogous to the Browsertrix importer (rustyweb-15z) but for Archive-It collections.

Behaviour:
- Authenticate to an Archive-It account and list content. Import EITHER specific collections/crawls OR everything marked ready/available.
- Archive-It does not (generally) expose WACZ files — it serves WARCs, primarily via WASAPI (the Web Archiving Systems API: e.g. GET /wasapi/v1/webdata returns WARC file records with download locations + checksums, filterable by collection/crawl/date). Verify exact endpoints + auth when building.
- So: download the WARC files for the selected content, then BUILD a WACZ from them via rustyweb-dlqv (the WARC→WACZ builder) and index it — reusing that feature rather than duplicating packaging.
- Map Archive-It metadata (collection name/description, crawl dates, seeds, subjects, access/rights) from its Partner API into rustyweb’s finding-aid Collection/crawl fields (rustyweb-findingaid-aoc3), the same way the Browsertrix importer maps its metadata (rustyweb-15z.6).
- Provenance + incremental sync (skip already-imported WARC sets), mirroring rustyweb-15z.5.

Sequencing: AFTER the Browsertrix importer (rustyweb-15z) lands, and depends on the WARC→WACZ builder (rustyweb-dlqv). Will be broken into tasks (API client, CLI/auth, download+build+index flow, metadata mapping, incremental sync, docs/tests) when scheduled.

title: Archive-It import: sweep stale .import-tmp staging at start

title: Archive-It import: verify downloaded WARCs against WASAPI checksums
description: Downloaded Archive-It WARCs are not verified against the WASAPI-provided md5/sha1 checksums (WarcFile.checksums). A cleanly-closed-but-truncated download (e.g. a proxy returning a short 200 body) would be packaged into a WACZ and indexed with no error — a fixity gap for a tool that otherwise emphasizes integrity (sha256 in datapackage.json, the verify command). Fix: stream-hash each download in archiveit::Client::download and compare to WarcFile.checksums (md5 or sha1). Needs a new hashing dep (only sha2 is present today; WASAPI gives md5+sha1). From code review of the kx53 importer.

title: Archive-It import UI: avoid re-paginating WASAPI on every crawl browse
description: ait_crawls (the import wizard's crawl listing) fetches the whole collection's WASAPI webdata (following all next pages) on every browse/refresh, solely to sum per-crawl WARC bytes for the size column, then also calls crawl_jobs. For a large collection this is a slow, repeated full listing on an interactive hot path each time the operator switches collections. Options: cache the per-collection totals for a short TTL, compute sizes lazily/async after the list renders, or drop sizes from the listing. Accepted trade-off for v1 (user chose to show sizes). From code review of the kx53 importer.

title: GET /logout is cross-site triggerable
description: Found during the auth review. /logout is a GET mounted in the public block (deliberately outside forward-auth, so it does not immediately re-set the display cookie). But that means `` on any page logs out a signed-in admin. Low severity -- annoying, not destructive, and it clears only indices display cookie, not the proxy session. The same-origin guard added in the CSRF fix does not cover it because the guard only gates state-changing METHODS and only on the management routes. Fix is making it a POST (a small form/button in the appbar instead of a link), which then falls under the existing guard. Deferred because it is a UI change, not a one-liner.
close_reason: Done in PR #141 (auth-cleanups), stale-open. /logout is now a POST (server/mod.rs:342) and the same-origin CSRF guard is layered over the whole router as the outermost middleware, so it runs before forward-auth does any cookie bookkeeping. Commit a0a7ec7 'server: make logout a POST, and apply the CSRF guard server-wide'.

title: Manifest provenance: added_by / created_by / updated_by
description:
Nothing records WHO performed a mutation. Wacz and Collection (collections.rs) have no created_by/modified_by -- `operator` on Wacz is the crawlers operator from the WARC warcinfo, not the indice user. The request span (server/mod.rs) logs method/uri/client_ip, and behind a proxy client_ip is the proxys. No management handler emits a tracing statement at all. After a collection is deleted, indice retains nothing about who did it.

That is a notable gap for a tool whose value proposition is provenance, and DESIGN.md cites Light & Hyry on governance.

It is also LOAD-BEARING for the permission model (rustyweb-authz-roles-odc6): "a curator may delete a crawl they added" needs Wacz.added_by to exist. Eds role instinct is what promotes this from nice-to-have to required.

SCOPE:
- Wacz.added_by: Option<SubjectId>, #[serde(default, skip_serializing_if)] so old waczs.json loads and untouched records dont churn.
- Collection.created_by / updated_by -> new optional keys in the finding-aid YAML front matter beside `created` (write_finding_aid / parse_finding_aid). The existing dirty-set design already means untouched finding aids are never rewritten, so no formatting churn.
- Store the SubjectId, resolve to a display name at RENDER time via users.yaml -- otherwise the public crawl page starts printing login emails and we recreate the leak that PR (this one) just fixed in annotations.
- CLI-side mutations set actor = urn:indice:user:local.

Test: a waczs.json fixture without added_by still loads (pin the serde default).
close_reason: done

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
KNOWN EDGE (from code review, fixed as far as is reasonable): Archive-It's importer is a single orchestrator call (archiveit::import_crawls) that returns Result<Outcome>, so on failure it reports nothing — any crawls it committed before erroring stay unattributed. Safe rather than misattributed (unattributed = only an admin can remove), but it means a partially-failed Archive-It import leaves crawls their own curator cannot undo. Browsertrix does not have this problem: its loop collects each crawl id as it goes, so a partial import still attributes what landed.

Fixing it properly means having import_crawls report partial progress — either returning the ids committed so far alongside the error, or taking a callback per crawl. Worth doing if partial Archive-It imports turn out to be common; not worth it speculatively.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Follow-up (crawl-custody branch): the known edge recorded when this closed is gone, because custody is now written by the ingest itself (Ingest::actor, read in record::upsert) rather than stamped on afterwards.

- The Archive-It partial-import edge noted here ('on failure it reports nothing, so anything it partially committed stays unattributed') is closed. import_crawls attributes each crawl as it indexes it, so an import that dies part way attributes exactly what landed. Guarded by archiveit::tests::a_partial_import_attributes_the_crawls_that_landed.
- Both of PR #126's review findings became unreachable rather than fixed: there is no second manifest write to race with (the lost-update that erased a concurrent job's entry), and 'which crawls are new' is never asked (the fail-open that would have handed one curator every unattributed crawl).

set_added_by and crawl_ids are deleted; they had no callers left. title: Expose an MCP endpoint so agents can search & retrieve the archive
description:
Serve a Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint from the rustyweb server so LLM agents (Claude, etc.) can discover and use a web archive as a tool — search full text, list collections/crawls, resolve a URL to its captures, and fetch a page's archived text/metadata — without scraping the HTML UI.

## Why
rustyweb already has the retrieval primitives (Tantivy full-text search, the collections/crawls model, CDX URL resolution). MCP is the emerging standard for handing those to agents. This turns the archive into a first-class research tool an agent can call, and dovetails with the read-only JSON API in the federation epic (rustyweb-federation-shwl.2/.3) — same data, agent-facing framing.

## Sketch (to be designed)
- Transport: MCP over HTTP (streamable HTTP / SSE) mounted on the existing axum server, e.g. under `/mcp`. Consider a Rust MCP server crate vs. a hand-rolled JSON-RPC handler; keep deps light (the project avoids heavy deps).
- Tools to expose (read-only first):
  - `search(query, limit, collection?)` → ranked hits (url, ts, crawl, snippet).
  - `list_collections()` / `get_collection(slug)` → finding-aid metadata.
  - `list_crawls(collection?)` / `get_crawl(id)` → crawl provenance.
  - `resolve_url(url)` → captures/timestamps for a URL (Memento-ish; overlaps shwl.3 `/api/resolve`).
  - `get_page(crawl, ts, url)` → archived text + headers/metadata (not raw replay bytes).
- Resources: optionally expose collections as MCP resources.
- Auth/safety: read-only; respect any access controls; bound result sizes; no replay-bytes firehose.

## Open questions
- Reuse the shwl.2 JSON API handlers under the hood (share a service layer) vs. a parallel implementation.
- Which Rust MCP library, if any, meets the light-deps bar.
- Whether to gate behind a `--mcp` serve flag or always-on.

Best built on top of the read-only JSON API (rustyweb-federation-shwl.2) so both share one query/service layer.

title: Ingest: duplicate captures of a URL get last-wins timestamp
description:
In index_merged (crates/indice-lib/src/index/ingest/pages.rs), RawRecord::Html
sets `e.timestamp = timestamp` unconditionally. When one WACZ contains two or
more captures of the SAME url, the last record processed wins, so the single
indexed doc's replay timestamp is whichever capture came last in the record
order.

NOTE on determinism: /code-review flagged this as depending on rayon/HashMap
ordering, but that appears to be wrong -- rayon's collect() preserves sequential
order, and the timestamp is assigned while iterating the `raws` Vec, not the
HashMap (HashMap order only affects which page doc gets indexed first). So the
winner is deterministic: the last capture in record/CDX order.

Still worth deciding deliberately rather than by accident: arguably the LATEST
capture timestamp should win (or the one whose body we actually indexed), and
search already collapses repeat captures of a URL and reports capture_count.
Decide the rule, document it, and add a test with a two-capture fixture.

Pre-existing; predates the WaczAccess refactor (PR #118). Found by /code-review
of #118, 2026-09-07.

title: Optionally back the indice home (index + archive) with object storage
description: Let the indice home be (optionally) backed by object storage (S3/MinIO/GCS) rather than a local filesystem, for cloud deployments and horizontal read scaling. Two parts, both feasible without abandoning the single-binary model: (1) INDEX — Tantivy can open an index over a custom Directory, so index/ could live in a bucket with a local NVMe read-through cache; one writer publishes an immutable versioned index, N read-only serve replicas mirror shards on demand (cf. tantivy-object-store crate). (2) ARCHIVE — the archive/ WACZ store could also live in a bucket; WACZs are already served via HTTP range reads at GET /files/{id}, so serve_file could range-proxy or redirect to presigned URLs. Deletes stay workable via versioned rebuilds. Not needed until ~10M docs / ~10GB index (see qw5 scale model + DESIGN 'Distribution & object storage'). Excludes Quickwit (append-only, cluster; clashes with indice's mutability + single-binary). Research + DESIGN note landed 2026-08.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: 2026-10-03: the ARCHIVE half of this is now being built under epic rustyweb-demo-instance-5b9k (.1 S3 client + storage: config, .2 ingest offloads WACZ bytes and records Source::Url, .3 delete removes the object), driven by the app.indice.page demo rather than by scale. Scope here narrows to the INDEX half: Tantivy over a custom Directory with an NVMe read-through cache, one writer / N read-only replicas. Still not needed until ~10M docs / ~10GB index.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
2026-10-03 (later): the ARCHIVE half is DEFERRED again, back to this bead. Ed's call on the demo: with content deleted daily, uploads size-capped, and only approved people able to upload, disk use on the UpCloud VM is bounded, so block storage is enough and an S3 client is unneeded complexity for app.indice.page. 5b9k.1/.2/.3 closed as not-doing.

Design work done before the reversal, worth keeping here so it isn't re-derived:
- USE A SANS-IO SIGNING CRATE, NOT A HAND-ROLLED SigV4 AND NOT AN SDK. rusty-s3 (BSD-2, sans-IO, 1.16M downloads, released 2026-08-01) with --no-default-features --features rustcrypto adds exactly THREE crates to indice's shipped tree: rusty-s3, jiff, jiff-core. It generates presigned URLs you execute with the ureq agent we already have, so no second HTTP stack and no async/sync impedance (object_store is ~50 crates incl. reqwest+hyper and is async-only, awkward from the sync Ingest path; aws-sdk-s3 is 100+ crates and defaults to aws-lc-sys, i.e. cmake). UrlStyle::Path covers UpCloud/Ceph. Add the xml feature (3 more crates) only when ListObjectsV2 response parsing is actually needed.
- THE SEAM IS acquire::open's (effective_source, access) RETURN PAIR. --download turns a Source::Url into a locally-read Source::File; object storage is the exact inverse. Add store: Option<&Bucket> to Ingest (one field + one setter, as its doc comment invites), have resolve_sources skip place_local_wacz when a store is set, and add a first arm in open guarded on Source::File that PUTs and returns (Source::Url(public_url), WaczAccess::Local).
- DO NOT rewrite the source in record::upsert: wacz_id(&effective_source) is computed in index_one right after open (ingest/mod.rs:408) and stamped onto every Tantivy document by pages::index, so the source must be settled before indexing.
- KEY NAMING CONTENT-ADDRESSED (<prefix><slug>/<sha256[..12]>-<name>.wacz) rather than porting pick_archive_dest's -2/-3 scheme: you can't cheaply compare bucket contents (ETag is MD5, md5 isn't in the tree), and it makes re-PUT idempotent and the URL predictable before upload.
- RESUMABILITY BREAKS without a helper: the skip-already-indexed guard (ingest/mod.rs:313-325) hashes the pre-effective Source::File, whose id won't match the recorded Source::Url. Needs an acquire::stored_source() that derives the URL without uploading, with the guard checking both ids.
- VERIFY REGRESSES SILENTLY: run_verify (main.rs:1924) skips Source::Url as 'not re-fetched', but a bucket crawl has a NON-EMPTY recorded sha256 (hashed locally pre-upload), so it would look verified and never be checked. See rustyweb-streamed-wacz-fixity-zle5.
- CORS IS THE SILENT KILLER: viewer_source (server/util.rs:38), not serve_file, is the load-bearing replay path - it hands the raw URL to the viewer, so wabac.js reads the bucket directly. Without Access-Control-Expose-Headers containing Content-Range and Accept-Ranges the browser gets the bytes but fetch() hides the headers, so wabac.js never learns the total length and replay breaks with nothing in the console. Any future bucket work should ship an 'indice storage check' preflight (signed PUT/HEAD, anonymous ranged GET asserting 206 + exact Content-Range + expose-headers, OPTIONS preflight asserting range in Allow-Headers) before anything else.
- hmac 0.13 is ALREADY in indice's shipped tree via zip 8 -> pbkdf2, so auth.rs's hand-rolled hmac_sha256 is avoiding a dependency that is already compiled in.

Also note what indice can ALREADY do, which is why this is deferrable: POST /api/archives and the accession desk's path/URL tab accept an http(s) URL, and Ingest stream-indexes it over HTTP ranges while replay reads it straight from that URL. Anyone who wants bucket-hosted WACZs can host them and point indice at them today. What is missing is only 'indice puts your uploaded bytes in a bucket for you'.

title: Index outbound link hosts and domains (link graph)
description:
Extract outbound hyperlink targets (a[href], resolved against the page URL) and index their hosts and registrable domains as multi-valued fields (e.g. links_hosts, links_domains), enabling queries like links_hosts:youtube.com (pages that link to a host) and a future link-graph view of the archive. Mirrors warc-indexer links_hosts / links_domains / links_images. Extraction is easy with scraper.

Deferred from the search-enrichment epic (rustyweb-search-enrichment-6by.4) over index-size concerns: storing/indexing many link targets per page can add materially to the index (unlike the other enrichment fields, which are cheap). Revisit alongside the scale-footprint epic (rustyweb-scale-footprint-qw5) once the index-size levers are understood, and when there's a concrete link-graph use case (the maintainer is interested in representing the archived web as a graph).

Decisions to make: whether to also capture links_images; index-only vs stored (stored enables a link-graph view but is the expensive interpretation). Requires reindex.

title: Use Browsertrix screenshot records as the preferred crawl thumbnail
description: Browsertrix crawls (when screenshots are enabled — common) store a rendered screenshot of each page in a screenshots WARC, surfaced in the CDX as: - urn:thumbnail: → a small, ready-made thumbnail (image/jpeg, ~20-30KB) - urn:view: → the full viewport screenshot (image/png, larger) keyed by the EXACT page URL. Verified in a real crawl: urn:thumbnail:https://lawfaremedia.github.io/jan6-doj-archive/ → image/jpeg 22854 bytes; urn:view:... → image/png 169525 bytes. Our thumbnail picker (thumbnail.rs generate()) ignores these entirely, and its tier-3 "largest on-site captured image" actively EXCLUDES them: it filters candidates by site_of(main_page_url) (registrable domain), and a urn:thumbnail:/urn:view: URL does not parse to that host, so it never matches. Result: JS-rendered pages (SPAs, github.io, SUCHO, etc.) with no og:image and no raw-HTML get NO thumbnail even though a perfect screenshot exists in the WACZ. Fix — add a TIER-0 (highest priority) in generate(), before og:image: 1. find_image_record(cdx, &format!("urn:thumbnail:{main_page_url}")) — use it if present (already thumbnail-sized JPEG; skip the size window / on-site checks, it is purpose-built). 2. else find_image_record(cdx, &format!("urn:view:{main_page_url}")) — the full screenshot; downscale via the existing write_thumbnail (400px). Fetch the record bytes with the existing fetch_record_bytes (works local + streaming), then write_thumbnail as today. Respect a pinned thumbnail (curator override) first, as now. Notes: - Broadly beneficial: this becomes the primary thumbnail source for Browsertrix-crawled content (the importer’s bread and butter) and fixes the "no image" cases we saw on SUCHO/reallifemag-style JS pages. - Regenerated on (re)index like other thumbnails, so a reindex picks it up. - main_page_url must match the screenshot record’s page URL exactly (datapackage mainPageUrl / first seed); handle a trailing-slash mismatch defensively. - Relates to the existing thumbnail heuristic (three-tier), the per-page og:image gallery idea (rustyweb-crawl-ogimage-gallery-vi3n), and thumb GC (rustyweb-thumb-gc-2x5c). Files: thumbnail.rs (generate + a screenshot lookup helper), maybe a small is_screenshot_url helper; DESIGN "Representative-image thumbnails" section. Test: a fixture WACZ with a urn:thumbnail record → generate() picks it.
close_reason: Landed in PR #49: tier-0 Browsertrix screenshot (urn:thumbnail/urn:view) in thumbnail::generate.

title: Page-level curator annotations (Web Annotation / JSON-LD)
description:
Let curators annotate individual archived PAGES with notes — page-level contextual information (why a page matters, what is absent or misleading, provenance caveats). This is important context that the existing collection- and crawl-level notes cannot capture, so annotation belongs at the page level.

PRIOR ART: this has been done before by layering hypothes.is over pywb (that deployment is probably no longer live). Worth studying how it anchored and stored annotations, and why it may not have persisted.

STORAGE (proposal — open to alternatives): use the W3C Web Annotation Data Model (the successor to the Open Annotation Collaboration model) and persist annotations as JSON-LD alongside the collection, consistent with indice's "source of truth is a committable file next to the collection" design (the finding-aid README.md and crawl notes). Likely collections/<slug>/annotations.jsonl (one annotation per line) or an annotations.json AnnotationCollection. Each annotation carries a target (the archived page URL + the memento/capture timestamp so it pins to a specific capture + an optional selector) and a body (the note, Markdown or HTML), plus creator/created. Keying on URL + timestamp lets annotations survive reindexing.

ANCHORING: attaching a note to a REGION of a page likely needs JS-driven text selection + highlighting. In the Web Annotation model, TextQuoteSelector (the quoted text plus prefix/suffix) is the most robust anchor across layout/markup changes; TextPositionSelector / RangeSelector / FragmentSelector are alternatives. A v1 could anchor at the whole-page level (a note attached to the page/memento, no sub-page region), which sidesteps the hard part and still delivers most of the curatorial value.

DISPLAY: show annotations in a side column beside the replayed page, and/or list them on the crawl and collection pages.

BIG OPEN QUESTION — ReplayWeb.page integration: the archived page renders inside ReplayWeb.page's web component, which embeds content in a service-worker-backed iframe. Capturing a text selection and injecting a highlight layer INSIDE that replay frame is the crux and may not be supported. This needs a spike (see child). If in-frame highlighting is not feasible, fall back to page-level annotations shown beside the replay (no in-page highlight), with region anchoring as a later enhancement, or explore an alternate rendering path we control.

RELATIONSHIP TO EXISTING WORK: this extends the current curator-note concept (crawl notes at collections/<slug>/crawls/<id>.md) from crawl-level down to page-level. Creating/editing annotations should be management-gated (serve --manage), like the other curation actions.

SUGGESTED PHASING:
1. Spike the ReplayWeb.page anchoring/highlighting question (gates all region-level work).
2. Storage model: Web Annotation JSON-LD alongside the collection + lib read/write.
3. UI: create (select region or whole page, then note) + display in a side column; management-gated.

REFERENCES: W3C Web Annotation Data Model (https://www.w3.org/TR/annotation-model/); hypothes.is; the older Open Annotation spec.
notes:
V1 DESIGN — settled 2026-09-06 via a design spike (after gnqf.1 proved in-place highlighting works).

FRAMING: a public, page-level provenance/annotation layer. Two user stories: (1) an ANNOTATOR deposits interpretive traces so they can re-find + understand documents; (2) a READER/searcher discovers others' notes serendipitously — so discovery is a first-class goal, not a byproduct. Conceptual grounding: Light & Hyry, "Colophons and Annotations" (American Archivist 65:2, 2002) — the finding aid as a living, layered, transparent record; annotations are that interpretive layer pushed down to individual captures (each note = a small colophon: author + date + observation). [DESIGN.md write-up pending a read of the paper.]

VISIBILITY: display is PUBLIC (same pattern as finding aids/crawl notes: public read, gated write); creating/editing is AUTHENTICATED. Rationale: notes live in the clear in the committed JSONL, so signed-in-only view would be false privacy.

AUTHORS: any signed-in user (identity from forward-auth); edit/delete OWN notes only. Caveat: a loopback --manage instance has a single local identity, so "own only" collapses to all-editable — real multi-author attribution needs forward-auth/SSO. Public attribution shows a human DISPLAY NAME, not the login email (derived, overridable).

CONTENT: freeform Markdown. FLAT (no replies in v1).

ANCHOR: a specific capture (page URL + timestamp); whole-page OR a highlighted region via W3C TextQuoteSelector (quote + prefix/suffix), re-anchored on load, degrading to an unanchored (still-listed) note if the captured text moved. NB: in-place highlighting reaches RWP-internal DOM — re-test on ReplayWeb.page upgrades (see gnqf.1).

SURFACING (all): side column beside the replay with in-page highlight; an "Annotations" section on crawl + collection pages; PUBLIC search (index note text as a distinct doc_type; show as "note on <page> by <author>" + a signal on page hits); a per-collection annotations index/browse.

STORAGE: collections/<slug>/annotations.jsonl — one W3C Web Annotation (JSON-LD) per line; committable public provenance (git history = the colophon audit trail); keyed by URL+timestamp to survive reindexing.

PHASING: gnqf.2 storage first (no UI risk) -> gnqf.3 public display + gated authoring.

title: Spike: can we anchor + highlight annotations inside ReplayWeb.page?
description:
Gating spike for the page-annotations epic. Determine whether we can (a) capture a user text selection and (b) inject a highlight/anchor layer INSIDE the ReplayWeb.page replay frame (a service-worker-backed iframe within the RWP web component).

Investigate: does RWP expose any supported hook (postMessage API, events, an extension/inject point, or a configuration) to run script in or overlay the replayed content? What are the cross-origin / shadow-DOM / service-worker constraints? Is there an alternate replay/render path (e.g. our own extracted-HTML view) where we control the DOM and can inject highlights?

Output: a go/no-go on region-level (sub-page) anchoring, plus a recommended approach. If no-go, the fallback is page-level annotations displayed beside the replay (no in-page highlight); confirm that is viable. Anchor recommendation should note which Web Annotation selector to use (TextQuoteSelector is the leading candidate).
notes: SPIKE RESULT 2026-09-05: GO for in-place highlighting. indice serves replayed content SAME-ORIGIN (wabac SW under the app origin), so from the top page we can pierce shadow DOM + two nested same-origin iframes (RWP app frame -> archived-content frame at /replay/w/<coll>/<hash>/<ts>mp_/<url>) and reach the archived document. Verified via CDP: read its DOM, window.getSelection + document.createRange available, and injected a highlight (Range.surroundContents succeeded; a <mark>/CSS class rendered visibly in the replayed page). => region-level (TextQuoteSelector) anchoring INSIDE the live replay is feasible, not just the page-level fallback. CAVEATS: (1) reaching RWP/wabac private DOM (frame nesting, /w/ URL shape) is unsupported and may break on RWP upgrades -- use resilient traversal (deepest same-origin doc whose URL matches /replay/w/.../mp_/) and re-test on upgrade; (2) naive surroundContents only handles single-node ranges -- robust cross-node highlighting needs the standard multi-range approach (rangy/hypothes.is style); (3) highlights are ephemeral -- persist in the annotation store and re-anchor on load via TextQuoteSelector. Recommendation: proceed with storage (.2) now; build UI (.3) with region-level via this path.
close_reason: GO: verified in-place highlighting is feasible — replayed content is same-origin (wabac SW), reachable through nested same-origin iframes; Range.surroundContents injected a visible highlight. Region-level anchoring via TextQuoteSelector on the live replay is viable. Caveat recorded: RWP-internal DOM coupling; re-test on RWP upgrades. Full findings in the bead notes.

title: Web Annotation storage: JSON-LD annotations alongside the collection
description:
Define and implement the on-disk annotation store for the page-annotations epic (independent of the ReplayWeb.page spike).

Use the W3C Web Annotation Data Model. Store per collection as a committable file next to the finding aid (proposal: collections/<slug>/annotations.jsonl, one annotation object per line). Each annotation: target = archived page URL + memento/capture timestamp + optional selector; body = note text (Markdown/HTML); plus creator + created. Add lib read/write helpers (mirroring the crawl-note / finding-aid helpers), keyed so annotations survive reindexing (URL + timestamp, not internal doc ids). Decide single AnnotationCollection vs JSONL, and how annotations map to a crawl/collection for display. Open to alternative storage if the spike suggests one.
design:
Web Annotation Data Model, one JSON object per line at collections/<slug>/annotations.jsonl (JSONL: appends cleanly, diffs well, mirrors crawl notes). Each annotation:
- id: uuid/urn
- type: "Annotation"; @context: the Web Annotation context
- created (ISO-8601), creator (identity + display name)
- target: { source: <page URL>, state/refinedBy: capture timestamp (pins to the memento), selector?: TextQuoteSelector { exact, prefix, suffix } for a region; absent = whole-page }
- body: { type: TextualBody, format: "text/markdown", value: <note> }
Keyed by URL + timestamp (not internal doc ids) so annotations survive reindex. lib read/write helpers mirroring the crawl-note / finding-aid helpers (append, list-by-collection, list-by-page(url,ts), update/delete-by-id-if-author). Public read; writes go through the management/auth path. Independent of the RWP UI, so this is the safe first build.

title: Annotation UI: create + display page annotations (side column)
description:
The curator-facing UI for the page-annotations epic. Blocked by the ReplayWeb.page spike (its outcome decides region-level vs page-level anchoring).

Create: while replaying a page (management mode), let a curator attach a note — to a selected region if the spike says that is feasible, otherwise to the whole page — and save it to the annotation store. Display: show annotations in a side column beside the replayed page, and surface them on the crawl/collection pages. Gate creation/editing behind serve --manage (like the other curation actions); display is public.

title: Production deployment in the cloud (reverse-proxy fronted)
description:
Set up a production deployment of rustyweb in the cloud, fronted by a modern reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy, or similar) for TLS and public-facing concerns. rustyweb is a single self-contained binary that serves HTTP via axum (default 127.0.0.1:8080); the deployment wraps that for real-world hosting while keeping the 'range' ethos: the same setup should suit a small VPS and scale up toward an institutional host.

Goal: a documented, reproducible way to run rustyweb publicly (TLS, a domain, restart-on-failure) with the reverse proxy handling the edge and rustyweb serving search + WACZ bytes.

rustyweb-specific considerations:
- BYTE-RANGE PASSTHROUGH is critical: replay is WACZ-direct — the browser reads GET /files/{id} with HTTP Range requests via wabac.js. The proxy must pass Range/Accept-Ranges/Content-Range through untouched and not buffer whole (multi-GB) WACZ responses (e.g. nginx: proxy_buffering off / proxy_max_temp_file_size 0, or use a proxy that streams ranges well). Verify large-file range serving end to end through the proxy.
- TLS termination at the proxy (Let's Encrypt). Caddy does this automatically; nginx needs certbot. Pick one.
- Run rustyweb bound to localhost, as a non-root user, index opened read-only (serve already opens read-only); only the proxy is public.
- Persistent storage for <home> (archive/ + index/). Streaming remote WACZs keeps disk small (index only); a local archive needs a durable volume. Decide the storage model per target.
- Compression is already done in-process (tower-http); avoid double-compressing at the proxy. Don't gzip byte-range responses.
- CORS: same-origin replay (WACZ served by rustyweb) needs none; replaying a *remote* WACZ needs that remote host's CORS — document the distinction.
- Health/readiness endpoint for the proxy / orchestrator (likely need to add a lightweight /health route — none today).
- Observability: tracing logs to stdout/journald; access logs at the proxy.

Deployment shapes to evaluate (pick 1-2):
- Container: single static binary -> tiny distroless/scratch OCI image; run on a VM, Fly.io, Cloud Run, ECS, etc. Assets are embedded at build time, so the image is self-contained.
- VM + systemd: a systemd unit for rustyweb + the proxy config on a VPS/EC2/droplet.

Open decisions: which reverse proxy (Caddy = simplest TLS; nginx = ubiquitous), which cloud target (VM vs managed container platform), container vs systemd, and where <home> lives (ephemeral + stream-only, or a persistent volume).

Deliverables (candidate child tasks): reverse-proxy config with verified range passthrough (nginx + Caddy examples); Dockerfile / OCI image (distroless); systemd unit + VM deploy guide; /health endpoint; a Deployment section in README/DESIGN. Relates to the scale-footprint direction (rustyweb-scale-footprint-qw5) and to streaming (remote-only deploys need little disk).
close_reason: Closing as stale (2026-08-22): a year of accumulated assumptions, much now shifted — streaming ingest shipped, scale measured (one node fine to ~10M), forward-auth + reverse-proxy docs landed, object-storage-home direction filed (rustyweb-object-storage-home). Re-planning deployment from scratch with the maintainer; the technical requirements here (byte-range passthrough, no double-compress/gzip-on-range, non-root loopback, CORS same-origin-vs-remote, /health) will be carried into fresh, scoped beads.

title: Make reindex resilient to transient remote-fetch failures
description:
`rustyweb reindex` currently fails fast: it drops the old full-text index up front, then re-indexes every registered source, and the first error (e.g. a transient network read on a remote WACZ) aborts the whole run — leaving the index partially rebuilt. With a collection of remote WACZs (e.g. the `sul` Stanford stacks collection) a single flaky fetch means the entire reindex is lost and must be restarted from scratch (re-fetching everything, ~20+ min), where it may fail again.

This bit us during the faceting work: reindex died at 9/19 on a transient read of a remote WACZ, and the Browsertrix collections (later in the manifest) never got indexed.

Desired behavior: a transient remote-fetch failure should be treated like a missing local file already is — logged as a warning and skipped, preserving the WACZ's manifest entry — so the rest of the reindex completes. At the end, print a summary of any skipped sources and exit non-zero (so cron/CI notices) while still leaving a usable, mostly-complete index.

Scope / considerations:
- Distinguish transient/remote-fetch errors (skip + warn) from programmer/logic errors (still fail). Start by making remote fetch/parse failures non-fatal; keep local validation (path outside archive, non-.wacz) fail-fast as today.
- Consider ret/retries with backoff for remote fetches before giving up on one.
- Consider not dropping the old index until the rebuild succeeds, or building into a temp dir and swapping — so a failed reindex doesn't destroy a working index. (Bigger change; could be a follow-up.)
- Report a clear end-of-run summary: N indexed, M skipped (with reasons).
- Tests: a source that errors is skipped and the run completes over the rest.

Relates to the remote-WACZ collections use case and the Browsertrix importer epic (rustyweb-15z), which will add more remote sources.
close_reason: Both remaining follow-ups delivered: reindex skip-on-failure (with non-zero exit + summary) and per-host concurrency cap (MAX_CONCURRENCY=64).

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Scope (maintainer concern): broaden this beyond "retry transient failures" to robust AND POLITE remote fetching. Now that CDX-guided record fetch is concurrent (r0n.7, default --concurrency 16), a single WACZ's requests all hit ONE host, so we can overload a small/self-hosted server or get IP-blocked when the target isn't a big object store like S3.

Key measure: honor HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) and 503 + the Retry-After header with exponential backoff, for both the range fetches (http_range::HttpFetch) and the whole-file downloads. This is simultaneously resilience (recover from transient/overload errors, per this task's original intent) AND politeness (back off when a host pushes back, instead of hammering -> far less likely to get blocked).

Also consider:
- A per-host rate and/or concurrency cap (proactive politeness), separate from the raw --concurrency worker count.
- Revisiting the default --concurrency: 16 is tuned for object stores; a lower default (or a "be gentle" mode) may be safer when pointing rustyweb at arbitrary hosts, which matters for the self-serve / adoption story.
- Retry with jittered backoff on transient network errors, and a bounded retry budget, so a long ingest survives blips without giving up or busy-looping.

Ties to the streaming epic (r0n) and the shareable/self-serve goal (others will point rustyweb at arbitrary hosts, not just S3).

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Core delivered in PR #36 (resilient + polite remote fetching):
- Retry transient failures (network errors + HTTP 429/502/503/504) with capped exponential backoff + jitter, honoring server Retry-After — applied to the range GETs (HttpFetch::open/fetch) and the whole-file downloads (get_reader).
- Agent built with http_status_as_error(false) so 4xx/5xx are inspectable (status + Retry-After).
- Gentle default --concurrency (4 remote / CPU count local) so we don't overload/get-blocked by default.
- Tests: with_retry unit tests + an axum 503-then-200 integration test (get_reader_retries_a_transient_status).

Remaining follow-ups (keep this task open for them):
- reindex skip-on-failure: don't abort the whole `reindex` run when one source fails after retries — skip it with a warning (like missing local files) so a long rebuild survives one bad/blocked source.
- Per-host rate/concurrency cap (proactive politeness beyond the raw worker count).

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Remaining follow-ups delivered (this closes the task):

1. reindex skip-on-failure — `reindex` no longer aborts the whole rebuild when one source fails. A source that can't be indexed (missing local file, or a remote source still failing after the retry budget) is skipped with a per-source warning, and its manifest entry is preserved. The rebuild always runs to completion and the mostly-rebuilt index is committed (usable). Per the desired behavior here, if anything was skipped the command exits non-zero with a summary count (indexed N of M, skipped K) so cron/CI notices while still leaving a usable index. Test: reindex_skips_a_failing_source_and_keeps_going (good + corrupt source → completes over the good one, returns non-zero, both manifest entries preserved).

2. Per-host concurrency cap — the resolved fetch worker count is clamped to a per-host ceiling (MAX_CONCURRENCY = 64), so no --concurrency value (or high local core count) can put an unbounded number of range requests in flight against a single host. A mis-typed --concurrency 500 logs a warning and is capped. Proactive politeness on top of the existing retry/backoff + gentle default (4 remote).

Docs updated (README + DESIGN). Not doing the bigger "build into a temp dir and atomic-swap so a failed reindex never touches the working index" idea from the original scope — the resilience + non-zero-exit here covers the immediate need; can be a separate follow-up if wanted.

title: reindex silently drops Browsertrix sources (wrong is_url guard)
description:
reindex() in crates/indice-lib/src/index.rs (~line 538) guards the local-file
existence check with `if !source.is_url()`. is_url() is true ONLY for
Source::Url, so Source::Browsertrix and Source::BrowsertrixPublic fall into the
block; source.resolve(home) returns None for them, hitting the `_` arm ->
"skipping missing local WACZ", skipped += 1, continue. This happens BEFORE
index_one, so the BrowsertrixResolver the CLI passes (main.rs:1117) never gets a
chance to re-resolve a fresh presigned URL.

Effect: every `indice reindex` silently drops all Browsertrix-imported crawls
from the freshly-built index (and exits non-zero), with a misleading "missing
local WACZ" message. Fresh `import`/`browsertrix` runs are unaffected (they call
the indexer directly and bypass this guard); only reindex loses them.

Fix: gate the existence check on File sources only, using the same distinction
delete_crawl already uses at index.rs:823 (`if wacz.source.is_remote()`):

    if !source.is_remote() {   // only Source::File; Url + Browsertrix pass through
        match source.resolve(home) { Some(p) if p.exists() => {} _ => { skip } }
    }

index_one already handles both Browsertrix variants via the resolver
(index.rs:~1315). Add a regression test: a manifest with a Browsertrix source +
a stub resolver should reindex it rather than skip it. Do as its own PR off main
(not stacked on annotations). Discovered 2026-09-06 while working on the
annotations PR (#111).
notes: Fixed in PR #115 (branch reindex-browsertrix, off main): guard changed !is_url() -> !is_remote() in reindex (index.rs:543); Browsertrix/Url sources now flow to index_one. Regression test reindex_does_not_skip_browsertrix_sources_at_the_guard (spy resolver) — verified fails on old guard, passes on fix. fmt/clippy/212 lib tests green. Close when #115 merges.
close_reason: Fixed + merged via PR #115 (guard !is_url()->!is_remote(), regression test).

title: Rename rustyweb → indice
description:
Rename the project from 'rustyweb' to 'indice'.

WHY RENAME
- 'Rusty Web' was conceived around content aging in place at its original origin, but the tool actually gathers WACZ files and serves them from a reading room — the name never fit.
- 'rusty-web' also collides with an unrelated Rust web framework on crates.io (human/semantic collision).

WHY 'indice'
- Triple resonance: Suzanne Briet's indice (a document is 'un indice concret ou symbolique, conserve ou enregistre... pour prouver un phenomene'); Charles S. Peirce's index (a sign bound to its object by a real, existential connection — a web capture is a trace of a moment of the live web); and the Tantivy full-text index the tool builds.
- crates.io: indice, indice-lib, indice-bin all free (verified 2026-07-30).
- Collision sweep (2026-07-30): absent from IIPC / DigiPres / awesome-web-archiving tool lists — no clash in the web-archiving domain. Caveats (non-blocking): common Romance-language word (weak SEO); unrelated GitHub handle github.com/indice (our repo will be github.com/edsu/indice) and a Greek identity-software company using an @indice npm scope.

DECISIONS
- Tracker prefix stays 'rustyweb' and this epic's ID keeps '-fonds-' — issue IDs are an immutable internal namespace; 'fonds' here is a historical artifact of an earlier candidate name.
- Keep the lib/bin crate split: indice + indice-lib + indice-bin.

SEQUENCING
- Execute on a dedicated branch off main. This rename gates the desktop-app packaging issue (rustyweb-desktop-app-i91t.6).
close_reason: Rename to indice complete (crates indice/indice-lib, CLI indice, repo edsu/indice, docs+branding). .5 crates.io closed won't-do; .7 done.

title: Replay cache invalidation: version the wabac source/coll by WACZ content hash
description:
ReplayWeb.page/wabac.js caches a loaded collection in the BROWSER (IndexedDB + Cache Storage) keyed by the coll name + source URL. indice's crawl id and /files/{id} URL are STABLE across a content change (wacz_id is derived from the WACZ's path, not its bytes), so replacing/reindexing a crawl in place leaves returning browsers serving the OLD cached replay until the user manually clears storage / unregisters the service worker.

When it bites:
- reindex,  overwrite, delete+re-add, or --force re-index of an updated WACZ at the same path -> same id/URL/coll -> stale replay.
- Append-only (new crawls get new ids/URLs) is UNAFFECTED — the common case is fine.
- Operators hit it during curation (fixable by clearing their own cache). Worse case: visitors to a SERVED indice site keep seeing stale replay after an operator fixes/replaces a WACZ — you can't ask every visitor to clear storage.

Discovered 2026-08-21 building a wget WACZ of ducklake.select: after the angle-bracket fix + rebuild, replay stayed stale in Zen/Firefox until IndexedDB/CacheStorage were cleared; a fresh Chrome replayed correctly, confirming server-side was fine and the browser cache was stale.

Fix idea: include the WACZ's content hash (sha256 — already stored per-WACZ in the manifest) in what indice hands the viewer — the replay source URL and/or the coll param (e.g. coll={id}-{shortsha}, or source .../files/{id}?v={sha}) — so a content change yields a new cache key and wabac re-fetches instead of reusing its stale local copy. Verify which key (coll name vs source URL) wabac actually uses for its IndexedDB collection reuse. Also consider ETag/Cache-Control on serve_file (/files/{id}), though wabac's IndexedDB persistence likely needs the key-versioning approach, not just HTTP caching. Files: server.rs (replay viewer URL / replay.json / serve_file), views (replay embed).

membership changes, the cached copy under that coll name goes stale and replays
the old (or an empty/broken) state — no member WACZ requests fire and deep-links
404 (GET /replay/w/<coll>/<ts>mp_/<url>). Confirmed live: a collection that
404'd in the normal profile replayed fine in an incognito window (clean
storage). Curators shouldn't need DevTools -> Application -> Clear site data.

Options (A recommended):
A. Scoped "Reload from server" button in the replay banner (next to Notes):
   deletes THIS collection's wabac storage (SW message to drop the coll +
   matching Cache Storage entries) and reloads the viewer. Discoverable,
   targeted, low-risk. Confirm the exact @webrecorder/wabac SW purge call
   during implementation.
B. Blunt "Clear all replay cache" action (settings/collection page): wipe all
   wabac IndexedDB + caches + unregister SW. Simpler, heavier-handed.
C. Automatic invalidation: version the `coll` namespace with a content hash
   (member ids + sha256/mtime) so a changed collection loads fresh
   automatically. Best UX but orphans old namespaces -> needs a cleanup pass.

Suggest shipping A first, C later as the "never think about it" version. Its own
PR off main. Discovered 2026-09-06 debugging collection replay while testing the
annotations PR (#111); affects annotation "Open page" deep-links too (same path).

title: Scale: from a laptop to institutional TBs
description:
Keep rustyweb's index frugal, predictable, and fast as a corpus grows from a laptop's handful of WACZs to an institution's TBs of WARC — without degrading the small/local experience. rustyweb's identity is small→institutional (unlike SolrWayback/SHINE, which assume a Solr cluster), so scale has to be a first-class concern of the single-binary design.

Measured baseline (2026-07, ~21.7k docs / 118 MB index): stored text (.store) is ~64% of the index and scales linearly with the corpus; term positions (.pos) ~20%; the inverted index (.term/.idx) ~16%; fast fields / facets ~0%. So the dominant, corpus-linear cost is the text we store for snippets — that is the thing to attack at scale.

The levers interact: capping stored body text shrinks .store AND makes the per-query URL-grouping pass (which reads up to CANDIDATE_CAP stored docs) cheaper. Frugality should be configurable: a laptop keeps generous snippets, an institution dials it down.

Scope covers on-disk footprint, query-time performance/memory, index build at scale, and the one-index-vs-sharding architectural question. Every decision should be driven by the size/scale model (first task), not intuition — several child tasks are investigations that may resolve to "leave as is".

title: Size and scale model (measure-first)
description: Measure-first foundation that gates the rest of the epic. Build a repeatable size/scale model: bytes-per-doc broken down by Tantivy file type (.store, .pos, .term, .idx, .fast, .fieldnorm), projected to 1M / 100M docs and to TB-scale corpora; plus index build time and peak RAM for a known corpus. Output a short written model (checked into the repo or DESIGN.md) and a script/command to re-measure after changes. Goal: choose every other lever from data, and know how alarmed to actually be. Baseline today: ~21.7k docs / 118 MB, .store ~64%.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #80 (size/scale model, zstd docstore, stored-body cap + snippet fallback, positions audit, resumable per-WACZ ingest, config.yaml frugality knobs).

title: Replay-client footprint: server-side pagesQueryUrl pagination for large collections
description:
The client-side instance of qw5's laptop->institutional goal. Multi-WACZ collection replay (bukh Phase 1) works natively for small/medium collections, but wabac then loads EVERY member WACZ's page index into the browser — infeasible for institutional collections (e.g. usgov-archive 570k pages / hundreds of WACZs).

The scale valve: set metadata.pagesQueryUrl on the collection JSON (server.rs collection_replay_json) when the collection is large (threshold from qw5.1's size/scale model), and serve a pagesQueryUrl-shaped endpoint from the Tantivy index so wabac defers URL->WACZ resolution to the server and lazily loads only needed members — flat browser footprint regardless of collection size.

wabac contract (from the sw.js trace on dk4): accepts ?url=<exact>, ?search=<q> (page-list + url fallback), ?page=<n>, ?pageSize=25; returns {total, items:[{url, ts|date, title, filename}]} where item.filename must match resources[].name (= the WACZ id, already emitted by collection_replay_json).

Consumers/relations: enables bukh at scale; is the page-list/resolution backend for dk4 (cross-WACZ); its query cost belongs with qw5.5 (faceting/grouping cost), qw5.3 bounds title/snippet size, and its latency depends on a compacted index (qw5.9). Reconcile the resolver with rustyweb-federation-shwl.3 (/api/resolve) — likely one shared core.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
MEASURED, then DEFERRED (2026-07-26). Ran a headless-browser probe that records every /files/{id} request the server sees (axum middleware layer + Chrome for Testing/chromedriver), replaying a page that lives in ONE member of a 2-member collection.

Result: BOTH member WACZs are fetched, in BOTH modes:
- with metadata.pagesQueryUrl set: /files fetched for every member
- native (no pagesQueryUrl): /files fetched for every member too

So the assumed benefit -- pagesQueryUrl lets wabac lazy-load only the member a URL resolves to -- is FALSE for this wabac build (replaywebpage 2.4.6). loadWACZFiles does this.pagesQueryUrl ? await r.init(e) : r.path=e, i.e. pagesQueryUrl EAGERLY opens every member; native sets paths lazily. Neither reduces member-WACZ opens; both touch all members.

What pagesQueryUrl actually changes: it skips loading each member page index (pages.jsonl) into the browser and defers page-list + URL lookups to the server. That is a real footprint win ONLY when member page counts are large (institutional scale). At current scale it is marginal, and it costs resolution fragility (exact-match index vs wabac native CDX) + sidebar coupling.

The /pages endpoint + the recording-middleware test pattern are the tools for that.

title: Auto-optimize a fragmented index after ingest (+ serve-startup warning)
description:
Split out of qw5.9 (the optimize command shipped; this makes it run when needed). Preflight/free-space and segment throttling were considered and dropped (running out of disk mid-ingest isn't a correctness problem — Tantivy commit is atomic; the real gap is a valid-but-fragmented index silently making every query slow, esp. the homepage facet_overview which fans out across all segments).

Motivation: Ed indexed a batch of WACZs, noticed the homepage was sluggish, and had to REMEMBER to run `indice optimize`. The tool should just do it when it clearly helps.

Work — auto-optimize at the END of an ingest run, but only when the index is actually fragmented:
- After a CLI `index` run and after a server bulk import (bx_import), check segment_count(); if over a generous threshold (well above a healthy/actively-merging index; optimize's default target is 8), run optimize once, logged transparently ('compacting index: N -> M segments').
- The threshold gate is what makes it 'sometimes': a healthy index, or a single incremental add to an already-tidy index, stays under the threshold and is untouched (protects the manage-UI add-one-crawl path from re-merging the whole index each time).
- Opt-out flag `--no-optimize` on `index`; when set and the index is fragmented, fall back to LOGGING the hint instead of running it, so nothing is silent.
- If disk is genuinely full the auto-optimize fails gracefully — index stays valid, only fragmented (same as today).
- Backstop: at `serve` startup (read-only; segment_count works without a writer), warn with the optimize hint if the opened index is fragmented (covers indexes built by older versions / killed runs).

Verification: build a many-segment index (search.rs tests already do), assert the fragmentation check trips above threshold and is quiet below; assert auto-optimize reduces the segment count; assert --no-optimize logs the hint instead.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #84: index/import auto-compact a fragmented index at end of run (optimize_if_fragmented, threshold-gated so healthy/single-add is untouched); --no-optimize opts out with a reminder; serve warns at startup if fragmented. Review fixes applied (shared fragmentation_warning helper, debug-logged count errors, doc tidy).

title: Decide whether the single waczs.json manifest becomes unwieldy at scale
description:
The manifest (<home>/index/waczs.json) is a single JSON file loaded and saved WHOLESALE. Every ingest commits per-WACZ and calls manifest.save() (rewrites the whole file), and open() parses the entire file into memory. Today's collections are modest (e.g. Stanford ~373 WACZs), but at institutional scale (tens of thousands to 100k+ crawls) this could get unwieldy: O(n) rewrite on every per-WACZ commit during a large ingest (quadratic total write), full parse into memory on open, and no concurrent-writer story.

Investigate/decide (measure-first, per the qw5 ethos): at what crawl count does load/save become a problem (time + memory)? Options if it does: batch the save (don't rewrite per-WACZ — ties to the resumable-ingest granularity), an append-only log + periodic compaction, sharding per-collection, or moving the manifest to SQLite (Tantivy is already the heavy store; a small embedded DB for metadata may fit). Also consider crawl-list/query cost (rustyweb-... crawl list reads the whole manifest). Decide with a benchmark, not intuition; may be a no-op if JSON is fine to 100k. Parent epic: qw5.

Potentially a large, zero-behavior-change win before we cap anything. Deliver: current setting documented, a size/CPU comparison, and a recommendation (and switch, if clearly better). title: Query-time cost of faceting/grouping at scale
description: Benchmark query-time cost at scale on a large synthetic index: facet terms aggregations and the URL-grouping pass in search_faceted (which currently reads up to CANDIDATE_CAP=1000 *stored* docs per query just to read each candidate's URL). Concrete synergy with the size work: make `url` a FAST field so grouping reads a fast column instead of stored docs — cuts per-query latency and pairs with the stored-body cap (fewer/smaller stored reads). Also revisit whether CANDIDATE_CAP should scale with corpus. Requires reindex if url becomes fast.
close_reason: Measured via examples/scale_bench (PR #89): faceted search is sub-linear (~2x latency for 10x docs, bounded by CANDIDATE_CAP) and <100ms at 1M docs on a laptop; facet_overview ~16ms/1M; collection lookups flat. Query cost is not a bottleneck at target scale, so the url-as-FAST-field grouping optimization isn't needed now (revisit only if grouping shows up in a profile). Documented in the README Scaling section.

title: Index build at scale (RAM, merges, resumable ingest)
description: Make indexing large corpora practical: size the IndexWriter memory buffer (currently 50 MB) and document/parallelize ingest under a RAM ceiling, review the segment merge policy at high doc counts, and make large ingests resumable/incremental (skip already-indexed sources; recover from a partial run) — related to the reindex-resilience task. Deliver guidance + any config knobs for ingesting TBs without OOM or multi-day runs.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #80 (size/scale model, zstd docstore, stored-body cap + snippet fallback, positions audit, resumable per-WACZ ingest, config.yaml frugality knobs).

title: Sharding investigation (one index vs per-collection)
description: Research spike (not a build): at billions of docs / TBs, does one Tantivy index remain workable, or does rustyweb need to shard — e.g. one index per collection, or by time/size — with query-time fan-in? Weigh single-index simplicity against per-shard build/merge/memory limits and Tantivy's practical ceilings. Decide IF and WHEN sharding is needed and what the trigger metric is (doc count / index size / query latency from the scale model). Likely outcome: "not yet, revisit at threshold X" — documented so it is a conscious decision, not a surprise.
close_reason: Spike concluded via the qw5.5 benchmark (PR #89): a single Tantivy index handles 1M docs with sub-100ms queries at ~1.7KB/doc, projecting comfortably to ~10M+ on a laptop. Decision: no sharding needed now. Revisit if the index exceeds ~10GB or query latency (esp. facet_overview / phrase-matching-everything, which grow ~linearly) exceeds budget. Documented in the README Scaling section.

title: Configurable frugality (laptop vs institution presets)
description: Make frugality a first-class, configurable choice rather than hardcoded, so the same binary serves both ends of the range: a laptop keeps generous snippets while an institution dials size down. Surface the knobs from the other tasks — stored-body cap size, docstore compressor, (maybe) which fields keep positions — via config (file and/or flags), with a laptop-generous default and an institution "frugal" profile/preset. Depends on the cap and compression tasks landing first.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #80 (size/scale model, zstd docstore, stored-body cap + snippet fallback, positions audit, resumable per-WACZ ingest, config.yaml frugality knobs).

title: Compact/optimize command + robust merges (segment explosion on disk-full)
description:
Add an operator-facing way to COMPACT an existing Tantivy index (merge many small segments into few) WITHOUT re-streaming sources, and make ingest-time merges robust so segments don't silently explode.

## Motivation (measured, 2026-07-24)
Streaming ~115 public Browsertrix WACZs onto a nearly-full disk produced a pathological index:
- **1557 segments** (`meta.json`) vs. a healthy index's handful (a 897-doc index had **3**).
- Root cause: disk hit 100%; Tantivy background merges need transient ~2x space, so they **failed mid-merge** ("WARN tantivy … Merge of … was cancelled"), and segments never compacted.
- Effect on search: a per-query FIXED floor of ~0.4-0.6s (debug build) that is **independent of hit count** — 0-hit, "snow" (20 hits), and "the" all cost about the same — because every query, plus the homepage `facet_overview` and search's URL-grouping, must fan out across all 1557 segments (open term dict + postings per segment) before doing real work. This is NOT faceting cost; it's segment fan-out.
- Freeing disk does NOT fix it: the segments already on disk stay 1557 until a *writer* runs and merges. `serve` is read-only and never merges. Today the only built-in remedy is `reindex`, which re-streams every source and rebuilds the whole ~87 GB index — hugely expensive for what is really just a local compaction.

## Proposed work
1. **`rustyweb optimize` (a.k.a. `compact`/`merge`) subcommand** — open the existing index with an `IndexWriter`, gather `searchable_segment_ids()`, and `merge` them toward a small target, then `wait_merging_threads` + `garbage_collect_files`. No source fetches. `--home` like other commands; progress bar; `-v`.
   - Bound peak disk: merging 1557 → 1 segment needs transient space ~= the merged segment size (tens of GB here). Merge toward a **target segment count** or in **size-bounded batches** so peak disk stays well under the index size, and preflight a free-space check with a clear error if there isn't room.
   - Consider an `optimize` pass that also runs at the end of a large `import`/`index` so a big ingest leaves a tidy index.
2. **Robust ingest merges** — don't let background merges fail silently to disk-full:
   - Surface merge failures (warn→error with actionable text: "index not fully merged; free space and run `rustyweb optimize`").
   - Optionally preflight free-space before large ingests and/or throttle segment creation (fewer, larger commits) so streaming many WACZs doesn't create thousands of tiny segments in the first place. Relates to qw5.6 (merges/RAM at scale).

## Verification
- Unit/integration: build an index with many segments, run optimize, assert segment count drops to the target and search still returns the same hits.
- Measure query latency before/after optimize on a multi-hundred-segment index (expect the fixed floor to drop substantially).
- Disk preflight: optimize on a too-full disk fails fast with a clear message rather than a mid-merge cancellation.

Discovered while stream-importing usgov-archive public collections (rustyweb-15z.11). Parent epic qw5; closely related to qw5.6 (index build at scale) and the atomic-reindex task (7x3j) which should reuse the same build-into-temp-and-swap machinery.
close_reason: Part 1 (the optimize/compact command) shipped: index.rs::optimize + search.rs::optimize (size-bounded batch merges toward --max-segments, garbage_collect, segment_count() health signal), CLI 'indice optimize'. Part 2 (robust ingest merges: free-space preflight, surfaced merge failures, segment throttling) split out to rustyweb-scale-footprint-qw5.11.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Part 1 DONE — merged to main in #63 (commit bb97039): rustyweb optimize subcommand + SearchIndex::optimize (smallest-first bounded batches, --max-segments N=8, before→after report) + SearchIndex::segment_count() health signal; tests (merge-to-target/search-preserved, no-op-when-small, no-index error) + DESIGN/README docs.

Part 2 REMAINING (keeps this issue in_progress) — ingest merge-robustness, none of which is in the code yet:
- Preflight free-space check before large ingests, with a clear error.
- Surface background-merge failures loudly (warn→error: 'index not fully merged; free space and run rustyweb optimize') instead of silently accumulating segments.
- Throttle segment creation (fewer, larger commits) so streaming many WACZs doesn't create thousands of tiny segments in the first place.

Relates to qw5.6 (merges/RAM at scale) and 7x3j (atomic reindex build-into-temp-and-swap).

title: Search enrichment inspired by SolrWayback / warc-indexer
description:
Index more per-record and HTML signals as queryable fields to improve archive search, inspired by SolrWayback and the British Library warc-indexer (which runs Tika/DROID and derives a large Solr schema). rustyweb adopts only lightweight, pure-Rust pieces that fit the single-binary, no-heavy-deps philosophy; full-text search over HTML/PDF/rendered-text stays the core and is unaffected.

Each new field is a schema addition, so it requires a rebuild via rustyweb reindex (the schema guard already errors and points there). Extraction lives in extract_html_text / collect_page_records; schema in build_schema; query wiring in SearchIndex::search.

In scope (child tasks):
- meta keywords + author (HTML metadata)
- content-based language detection fallback (whatlang)
- registrable-domain (public suffix) for a site: filter spanning subdomains
- outbound link host/domain fields (link-based discovery / future link graph)
- last-modified date facet

Deferred / out of scope for now (keep it minimal): image enrichment (dimensions, EXIF geo, perceptual/PDQ image search), entity/geo extraction (locations, postcodes), fuzzy near-duplicate hashing (ssdeep), elements-used analytics, and Tika-style text extraction from arbitrary binary formats (needs a heavy extractor). Open question also deferred: whether to index non-text resources (images/js/css) as stub docs to power a real media-type facet.

Refs: https://github.com/netarchivesuite/solrwayback and warc-indexer SolrFields.java in https://github.com/ukwa/webarchive-discovery
notes: Its new fields (registrable-domain site:, keywords/author, outbound links) feed the facets in rustyweb-faceted-discovery-4js (faceted discovery epic).
close_reason: done

title: Index HTML meta keywords and author
description: Extract meta keywords (meta[name=keywords]) and author (meta[name=author], with og/article fallbacks) during HTML extraction and index them. Add keywords (TEXT, searchable via the default query fields) and author (TEXT, searchable and usable as author:name) to the schema; populate via HtmlText and the Page struct, mirroring the existing description/headings work. Mirrors warc-indexer keywords/author. Low effort. Requires reindex.
close_reason: done

title: Content-based language detection fallback
description: When a page has no html lang attribute, detect the language from the extracted body text with a lightweight pure-Rust detector (whatlang) and store its primary subtag in the existing lang field. Keep the html lang attribute as the primary source; only fall back when it is absent or empty. Improves coverage of the lang: filter. Mirrors warc-indexer content_language (which uses Tika). Adds the whatlang dependency (small). Requires reindex.
close_reason: done

title: Registrable-domain field for a cross-subdomain site: filter
description: Add a registrable-domain field (the private domain: one label above the public suffix, via the public suffix list / psl crate) so a site: filter matches a whole site across subdomains and handles multi-level suffixes like example.co.uk. Today domain holds the raw host (www.example.com), so subdomains and the bare domain do not unify. Keep domain (host) for exact host filtering and add site (registrable domain) for cross-subdomain filtering; both derived from the page URL. Mirrors the warc-indexer host / domain / public_suffix split. Adds the psl dependency (bundled public suffix list) - confirm it fits the single-binary goal. Highest search-quality win for archives with many subdomains. Requires reindex.
close_reason: done

title: Index outbound link hosts and domains
description: Extract outbound hyperlink targets (a[href], resolved against the page URL) and index their hosts and domains as multi-valued fields (links_hosts, links_domains), enabling queries like links_hosts:youtube.com (pages that link to a host) and a future link-graph view. Mirrors warc-indexer links_hosts / links_domains / links_images. Extraction is easy with scraper; note the index-size cost of storing link targets. Decide whether to also capture links_images. Requires reindex.
close_reason: Moved to standalone task rustyweb-outbound-links-ind (deferred)

title: Last-Modified date facet
description: Capture the HTTP Last-Modified response header (response records already parse http_headers) as a second date signal: store last_modified and/or last_modified_year for filtering, complementing crawl year. Mirrors warc-indexer last_modified / last_modified_year. Small; helps distinguish when content was authored vs when it was crawled. Requires reindex.
close_reason: done

title: Index HTTP status_code for capture-level status filtering
description: Index the HTTP status_code (and optionally expose per-capture status/mime/digest) so results can be filtered, e.g. status:200 vs redirects/errors. Moved from the provenance epic (was rustyweb-provenance-imd.6); it is a search/filter feature rather than provenance.
