title: Optional golden search integration test (full-featured WACZ)
description:
Add an OPTIONAL, opt-in integration test that indexes a known full-featured WACZ and asserts search results look correct end to end -- a "golden" search test.

Motivation: the committed fixtures (a.wacz, simple.wacz, pdf-doc.wacz) are small, so they don't exercise search the way real content does -- diverse sites/dates/languages/types for faceting, phrase search over real prose, ranking across many docs, PDFs + Browsertrix rendered urn:text together. This would catch regressions that small fixtures miss (e.g. the phrase-search behavior the maintainer found confusing) and guard the search feature as indexing internals change (parallel fetch, setup consolidation, etc.).

Optional / opt-in because a full-featured WACZ is large and not a good committed fixture in the default test run:
- Gate with #[ignore] (run via `cargo test -- --ignored`) and/or an env var pointing at the WACZ (e.g. RUSTYWEB_SEARCH_WACZ=path-or-url), skipping cleanly when unset so normal CI stays fast.
- Source options to decide: a curated medium fixture committed via git-lfs; a stable public WACZ URL (streamed); or a local path supplied by the developer.

Assertions to cover (the "looks correct" part):
- Representative queries return the expected top page(s) with the right fields (title/url/collection).
- Phrase search: a quoted phrase matches the page containing that exact adjacent phrase and excludes near-misses (the per-field, OR-across-fields semantics).
- Filters: site:, domain:, type:, lang:, status:, year: (and ranges) narrow as expected.
- Facet counts for the main dimensions match known values for the corpus.
- Ranking sanity (title match outranks body match), snippets present, PDF text and rendered urn:text both searchable.

Relates to the search feature generally and the phrase-search question raised during the r0n.7 work.

title: Searchable page metadata: domain, URL tokens, title boost, AND-by-default + in-app search help
description:
Improve full-text search relevance and expressiveness, and document the query syntax in the app.

Current state: QueryParser has default fields [title, body] only; url/timestamp are STRING (exact-match only) so domain/URL search does not usefully work; multi-word queries are OR by default; no in-app help.

Scope (this slice):
- Schema: add 'domain' (STRING|STORED, exact host for domain: filter + display) and 'url_tokens' (TEXT, tokenized URL words) to the Tantivy schema.
- Extraction: derive host + tokenized URL text from each page URL (url crate).
- Query: default fields become [title, body, url_tokens]; set_conjunction_by_default() (AND); boost title over body; use lenient parsing so malformed queries do not 500.
- Docs: in-app 'Search tips' disclosure on homepage + results page documenting the real working syntax (phrases, field search title:/domain:, +/-, OR, grouping, boost).
- Update DESIGN.md schema table + README search note.
- Tests for domain extraction, url tokens, domain: filtering, AND semantics.

Note: adding schema fields requires re-indexing existing collections (idempotent upsert).

Deferred follow-ups: crawl-date as DATE/numeric range field, meta_description/OpenGraph, headings, lang/mime filters.
close_reason: Implemented: domain + url_tokens fields, AND-by-default, title boost, lenient parsing, in-app Search tips, DESIGN/README updates. Tests green.

title: search-url panics on remote (non-file) sources (unwrap on Source::resolve None)
description: run_search_url (main.rs ~1804) calls col.source.resolve(home).unwrap(), but Source::resolve() returns None for remote sources (Url / Browsertrix / BrowsertrixPublic), so 'indice search-url <URL>' panics when the manifest has any remote-source crawl. Should skip remote sources (they have no local CDX to scan) or handle None gracefully, like the neighboring code already does for the not-found case. Found while verifying index integrity after the optimize orphan-sweep work.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #91 (merged): search-url now skips all remote sources via Source::is_remote() and handles a None path instead of unwrapping.

title: Collection storage model: mandatory collections, curator/derived split, filesystem layout
description:
Rework the on-disk model around a clean split by OWNER: one curator-edited source of truth (git-committable Markdown) and one derived cache rebuilt from the WACZs (never hand-edited). Decided with the maintainer:

- Mandatory collections; retire singletons. A crawl is always in a curated collection. Import (Browsertrix/Archive-It) supplies it automatically; hand-index REQUIRES --collection (deliberate friction, per Maemura -- ask 'what is this a part of?' at ingest). No more collection-of-one whose id == the WACZ id.
- Curatorial dir: collections/<slug>/README.md (per-collection subdirectory; README so the dir name identifies it). Holds the finding aid + committable pinned assets.
- Derived cache: index/{waczs.json, full_text/, thumbs/} stays git-ignored and rebuildable; waczs.json is demoted to a pure per-file cache (loses membership; never hand-edited).
- Archive layout mirrors the model: archive/<collection-slug>/<wacz> for local WACZs, archive/<collection-slug>/<item-id>/ for imports. MEMBERSHIP IS THE FOLDER (a WACZ under archive/sucho/ is in 'sucho'), so browsing the filesystem is self-describing.
- Thumbnails: curator-pinned crawl thumbnails become committable in collections/<slug>/; auto-selected thumbnails stay in index/thumbs/. Add a collection-level representative thumbnail too.
- Nesting stays DEFERRED (flat single-level) but the slug scheme + on-disk form must keep an optional parent addable later without migration.

Pre-release, so migration is minimal. Supersedes/rewrites the storage layer of the finding-aid work (PR #56, rustyweb-findingaid-aoc3); #56 is parked and reconciled onto this model afterward. Full design recorded in DESIGN 'Two-level collection model' + the session discussion.
close_reason: done

title: Mandatory collections; retire the singleton fallback
description: index requires --collection when hand-indexing (clear error/guidance if omitted; a glob into one collection is the intended 'decide once' UX); import supplies the collection automatically. Remove singleton creation (index_one's 'None => (id, name)' branch) and singleton reading/migration in Manifest::open. Homepage no longer shows a card per loose crawl. Decide handling of any existing singleton homes (pre-release: minimal).
close_reason: done

title: Archive layout archive/<collection-slug>/ + membership-by-folder
description: Local WACZs stored at <home>/archive/<collection-slug>/<wacz>; imports at <home>/archive/<collection-slug>/<item-id>/. A WACZ's collection membership is DERIVED from its parent folder rather than stored per-entry. Update Source/for_file path handling, index placement, the importer's download target, and portability (relative-to-home). waczs.json loses its 'collection' field as authoritative.

title: Update DESIGN + README/CLI docs for the new model
description: Revise the DESIGN filesystem-layout + Collection Management + Two-level-model sections for: mandatory collections, curatorial-vs-derived split, collections/<slug>/README.md, archive/<slug>/ + membership-by-folder, waczs.json-as-cache, thumbnails (pinned + collection-level). Update README and CLI --help/reference. DESIGN is the architecture of record.

description:
Several crates/indice-lib/src files have grown large enough to be hard to read

title: Show HTTP status on search results; evaluate faceting by status
description:
Idea (maintainer): surface HTTP response status on the search results page, and assess whether faceting by status is worthwhile.

Current state (already partly there):
- HTTP status IS indexed: FIELD_STATUS ("status"), INDEXED | STORED, populated from page.status (WARC http_status).
- It IS queryable: status:200 and range syntax status:[200 TO 299] (shown in the search tips).
- It IS an EXTRA_FILTER (a filterable field, labelled "Status") -- so it can be filtered, but it is NOT one of the primary sidebar FACET_DIMENSIONS (collection, site, date, type, language), and it is NOT displayed on individual result cards.

Part 1 -- show status on results (cheap, worthwhile): add the status code to each result card. Most indexed pages are 200, so the real value is flagging the exceptions (archived 404 / 500 / error pages, or non-200 captures), e.g. a small badge shown prominently only for non-200 and subtle/omitted for 200.

Part 2 -- is faceting worthwhile? (measure first): page documents are overwhelmingly 200 -- we index HTML/PDF response records that became pages; redirects and no-body records generally aren't page docs -- so a full status facet likely has low diversity and limited value for a scarce sidebar slot. Options:
- Leave as-is (queryable via status: + the existing EXTRA_FILTER).
- Add a lightweight "non-200 only" filter/toggle -- probably the highest-value slice (find archived error pages).
- Promote status to FACET_DIMENSIONS only if a real index shows meaningful spread. Measure the actual status distribution before committing a facet.

Caveat: soft-404s (HTTP 200 with "not found" content) won't be caught by status alone -- status is not a content-correctness signal.

Relates to the faceted-discovery work and the EXTRA_FILTERS mechanism.
close_reason:
Done (working tree, 2026-07-26).

Part 1 (show status on results): SearchResult now carries status: Option<u16> (read from FIELD_STATUS via a new get_u64), surfaced on each result card as a red 'HTTP <code>' badge with a reason-phrase tooltip (http_status_label) shown ONLY for non-200 — 200 stays unmarked (the value is flagging archived 404/500/etc.). Also added to the /api/search JSON. Unit test search_results_carry_http_status covers 200/404/None.

Part 2 (evaluate faceting): measured — page docs are 200 or unrecorded (no non-200 in the sample index); low diversity, so status is NOT promoted to a sidebar FACET_DIMENSION. It stays queryable via the existing EXTRA_FILTER (status:200, status:[300 TO 599]). Decision: leave faceting as-is; the non-200 badge is the high-value slice.

fmt/clippy clean; full suite green (162 lib + 48 integration + 6 collection-replay).

title: Streaming index: HTTP agent has no timeouts, so one slow record stalls the fetch tail
description:
Symptom (seen live on a Browsertrix remote index): the record-fetch progress bar
sits at N-1/N (e.g. 13783/13784) for many minutes at 0/s with a nonsense ETA
("eta 6d"), then eventually completes and moves on to "building index". Not a
true hang — it finishes.

Root cause: http_agent() in crates/indice-lib/src/http_range.rs builds the ureq
agent with NO timeouts. The CDX-guided fetch loop (index.rs ~2318) fans out with
rayon (default remote concurrency 4); each record does fetch.fetch() ->
with_retry(range GET) -> resp.into_body().read_to_end(). with_retry (5 attempts,
exp backoff) only retries when a request ERRORS (connect error or a mid-stream
read error -> Attempt::Retry). A connection that is merely SLOW/STALLED — sends
headers then dribbles/hangs the body — never errors, so read_to_end blocks with
no idle/read timeout. Near the end there are <=concurrency records left, so one
slow record holds the determinate bar at N-1 until the server delivers. The
"eta 6d" is the rate->0 extrapolation.

Note: what the user sees here is the FETCH tail, not the index write (that is a
separate phase labeled "building index", index.rs:2376). The earlier work fixed
the 100%-tail *display* (switch to a spinner for the local-file merge) and added
retry for *failing* requests, but neither covers a slow-but-not-failing remote
record.

Fix: set timeouts on the ureq 3.4 agent (config_builder) so a stalled read trips
an error that with_retry can retry a fresh range GET for, bounding the tail:
- timeout_connect (~15-30s)
- timeout_recv_response (~30s)
- timeout_recv_body (generous, ~60-120s) — per-record WARC bodies are small, but
  keep headroom for large PDFs; do NOT set an aggressive global timeout that
  could kill a legitimately large-but-flowing body.
Consider also: clamp/hide the ETA when rate hits 0 (cosmetic), and maybe a debug
log when a record fetch exceeds N seconds. Verify the thumbnail fetch + range
probe still work with the new timeouts. Own PR off main.

title: Fixity/integrity model for streamed (not fully downloaded) WACZs
description:
Split out of the (now essentially complete) streaming-index epic rustyweb-streaming-index-r0n as standalone follow-up work.

Whole-file SHA-256 fixity (stored in the manifest, checked by `verify`) can't be computed when we never read the whole WACZ. Decide and implement the integrity model for streamed sources: prefer per-record WARC-Payload-Digest values (present in the CDX) and/or the WACZ datapackage-digest, or explicitly record 'no whole-file fixity' for streamed WACZs. Update `verify` and the manifest accordingly, and make sure a WACZ indexed by streaming vs by download is still verifiable in some meaningful way. Decision task first, then implementation.

Current state (from the streaming work): verify ALREADY skips remote (URL) sources ('REMOTE - skipped, not re-fetched'), so streaming doesn't regress it. The streaming path does the minimal handling: a streamed entry stores empty sha256 + file_size from HTTP Content-Length. THIS issue is the RICHER model: record & check the WACZ's own per-resource integrity from datapackage.json / datapackage-digest.json (already read for metadata) so streamed WACZs are verifiable without re-download; update verify to report/check it.

Relates to the authenticity epic (rustyweb-authenticity-671, WACZ signatures).

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: 2026-10-03: this gets sharper under rustyweb-demo-instance-5b9k.2. Once ingest offloads WACZ bytes to a bucket, a Source::Url crawl has a NON-EMPTY recorded sha256 (it was hashed locally before upload), but run_verify (main.rs:1924) still skips every Source::Url as 'not re-fetched'. So those crawls will look verified and never be checked - worse than today, where a streamed remote has an empty fixity() and is honestly reported as unverifiable. Minimum fix in 5b9k.2: branch on !col.sha256.is_empty() and report REMOTE (sha recorded, not re-hashed).

title: Streaming / CDX-guided indexing (index WACZs without full download)
description:
Index WACZ content selectively via the WACZ's internal CDX instead of downloading the whole WACZ and parsing every WARC record.

Today (index_one -> download_to_temp): a remote WACZ is fully downloaded to a temp file, opened as a ZIP, and every archive/*.warc.gz record is decompressed and inspected. The CDX index inside the WACZ (indexes/index.cdx.gz) already lists, per capture, the mime, WARC filename, offset, and length — and rustyweb already parses these (wacz.rs search_cdx / CdxjRecord). So we can identify just the html/text/pdf (and Browsertrix urn:text) records and seek to them: the CDX offset/length is into the named WARC, and that WARC is a stored (uncompressed) ZIP entry in the WACZ, so absolute range = zip_data_start(filename) + offset .. +length; the slice is one gzip member -> one WARC record.

For remote WACZs this is done with HTTP range requests, exactly like the wabac.js replay client. Make streaming vs full-download an OPT-IN choice; keep download-to-temp as the default/fallback.

Wins: avoid full remote download (bandwidth, transient disk / the TMPDIR problem) — big for media-heavy crawls where text is a small fraction of bytes; skip decompressing/parsing media records even locally (CPU). Costs: many small range requests are round-trip-latency-bound and can be SLOWER than one big GET for text-heavy remotes (coalescing adjacent records helps only when text clusters); more code (HTTP-range ZIP reading, per-record gzip seeking).

Two gotchas to decide up front: (1) whole-file SHA-256 fixity can't be computed without reading the whole file, so streamed sources need a different integrity model (per-record WARC-Payload-Digest from the CDX, or the datapackage-digest); (2) the cross-WARC per-URL merge (rendered urn:text often lives in a different WARC than the HTML) and PDF handling must be preserved by the CDX-guided selector.

Relates to the scale epic (rustyweb-scale-footprint-qw5) and reindex resilience (rustyweb-reindex-resilient-aev). Measure-first: benchmark before committing to defaults.
design:
Feasibility validated (2026-07) against a real Browsertrix WACZ:
- WARCs are Stored (uncompressed) inside the WACZ ZIP, so a CDX record's byte offset maps to an absolute WACZ position: abs = zip_data_start(entry) + cdx.offset, read cdx.length bytes = one gzip member = one WARC record. Proven end-to-end (offset -> gzip magic -> WARC/1.1 with matching WARC-Target-URI).
- The zip crate (2.4.2) exposes ZipFile::data_start() and ZipArchive<R: Read + Seek>, so it parses the central directory for us over ANY Read+Seek source.
- Gotcha: the CDX `filename` is the bare WARC name (rec-*.warc.gz); the ZIP entry is under archive/ — map by suffix.

Design: ONE CDX-guided extractor over a pluggable Read+Seek reader.
- Local source -> std::fs::File (Phase 1, .1).
- Remote source -> an HttpRangeReader (Read+Seek over ureq range GETs; total size from the first range's Content-Range; read-ahead buffer; coalesce adjacent wanted records) handed to ZipArchive (Phase 2, .2).
- Extractor: read all CDX records, select by mime (html/pdf + Browsertrix urn:text), seek to abs offset, gunzip the slice, parse the single WARC record, feed the existing merge/index pipeline. Reuses CDX parsing, WARC record parsing, HTML/PDF extraction, and the merge.

DEFAULT MODEL (decided with maintainer): a remote WACZ stays remote for both indexing and replay.
- Remote default = STREAM index (range) + replay from the URL (already the case). Nothing colocated.
- `--download` is the opt-in: colocate into <home>/archive (durable copy, faster bulk indexing, whole-file fixity, offline replay). Unifies with the Browsertrix always-download flow.
- Local WACZ unchanged.

Consequences: (1) fixity — streamed remotes have no whole-file SHA-256; v1 marks them "not locally verifiable" (verify reports that, not MODIFIED), per-record WARC-Payload-Digest is a later option; --download keeps full fixity. (2) robustness/perf — many small range requests can be slower and are exposed to flaky hosts; --download is the robust escape hatch. (3) streaming trusts the CDX to enumerate records (authoritative for Browsertrix).
close_reason: Feature complete: all core children (Phase 1/2 extraction, HTTP range reader, opt-in stream/download, parallel fetch, docs) shipped. Remaining follow-ups split into standalone issues: rustyweb-streamed-wacz-fixity-zle5 (fixity model) and rustyweb-streaming-setup-consolidate-850t (setup perf). Benchmark (.5) closed as optional.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Follow-up optimization spotted while using r0n.7 (parallel record fetch): now that the per-record fetch is concurrent, the serial "reading index" SETUP phase dominates for multi-GB remote WACZs.

The setup iterates all ZIP entries ~4 times, each a serial by_index pass that reads scattered local headers over the network:
1. remote_warcs_streamable / local_warcs_streamable (the stream-vs-download pre-check in index_one)
2. ensure_warcs_stored (in collect_page_records_via_cdx)
3. warc_data_starts (in collect)
4. find_warcinfo_streaming's name collection (in collect)

Biggest, safest win: CONSOLIDATE these into a single by_index pass that gathers, per WARC entry, its compression (storedness), data_start, and name, plus the first WARC's warcinfo -- and fold the storedness decision so the separate *_warcs_streamable pre-check isn't a fourth full iteration. No zip-internals reimplementation; should cut the setup roughly 4x.

Further (optional, measure first): parallelize the remaining single pass by fetching local headers concurrently via RangeFetch and computing data_start from the local-header extra-field length. Feasible but reimplements part of the zip local-header parsing, so only if consolidation isn't enough. Also: read the CDX as one large range rather than CHUNK-by-CHUNK.

title: CDX-guided record extraction for local WACZs (Phase 1)
description: Phase 1 (local, no HTTP) — de-risks the parsing/seeking before any networking. Use the WACZ CDX (mime, filename, offset, length; already parsed by wacz.rs) to seek directly to the html/text/pdf and Browsertrix urn:text records in the local WARCs, instead of iterating and decompressing every record. Each CDX offset points into the named WARC; that WARC is a stored ZIP entry, so seek to zip_data_start(filename)+offset and read `length` bytes = one gzip member = one WARC record. Preserve the existing cross-WARC per-URL merge (rendered urn:text may live in a different WARC than the HTML) and PDF handling. Factor the per-record extractor so Phase 2 (HTTP range) can reuse it. Benchmark local index time vs the current scan-everything approach.
close_reason: CDX-guided extractor + --stream opt-in landed; parity (same page count as scan) + deflate-guard tested on fixtures

title: HTTP range reader for remote WACZs (Phase 2)
description: Phase 2 — a reader that fetches WACZ bytes over HTTP range requests (like wabac.js) so remote WACZs can be indexed without a full download. Needs: read the ZIP end-of-central-directory + central directory (small, at file end) to map each WARC filename to its stored data offset; then for each wanted CDX record, range-fetch zip_data_start(filename)+offset .. +length and gunzip the single member. Coalesce adjacent wanted records into fewer, larger range GETs to cut request count. Reuse the Phase 1 per-record extractor. Requires the host to support range requests (already required for replay). Reuse ureq (already used for downloads and range serving).
close_reason: HttpRangeReader landed; verified streaming a real 323MB remote WACZ over range requests (8 pages, same as download+scan, ~3s, no download)

title: Opt-in stream vs download mode for index
description: Let the user choose streaming vs full download per index run, e.g. index --stream / --download (default download-to-temp, which stays the fallback). Consider auto-selecting stream for remote sources once it is proven. Wire the choice into index_one so it picks the CDX-guided range reader (Phase 2) or the current download path. Keep behavior identical for local files unless streaming is requested. Document that streaming trades bandwidth/disk for more requests (can be slower for text-heavy remotes).
notes: Reframed: remote WACZs STREAM by default; --download is the opt-in to colocate into archive (durable, faster bulk, whole-file fixity, offline replay). Local unchanged.
close_reason: remote streams by default; --download colocates into archive; range/deflate fallback to download. Verified on a 323MB remote WACZ.

description: Whole-file SHA-256 fixity (stored in the manifest, checked by `verify`) can't be computed when we never read the whole WACZ. Update `verify` and the manifest accordingly, and make sure a WACZ indexed by streaming vs by download is still verifiable in some meaningful way. Decision task first, then implementation.

This .4 is the RICHER model: record & check the WACZ's own per-resource integrity from datapackage.json / datapackage-digest.json (already read for metadata) so streamed WACZs are verifiable without re-download; update verify to report/check it.

title: Benchmark streaming vs download; when-to-stream heuristic
description: Benchmark streaming vs full-download across the two axes that matter: media-heavy vs text-heavy WACZs, and remote vs local. Report bytes transferred, request count, and wall-clock. From the CDX we can cheaply compute the wanted-record byte fraction (sum of html/text/pdf lengths / total) — use it to document (and maybe auto-pick) when streaming wins. Deliver a short guidance note and, if warranted, a heuristic default for --stream on remote sources. Measure-first input for the opt-in mode's defaults.
close_reason: Optional measure-first tuning; not needed for the shipped streaming feature. Closing per maintainer.

title: Docs: streaming vs download modes and trade-offs
description: Document the two indexing modes (download vs stream), the trade-off (bandwidth/disk vs request count/latency; media-heavy vs text-heavy), the fixity consequence for streamed sources, and the TMPDIR/temp-space behavior of the download path. Update README (Remote WACZ files section) and DESIGN.md (Indexing Pipeline).

title: Parallel CDX-guided record fetch (concurrent range requests)
description:
Streaming a remote WACZ currently fetches page records serially through a single Read+Seek HttpRangeReader cursor: fetch one record's range, block on the full round trip, gunzip+extract, then fetch the next. Measured on a 24.7 GB SUCHO WACZ (S3 eu-central-1, from the US) this runs at ~2 pages/sec.

Diagnosis: this is I/O bound but LATENCY-bound, not bandwidth-bound. Each page record is a separate small HTTP range GET (a single gzipped WARC record, tens of KB); the payloads are tiny and the downlink sits mostly idle while we wait ~100-150ms per transatlantic round trip. Throughput ~= 1/latency, not bytes/bandwidth. That is precisely the regime where concurrency helps: N requests in flight ~= N x throughput until another resource saturates.

Why it is a clean fit here: the CDX already gives (offset, length) for every wanted record up front, so the per-record fetches are INDEPENDENT - they do not need the shared Read+Seek cursor at all. Read the zip central directory + WARC data-starts once serially (cheap), then fan out the thousands of record fetches. rustyweb already uses rayon for the local scan path (index_wacz), so mirror that: parallel fetch + gunzip + record_to_raw into RawRecords, then feed the existing (serial) merge/index step behind the tantivy writer mutex.

Sketch: in collect_page_records_via_cdx, after computing the wanted CDX entries + starts, replace the serial for-loop with a bounded-concurrency parallel map issuing independent range GETs. Options: rayon par_iter with a shared ureq::Agent (Send+Sync, pools connections) doing HttpFetch::fetch(start, len) per record; or an async pool (reqwest) if we want finer control. Keep progress reporting (IndexProgress.set_records) thread-safe (atomic counter). Preserve ordering-independence: the merge is by URL so fetch order does not matter.

Expected win: ~5-15x wall-clock for latency-bound remotes (e.g. ~2/sec -> tens/sec). Ceiling shifts to (a) downlink bandwidth (page records are a small slice of the 24 GB; media we skip is the bulk, so this bites late), (b) CPU for gunzip + HTML text extraction + PDF extraction + tantivy indexing (the real ceiling at high concurrency; also parallelizable), or (c) S3 throttling (unlikely at sane concurrency, e.g. 16-32 in flight).

Caveats / testing surface: pick a sane default concurrency (config or fixed ~16-32) and consider a flag; be gentle to flaky hosts (--download stays the robust escape hatch); ensure errors on one record do not abort the whole run (already warn-and-skip); keep the tail-cache path correct if any shared reader remains for the central-dir/data-starts phase; add a test asserting parity of indexed pages between serial and parallel paths. Coalescing adjacent records (when text clusters in the WARC) is a possible complementary optimization but orthogonal.

Not part of the tail-cache + progress-bar PR (that PR keeps the serial fetch). This is a follow-up behavior change with its own testing surface.
close_reason: Delivered in PR #33: concurrent CDX-guided record fetch over RangeFetch (HttpFetch/FileFetch) on a dedicated pool with --concurrency (default 4 remote / CPU count local); scan-vs-CDX parity test runs through the parallel path.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: Code review (PR #7) surfaced a related redundancy to fold in here: the CDX-guided read path makes several separate passes over the ZIP central directory/entries — the *_warcs_streamable pre-check calls warcs_stored, then collect_page_records_via_cdx calls ensure_warcs_stored + warc_data_starts + find_warcinfo_streaming, each iterating all entries via by_index (a range fetch per entry for remote). The tail-cache absorbs most of the cost today, so it's not urgent on its own.

title: Deduplicate the config-load and writer-open sequence between index_location and reindex
description:
Deferred from PR #132 (rustyweb-ingest-params-mqls), where it was the plan's
commit 6. Filed so the remaining win is not lost with the type that was
supposed to carry it.

`Ingest::index_location` and `Ingest::reindex` each open the write state with
the same four steps in the same order:

    Config::load(home)
    SearchIndex::open_with_heap(dir, config.writer_heap_bytes())
    set_stored_body_cap(config.stored_body_cap_bytes())
    Mutex::new(..)

Two copies means `writer_heap_bytes` and `stored_body_cap_bytes` can drift:
a new knob added to one path and not the other is silent, and only shows up as
a reindex that behaves differently from the ingest that preceded it.

The plan's answer was a `Run<'a>` type (the open manifest + writer as a
receiver, with `open(cx)` and `rebuilding(cx, new_dir)` constructors, since the
two layouts genuinely differ: an ingest writes `index/full_text`, a rebuild
writes the sibling `full_text.new` and swaps it). It was dropped from #132
because its *main* justification had evaporated — it was to be the single
place PR 2 could demand a lock witness, and the locking design
(rustyweb-durable-writes-f4h5) concluded the lock attaches to the resource
instead. What is left is a refactor of the riskiest part of the pipeline for
its own sake, which did not belong in a PR whose safety rested on changing no
behaviour.

Second win, and the reason this is worth doing rather than closing: `reindex`
must load `Config` *before* `reconcile_index_swap` destroys anything, or a
malformed `config.yaml` leaves you with no index at all. That ordering is
enforced by a comment today (`reindex.rs`). Moving `reconcile_index_swap` +
`index_swap_paths` inside `Run::rebuilding` makes it structural.

Test to add with it, the twin of `tests/config.rs::index_aborts_on_a_malformed_config`:
a malformed `config.yaml` makes `reindex` error *and* leaves `index/full_text`
still searchable.

Worth noting for whoever picks this up: it is no longer blocked by anything,
and it is a prerequisite for nothing. Pure consolidation.

title: Theming: let operators customize the app's look (colors, wordmark, branding)
description:
Let a deployer restyle indice for their institution — accent colors, neutrals, the wordmark/instance name, maybe a logo — without forking the CSS.

FOUNDATION ALREADY IN PLACE (from the management-UI design refresh): app.css is a single token system built on CSS custom properties — ~12 :root variables drive the whole look (--ink, --muted, --line, --paper, --blue/--blue-dk reading-room accent, --clay/--clay-dk/--clay-tint workroom accent, --radius, etc.), and the two modes are just an --accent swap via .mode-manage. So a theme is largely 'override these tokens'; the hard part (tokenizing) is done.

MECHANISM OPTIONS to weigh:
- (a) Simplest: serve an optional operator-supplied stylesheet appended AFTER app.css (e.g. <home>/theme.css, or assets/custom.css), so it can override any token or rule. Zero config schema; full power; must be self-hosted (keeps the offline/no-CDN ethos).
- (b) Config-driven: a small theme.toml (or [theme] in a config file) mapping named tokens -> values, injected as a :root override <style> in layout(). Safer/curated surface; less powerful than raw CSS.
- (c) A few built-in presets (e.g. 'classic blue', 'slate', high-contrast) selectable by flag.
- Branding beyond color: swap the 'indice' wordmark for an instance name / logo (already partly relevant — the homepage h1 and title). Consider an --instance-name / --logo option.

CONSTRAINTS: keep it self-contained and offline (themes ship as local CSS/assets, no external fonts/CDN — same reason the app uses the system font stack). Accessibility: whatever the mechanism, keep the contrast/focus floor (don't let a theme break keyboard focus or contrast). Don't let a themed accent collide with the semantic error red.

Not urgent; parked for when there's demand. The token refactor means this is much cheaper than it would have been.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: Maintainer framing (2026-08-29): operator theming is important; a good way to showcase it is to ship a few different built-in themes (the token system makes this cheap). Concrete deliverable split out as a child: 'Ship a few showcase themes'. Priority still P3 unless bumped.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: 2026-10-03: rustyweb-demo-instance-5b9k.5 adds the first site: section to <home>/config.yaml (name, tagline, Markdown banner, request_access text) and folds layout()'s positional args into a Chrome struct. That is the same config seam an operator-supplied theme.css would hang off - coordinate so the two don't invent different shapes.

title: Ship a few showcase themes (demonstrating operator theming)
description:
Provide a small set of built-in example themes that both demonstrate operator theming (parent rustyweb-theming-5b4x) and give operators ready-made starting points to copy/adapt.

Once the theming mechanism lands (operator-supplied theme.css and/or token config — see 5b4x's options a/b), ship ~3 example themes as local CSS overriding the existing :root custom-property token set, e.g.: the default reading-room blue, a dark/slate theme, and a high-contrast theme. Each is essentially just token overrides (the app.css custom-property system is already in place), shipped self-contained — no external fonts/CDN (offline ethos).

Constraints: keep the contrast + keyboard-focus accessibility floor in every theme, and don't let a themed accent collide with the semantic error red. If the themes are selectable at runtime, wire a picker or flag (5b4x option c); otherwise they serve as documentation-by-example. Doubles as the 'showcase' that makes the theming feature tangible.

title: Pinned thumbnails are written non-atomically, and presence is the pin marker
description:
From the code review of PR #129. thumbnail.rs write_thumbnail still uses std::fs::write, so the commit claim "used by every file that holds state" was an overclaim.

Three of its four callers write DERIVED thumbnails (generated during indexing, rebuilt by reindex), where a truncated file is self-healing. The fourth, set_manual, writes the PINNED committable thumbnail at collections/<slug>/thumbnail.jpg or crawls/<id>.jpg -- and its mere presence is what marks the thumbnail as pinned. So a crash mid-write leaves a crawl rendering as pinned-with-a-broken-image, and re-indexing will not repair it because the pin is still there.

Not fixed in #129 because write_thumbnail(dest, bytes) has no `home` to pass to fsio::ensure_within, and threading one in is exactly the parameter workaround we agreed to stop making mid-PR. It is a small, contained change once the write path is settled: either give write_thumbnail a home, or have set_manual do the atomic write itself (it is the only caller that needs it).

Also worth deciding while there: derived thumbnails under index/thumbs/ arguably do NOT need atomicity or containment, since they are disposable. Being explicit about which of the two kinds a writer is would be clearer than treating them the same.

title: Garbage-collect orphaned crawl thumbnails on reindex
description:
The representative-image thumbnails (rustyweb-crawl-thumbnail-s1ff) are cached at <home>/index/thumbs/<crawl_id>.jpg (+ a <crawl_id>.pinned sidecar for curator-pinned ones). Nothing prunes them: when a crawl is removed from the manifest, or its id changes, its thumbnail + pin marker are left behind as orphaned files. reindex rebuilds the full-text index and regenerates thumbnails but does not sweep the thumbs dir; verify doesn't either.

Add a prune step (e.g. at the end of reindex, or a dedicated maintenance action) that removes thumbs/<id>.(jpg|pinned) for any id no longer present in waczs.json. Careful to key off the manifest ids, and to treat pinned thumbnails the same (a removed crawl's pin is also orphaned). Low priority - it's disk cruft, not a correctness issue. Found during the s1ff code review (finding C2).

title: Triage the 9 remaining CodeQL alerts (js/* + hard-coded-crypto + workflow perms)
description:
With the 28 rust/path-injection alerts dismissed (see
rustyweb-audit-path-injection-alerts-5j4h), 9 open CodeQL alerts remain. These
were NOT audited — do not assume they're noise:

- #37 js/xss (ERROR) and #36 js/client-side-unvalidated-url-redirection (ERROR),
  both crates/indice-lib/static/replay/ui.js:69. ui.js is Webrecorder's vendored
  ReplayWeb.page bundle, so this is likely minified-library noise we inherit
  rather than our code — but two ERROR-severity alerts deserve confirmation, not
  assumption. If it is vendored noise, consider excluding vendored assets from
  the scan rather than dismissing one-by-one (they'd return on every RWP bump).
- #34/#35 js/overly-large-range (warning), ui.js:3601 — same vendored bundle.
- #2,#3,#4 rust/hard-coded-cryptographic-value in browsertrix.rs (624, 641, 652)
  and #5 in archiveit.rs:824. HIGHEST PRIORITY of this set: that rule usually
  fires on a literal key/salt/IV, and these files handle API auth. Check whether
  it's a real embedded secret or a false positive on e.g. a constant header name
  or a test fixture.
- #1 actions/missing-workflow-permissions, .github/workflows/ci.yml:18 — genuine
  and trivial: add an explicit least-privilege `permissions:` block to the
  workflow.

Goal is the same as 5j4h: get the security tab to zero *honestly*, so a future
alert actually means something.
notes:
PROGRESS 2026-09-09 — 5 of 9 resolved, 4 remain (all vendored):

- #1 actions/missing-workflow-permissions — FIXED, not dismissed. ci.yml had no
  permissions block; added `contents: read` (least privilege; it only checks out
  + runs cargo). pages.yml/release.yml already scoped theirs. PR #120.
- #2,#3,#4 browsertrix.rs + #5 archiveit.rs hard-coded-cryptographic-value —
  DISMISSED as "used in tests" (GitHub's first-class reason). Verified all four
  sit inside #[cfg(test)] modules: canned JSON login fixtures and
  Client::with_transport(t, HOST, "user", "pass") driving a FakeTransport. No
  real secrets. My earlier guess that these were the highest-priority of the set
  was wrong — checking beat assuming.

REMAINING — #34, #35 (js/overly-large-range, warning) and #36, #37 (js/xss and
js/client-side-unvalidated-url-redirection, ERROR), all
crates/indice-lib/static/replay/ui.js. Confirmed vendored: header reads
"ui.js is part of ReplayWeb.page ... Copyright (C) 2020-2026, Webrecorder
Software", and it is minified — the flagged line 3601 is 55,303 characters, line
69 is 1,706. The xss/redirect pair is lit-html's unsafeSVG directive, a library
primitive that does unescaped insertion by design; not a defect at its
definition site, and not our code to fix.

Also confirmed the scanner is NOT blind to that directory: our own
static/replay/annotations.js has zero alerts. So any exclusion MUST be
file-scoped (ui.js, sw.js) and never directory-scoped, or we would silence our
own annotation JS — the one file there most worth scanning.

Ed to decide:
(a) exclude vendored files via advanced setup + paths-ignore — durable, survives

title: Upgrade vendored ReplayWeb.page 2.4.6 -> 2.5.3
description:
We vendor ReplayWeb.page via scripts/fetch-replay.sh, pinned at VERSION=2.4.6
(published 2026-04-29). Latest is 2.5.3 (2026-09-03) -- 5 releases and a minor
bump behind: 2.4.7, 2.5.0, 2.5.1, 2.5.2, 2.5.3. The bundled wabac.js goes
2.26.4 -> 2.27.2. This is the engine that does ALL of indice's replay, so being
4.5 months stale is worth closing.

WHY IT'S WORTH DOING -- 2.5.0 has things we specifically want:
- `navigateReplayTo` public method on <replay-app-main>: "allows embeds to
  control replay navigation directly without reloading entire UI". indice
  deep-links by url/ts today; this may be a cleaner mechanism (PR 521).
- "Enables reloading <wr-coll-replay> iframe even if source URL hasn't changed"
  -- possibly relevant to the stale-replay problem behind
  rustyweb-replay-cache-invalidation-vz16 / rustyweb-replay-clear-cache-button-24lm.
- "Allows hiding collection metadata in embed" (PR 529) -- we use
  embed=replayonly, so this may matter for the viewer chrome.
- Fixes: incorrect page count; non-seed pages enabled by default; ndjson parsing
  ignores invalid lines; wabac.js 2.27.x fixes.
- `part`/`exportparts` support for deep component customization -- could let the
  viewer chrome be styled properly instead of worked around.

WHY IT'S RISKY -- test these specifically:
- annotations.js reaches into RWP's *internal* frame structure (shadow-DOM +
  nested same-origin iframe traversal) and listens for `rwp-url-change`. 2.5.0
  "refactors lifecycle events to prevent unnecessary re-renders" and restyles
  components throughout. This is exactly the coupling DESIGN.md warns must be
  re-tested on every RWP upgrade. Verify: the Notes panel still finds the replay
  document, and passage highlighting still anchors.
- Collection (multi-WACZ) replay via /collection/{id}/replay.json.
- Deep links with url+ts (from search results and annotation "Open page").
- The `embed=replayonly` chrome and our banner/toggle layout, given the restyle.

HOW: ./scripts/fetch-replay.sh 2.5.3, bump the VERSION default in the script,
rebuild, then re-test the above in a real browser (headless can't run the RWP
service worker -- see the screenshot recipe in memory). Note the browser tests
in tests/browser*.rs are #[ignore] and need chromedriver.

Also: this will re-mint the 4 dismissed js/* CodeQL alerts on ui.js under new
fingerprints (dismissed 2026-09-09 as "won't fix"). Expect to re-dismiss, or do
rustyweb-triage-remaining-codeql-ggit's paths-ignore option first so it stops
recurring.

title: Slim the README + build a small illustrated user manual (docs site)
description:
The README has grown large and mixes overview, quickstart, deep internals, CLI reference, and deploy details. Slim it to an inviting overview + quickstart + links, and move the detailed material into a dedicated, better-organized user manual with screenshots (the UI is now worth showing).

WHAT THE README KEEPS: what indice is + the 'range' pitch, install, a 60-second quickstart (index a WACZ, serve, search), and links into the manual. Everything deep moves out.

WHAT MOVES TO THE MANUAL (proposed sections):
- Getting started / install
- Adding content: index (local + remote/streaming), collections & finding aids (DACS/EAD fields), reindex/optimize/verify
- Searching: the query language + facets/filters (with screenshots of the results page, timeline, facet sidebar)
- Management mode: local (loopback) + service (forward-auth behind a proxy), with the deploy checklist + example proxy config; screenshots of the workroom (add-archive, edit collection, accession desk)
- Importing from Browsertrix / Archive-It (once those UIs land)
- Replay & how WACZ-direct replay works
- Full CLI reference
- Architecture / design (link or fold in DESIGN.md)

SCREENSHOTS: reading room homepage, a collection finding-aid page, search results, the workroom (clay) with edit-in-place, the accession desk, replay. Worth a small convention for capturing/refreshing them as the UI evolves.

TOOLING (decide when we start):
- GitBook (user's idea): hosted, nice editing/search, easy image handling — but SaaS/hosted, content lives off-repo unless synced.
- mdBook: Rust-native, static site, content is Markdown versioned IN the repo, offline-friendly — fits indice's self-contained ethos and could publish to GitHub Pages. Strong default candidate.
- Others: MkDocs Material, Docusaurus/Astro Starlight (heavier, JS).
Consideration: indice's whole ethos is self-contained/offline, so a static, in-repo generator (mdBook) aligns better than a hosted SaaS; but GitBook may be faster to author and prettier. Weigh authoring speed vs. in-repo/offline/versioned docs.

Not urgent; a good milestone once the management UI + Browsertrix import have settled (so screenshots don't churn).

title: indice users list / migrate (cosmetic identity normalization)
description:
Follow-up to the SubjectId work. Correctness never depends on this: SubjectId::matches canonicalizes the STORED key at comparison time, so legacy annotation records keep working untouched forever. This is purely cosmetic tidying plus a users.yaml starting point.

- `indice users list` -- every distinct author found across all annotations.jsonl, its resolved display name, and whether that name comes from users.yaml or is derived.
- `indice users migrate [--dry-run]` -- canonicalize creator.id, set creator.name from the roster (else derived), rewrite via the existing write_atomic, and index_annotation_upsert each changed record so searchs author field follows without a full reindex. If users.yaml is absent, write a STUB listing each subject found with its derived name and its pre-migration id as an alias, so the curators next step is just editing names.
- Must be idempotent: assert by running twice and comparing bytes.

Depends on users.yaml existing (rustyweb-authz-roles-odc6).

title: Introduce validated CollectionId / CrawlId newtypes
description:
Today, "is this id safe to put in a filesystem path?" is answered by five
separate hand-rolled character checks with THREE different rule sets:

  server/assets.rs:210     alnum                 crawl id (thumb_handler)
  server/assets.rs:247     alnum + '-'           collection slug (collection_thumb_handler)
  annotations.rs:322       alnum + '-'           ensure_safe_collection
  collections.rs:972       alnum (constructor)   slugify
  index/paths.rs:58        alnum + . _ -         safe_component (filename, different job)

Each is correct today, but safety depends on every future handler remembering
to validate AND picking the right variant. That's how this eventually breaks --
not in reviewed code, but in the next handler someone adds.

Fix: "parse, don't validate" -- a newtype with a private field so it can only be
built through one allowlist:

    pub struct CollectionId(String);
    impl CollectionId {
        pub fn parse(s: &str) -> Option<Self>;   // the single source of truth
        pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str;
    }

Then change the path builders to demand it:
    collection_dir(home: &Path, id: &CollectionId)      // was &str
    collection_thumb_path / pinned_thumb_path / crawl_note_path / annotations_path

...and it becomes impossible to COMPILE a collection path built from an
unvalidated string. Consider the same for CrawlId (alnum, hex-ish). With axum,
implement FromRequestParts so the extractor parses it and handlers never see a
raw String.

Payoff: one definition of validity, compiler-enforced at every call site
including future ones; ensure_safe_collection and the ad-hoc handler checks all
collapse into it.

Context: raised by Ed reviewing CodeQL alert #45
(https://github.com/edsu/indice/security/code-scanning/45). The alert itself was
correctly dismissed -- an allowlist is CodeQL's own top-recommended remediation
and the code does exactly that -- but the SCATTERING of that allowlist is a real
structural weakness worth fixing. Relates to
rustyweb-audit-path-injection-alerts-5j4h.
notes:
PARTIALLY DONE in PR #119: CollectionId shipped (newtype with private field; parse/from_name the only constructors; all collection path builders take &CollectionId; Wacz.collection + Collection.id typed; ensure_safe_collection and the two ad-hoc handler allowlists collapsed into it; verified a &str at collection_dir is now E0308).

REMAINING = CrawlId only. server/assets.rs thumb_handler still hand-rolls
 for the crawl id. Real crawl ids are
wacz_id() = 8 lowercase hex chars, so the check is also looser than reality.
Same treatment: a CrawlId newtype with parse()/as_str(), taken by the thumbnail
path builders, so the check lives in one place and is tight. Note index/paths.rs
safe_component is deliberately NOT part of this -- it sanitizes externally-supplied
FILENAMES (Browsertrix/Archive-It names we must accept), a map-don't-reject job,
which is the right strategy there.

See also rustyweb-wacz-collection-option (Option<CollectionId> modeling).

title: WACZ builder: automated headless-Chrome replay test for a built WACZ
description: Follow-up to rustyweb-dlqv. v1 verifies CDX via a non-browser replay-contract + a reference oracle (warcio.js CDXIndexer diff) + manual ReplayWeb.page check. Add an automated assertion to the #[ignore]d headless-Chrome test (crates/indice-lib/tests/browser.rs, needs chromedriver): build a WACZ from a fixture WARC with the new builder, serve it, and assert a known page replays (200 + expected body). Confirms our SURT/CDX matches wabac end-to-end.

title: WACZ builder: headers-only WARC scan to bound memory on large inputs
description: Follow-up to rustyweb-dlqv (found in PR review). build_wacz's scan_warcs uses warc::iter_records, whose collect_records_gz buffers ALL records — including full payloads — into a Vec just to compute CDX offsets. For the large WARCs this feature targets (Archive-It, multi-GB) that's an OOM risk; the builder only needs per-record headers + (offset, length). Add a headers-only streaming pass (don't retain payloads) for CDX generation. This also lets us fold the currently-separate verbatim-copy read into the same pass and hash while copying (removes the double read of each WARC). Mirrors indice's existing scan-path memory behavior, but is avoidable here.

title: WACZ builder: extract HTML <title> for pages/pages.jsonl
description: Follow-up to rustyweb-dlqv. v1 generates pages/pages.jsonl with title = URL. Parse the HTML <title> from each seed page's response record (reuse the scraper the indexer already uses) so seed pages / thumbnails show a real title.

title: WACZ builder: POST fuzzy-match CDX keying (pair request+response, fold body into SURT)
description: Follow-up to rustyweb-dlqv, found during the CDX conformance spike. warcio.js's CDXIndexer pairs a POST request record with its response and folds the request method+body into the CDX key (?__wb_method=post&__wb_post_data=<base64>) plus method/requestBody JSON fields, so wabac can fuzzy-match POST replays. v1 emits a plain GET-style CDX line for such responses (won't POST-replay). Implement warcio's POST handling: read request records, base64/urlencode the body per warcio, rewrite the SURT key + add method/requestBody. Verified against the oracle (a.warc.gz has 2 POST records to cognito-identity.us-east-1.amazonaws.com that currently differ from warcio).

title: WACZ builder: --recompress opt-in to normalize non-per-record-gzip WARC inputs
description: Follow-up to rustyweb-dlqv. Default packaging copies WARC bytes verbatim. A plain uncompressed .warc or a non-standard multi-record-per-member .warc.gz won't CDX-stream (indice falls back to a full scan; wabac replay may degrade). Add an explicit --recompress flag that re-emits records as per-record gzip members so such inputs become CDX-streamable/replayable. Never the default (verbatim preserves original bytes).

title: WACZ builder: cryptographic WACZ signing (datapackage-digest.json signedData)
description: Follow-up to rustyweb-dlqv. v1 emits datapackage-digest.json with {path, hash} but no real signedData. Add optional signing (POST hash+created to an authsign-compatible signing service, like browsertrix-crawler's signingUrl/signingToken) to produce a signed, verifiable WACZ.

title: WACZ builder: ZipNum-clustered gzipped CDX (index.cdx.gz + index.idx) for large indexes
description: Follow-up to rustyweb-dlqv. v1 writes a plain uncompressed indexes/index.cdxj. Match Browsertrix at scale: when the merged CDXJ is >= ~50KB, write ZipNum-clustered indexes/index.cdx.gz (gzip blocks of ~256 lines) + an indexes/index.idx offset map, as browsertrix-crawler's mergeCDXJ/generateCompressed does. indice's reader already reads multi-member gz CDX (wacz.rs cdx_records); this is about the WRITE side + the .idx.

title: Model absent collection membership as Option<CollectionId>
description:
Wacz.collection is a non-optional CollectionId, so "this legacy record has no
collection yet" has to be encoded as a magic value -- currently the
CollectionId::default() sentinel "-unset", healed during Manifest::open.

That sentinel works and is now test-covered, but it is a workaround for a state
the type refuses to represent. It already cost us a HIGH-severity bug: when the
sentinel changed from "" to a non-empty string (commit 8c88843), the migration
guard `if w.collection.is_empty()` silently stopped matching and every crawl in
an oldest-layout archive was orphaned (members_of() == 0), with the next save()
about to make it permanent. Found in /code-review of PR #119, fixed in e0c1108.
A sentinel has exactly that failure mode: correctness depends on everyone
comparing against the *current* magic value.

Proposal (suggested by the reviewer):

    pub collection: Option<CollectionId>,   // None = legacy record, not yet migrated

- "absent" becomes representable, so the migration guard is `is_none()` and can
  never silently stop matching.
- Retires the "-unset" sentinel and its leading-dash trick (chosen so slugify
  could never collide with it -- a constraint that disappears with Option).
- The lenient_collection deserializer collapses into `Option` + a warn for a
  genuinely malformed id.

Cost: Wacz.collection is read in ~60 places, so this is the ripple avoided last
time. Mitigations: most sites can go through an accessor that returns the healed
id (membership is always Some after Manifest::open), so the Option is visible
only in the load/migration path.

While in here, also worth doing:
- Manifest::apply_fields still returns String; it should return CollectionId now
  that one exists (small API wart left behind in #119).
- Broaden the legacy-manifest test matrix. There are three on-disk layouts
  (collections.json-as-WACZ-records, collections.json-as-collections,
  waczs.json + finding-aid dirs) and coverage was thin enough that the HIGH bug
  above slipped through -- the existing legacy test only asserted waczs.len()
  and source, never membership.

title: Portable home directory layout (--home)
description:
Make an archive + its index a single portable folder that can move to another disk, mount point, or machine.

LAYOUT
  <home>/            (default: current directory; --home to override)
  ├── archive/       WACZ files
  └── index/         Tantivy index + collections.json

DESIGN
- One flag --home (default '.') on every subcommand; archive_dir = <home>/archive and index_dir = <home>/index are derived siblings. --home replaces --index-dir as the primary knob (pure --home; overrides can come later if needed).
- Storage: a local WACZ's source is stored RELATIVE to home (e.g. 'archive/docnow.wacz'); that is also what we display. Resolve with home.join(source) to open. Files outside home fall back to an absolute path. Remote http(s) sources still store their URL.
- collection_id derives from the (portable) relative source string, so IDs are stable across moves.
- Downloads (remote URL index, and the coming Browsertrix importer) land in <home>/archive/.
- Back-compat: old manifests with absolute paths still resolve (absolute path used as-is).
- Bonus: 'rustyweb index' with no path indexes everything under <home>/archive/.
- Portability test: index, move the whole home dir, serve/resolve still works.

Reindex is acceptable (single user). Touches CLI (all commands), lib signatures (index/serve/verify/search-url take home and derive/resolve), and collections (relative<->absolute resolution).
close_reason: Portable home-directory layout shipped.

title: Support re-collecting a crawl (crawl set --collection / re-home)
description: Today, re-indexing a WACZ that's already registered into a DIFFERENT collection is refused (place_local_wacz guard) because moving it changes its id (hash of home-relative path) and would orphan its old manifest entry + committed note/thumbnail + Tantivy docs. Add first-class re-homing: a 'crawl set <id> --collection <NAME>' that moves the WACZ to archive/<new-slug>/, updates the manifest entry, relocates committed assets (collections/<old>/crawls/<id>.{md,jpg} -> <new>/), and refreshes search docs — coherently, in one operation. Alternatively make crawl ids collection-independent so a move doesn't change identity. Surfaced in the storage-model review (rustyweb-sfaz).

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Custody constraint from PR #135 (crawl custody moved into the ingest).

Whatever shape first-class re-homing takes, it must not change `added_by`. The rule now in `record::upsert` is: custody is set once, at accession, and an entry already in the manifest keeps whatever it has, including nothing. That exists because re-homing via the plain-add path was a privilege escalation — the already-indexed skip guard is scoped to the collection, so adding the same URL under a different collection falls through and re-homes the entry, and crediting the actor there let a curator claim an admin-accessioned unattributed crawl (`may_delete_crawl` is owner-or-admin).

Guarded by `tests/integration.rs::re_homing_an_unattributed_crawl_does_not_claim_it`, which asserts the re-home happens (the collection does change) while custody does not. A `crawl set --collection` built here should keep that property and ideally reuse the same test shape.

Note the second option in this bead's description — making crawl ids collection-independent — would also remove the reason the URL path re-homes while the local-file path is refused, which is the asymmetry that made the escalation reachable in the first place.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Second constraint from the locking work (PR #140), alongside the custody one above.

A REBUILD WOULD SILENTLY REVERT A RENAME OR A MOVE. reindex snapshots each crawl's name and collection into `targets` before it starts, hands those to index_one, and writes them into the freshly-opened manifest at the end. Only browsertrix/archive_it/added_by are re-read from the current manifest, so those three are protected and name/collection are not. A manifest-only writer that renamed a crawl or moved it between collections mid-rebuild would have the change reverted when the rebuild applies.

Not reachable today, which is the only reason it was left: there is no rename or move endpoint. This bead is what would add one.

Note the tension before reaching for the obvious fix. The rebuild tags the *documents* with the snapshot name (crawl_name in the index), so simply preferring the fresh manifest value at upsert time would leave the index and the manifest disagreeing about the same crawl. Either the rebuild has to re-read name/collection early enough to tag documents with them, or a move has to be serialized against a rebuild the way an ingest is (it already would be, if a move takes the index lock — which it should, since re-homing changes crawl_id and therefore the documents).

title: Reconcile orphaned documents: repair the gap locking cannot close
description:
The index lock and the manifest lock (PRs #136/#138/#140) serialize writers, so no two operations lose each other's work any more. Neither closes one structural gap, and no amount of locking will: THERE IS NO TRANSACTION SPANNING TANTIVY AND THE MANIFEST.

An ingest commits documents to Tantivy and then saves the manifest entry. A crash, power loss or SIGKILL between those two leaves documents in the index with no manifest record. The reverse is possible too (manifest entry saved, a later commit lost), though the ingest's ordering makes the first far likelier.

Symptom for a curator: a crawl's pages appear in search results and the crawl page 404s, because rendering goes through the manifest. It cannot be deleted through the UI either, since delete_crawl plans from the manifest entry that is not there. This is the same end state as PR #126's lost-update bug, reachable by hardware instead of by a race — which is why locking does not help.

WHAT TO BUILD
A reconciliation pass that finds and repairs the disagreement. `indice verify` already walks this territory (it checks recorded crawls against what is on disk), so this is plausibly an addition to it rather than new machinery. Roughly:

- list the distinct crawl_id values present in the Tantivy index;
- compare against the ids in waczs.json;
- ids in the index but not the manifest are orphans: report them, and offer to drop their documents (`delete_crawl_docs` already exists and takes a crawl_id);
- ids in the manifest whose documents are missing are the other direction: report, and suggest `indice index --force` on that source to re-index it.

Take the index lock for the whole pass, and do any manifest read inside manifest_write, per index::lock's ordering rule.

DESIGN should then record this as the answer to the store-spanning gap, replacing the current admission that it simply exists. The 'what it does not protect against' list in the locking section is where it belongs.

Worth doing because the gap is permanent by construction: indice deliberately keeps human-readable files on disk rather than putting the manifest in a database (confirmed 2026-09-22), so a single transaction over both stores is not available. Repair is the alternative to prevention.
close_reason:
Shipped in PR #149 (merged 2026-09-27) as `indice reconcile` / `index::reconcile`.

WHAT LANDED, and where it differs from this bead's sketch:

- Not folded into `indice verify` as suggested. Fixity (do the files still match what was recorded) and reconciliation (do the two stores list the same crawls) are different questions with wildly different costs: re-hashing every WACZ is minutes to hours of I/O, comparing id sets is seconds. Bundling them means never getting the cheap answer without paying for the expensive one. `verify` prints a pointer instead.
- Read-only, by Ed's call. Each finding prints the command that repairs it rather than performing it, because one remedy (dropping documents) discards the last surviving copy of a crawl's text.
- Orphans are usually RECOVERABLE, which the bead did not anticipate. `wacz_id` hashes the home-relative location string rather than the contents, and a local ingest files the WACZ under `archive/<slug>/`, so rescanning the archive and recomputing ids finds the orphan's file. Then the remedy is a re-index that rebuilds the manifest entry with real provenance, not `delete_crawl_docs`. The collection comes off the orphan's own documents, since the missing manifest entry is what would otherwise name it.
- The reverse direction uses `Wacz::page_count` to separate real loss from a WACZ that never had extractable pages. Only confirmed findings set the exit code.
- DESIGN.md gained a section on the gap and this as its answer. Note it did NOT replace an existing admission: that text was only ever in the planning document, so DESIGN had been silent on the subject.

TWO TRAPS WORTH REMEMBERING (both were bugs caught in review of #149):
1. Tantivy keeps a crawl's term in a segment dictionary until that segment merges, so counting terms reports every correctly-deleted crawl as an orphan. Candidates come from the dictionary, counts come from the searcher so alive bitsets apply.
2. A crawl carries one `collection` document under the same crawl_id as its pages. Counting it inflates every count by one AND hides real damage: a crawl whose pages are lost but whose collection doc survives looks present, so 'missing documents' never fires. Queries filter `doc_type:page`.

STILL OPEN, split out rather than done: rustyweb-reconcile-stray-wacz-5epb, for the third state (a WACZ on disk that neither store knows about). The crash window for that is much wider, since the ingest files the WACZ before it opens the index at all, but a stray file is not unambiguously damage and needs a decision first.

Not covered by design: nothing detects the disagreement as it happens. This is a pass an operator runs. Surfacing it in the workroom needs a decision about when the check would run.

title: Request-path writes answer 503 before checking authorization
description:
Raised in two separate reviews of PR #138 and not fixed there.

delete_crawl_handler, update_annotation and delete_annotation take the bounded index lock BEFORE the permission check. So a curator who may not touch the object waits the full 10s budget, parks a tokio blocking-pool thread for it, and then gets 503 with the holder's description, operation name and pid — rather than 403. The Retry-After then invites them back for another 403.

Two costs: internal detail disclosed to someone with no permission for the action (mild — they are an authenticated curator, not anonymous), and a cheap way for any curator to park blocking threads.

NOT FIXED BECAUSE THE OBVIOUS FIX IS WORSE THAN IT LOOKS. The authoritative custody read is deliberately INSIDE the lock — server/manage.rs explains why: a crawl id is a hash of its source, so between an unlocked read and the delete the entry can be removed and the same WACZ re-added under a different owner, and the check would have passed against an owner who is no longer there. Moving the check out reintroduces that TOCTOU.

So a fix means an advisory pre-check outside the lock purely to reject early, with the real check still inside — deliberately duplicated authorization logic, which is its own hazard and needs to be written so the two cannot drift. For annotations it is harder still: may_edit is evaluated inside annotations::update via a predicate, so there is no cheap outside equivalent.

Decide explicitly rather than drifting into it. Doing nothing is defensible; doing it badly is not.

title: Consolidate the request-path lock plumbing
description:
Cleanup left after rustyweb-durable-writes-f4h5. No data loss; this is about the mechanism having grown five ways to say one thing, and the ordering rule being enforced by people remembering to paste a block.

FIVE ENCODINGS OF "BUSY". Acquisition::{Held,Busy}, Write::{Done,Busy}, CrawlDeleteOutcome::Busy, DeleteOutcome::Busy, and the anonymous Result<IndexLock, String> that acquire_index_for_request returns. One state, four translation steps between them. Acquisition is already the shape the callers need; returning anyhow::Result<Acquisition> and matching on it directly removes the wrapper, the nested Result, and the Ok/Err reversal that reads like an error when it is not.

THE ACQUIRE PREAMBLE IS COPY-PASTED INTO FIVE HANDLERS, comment and all (api.rs x3 byte-identical, manage.rs x2 the same shape with a different outcome enum). index/lock.rs's own module docs say the way to get this wrong is to add the acquisition to the library function and leave the handler alone: "it compiles, it looks tidier, and it hangs". That rule currently holds because five call sites each remember it. A with_request_index_lock helper taking a closure, or a tower layer over the write routes, makes it structural instead: the body cannot run without the guard. Worth doing BEFORE a sixth write handler exists.

DELETE AppState.write_lock. PR #140 removed it from the finding-aid save, which was the last holder that did not also hold the index lock. If that is still true when this is picked up, the in-process mutex is fully redundant with the two cross-process locks, and deleting it removes a whole lock tier, the poison-tolerance dance at every site, and the unbounded wait that sits after the bounded flock wait (a handler gives up on the index lock after 10s and then blocks on the mutex with no bound). CHECK EACH REMAINING HOLDER FIRST: the claim is that every one now takes the index lock first, and that should be verified rather than assumed.

BOUNDED MANIFEST ACQUIRE, only if it bites. lock_manifest is Wait::Forever with no bounded variant, justified by the hold being short. That is false for exactly one caller: a rebuild applies every crawl it rebuilt in a single closure, so that hold is proportional to the archive (a linear scan per upsert plus a rewrite of every dirty finding aid). A request-path writer blocks for all of it, past the 10s budget it gets on the index lock, with no 503. The docs say so honestly now. The fix would be a lock_manifest_within mirroring lock_index_within, plus having the rebuild apply in batches.

MEASURE BEFORE OPTIMISING. Two costs noted in review and never measured:
- index_location now does two full Manifest::open per call (the planning snapshot plus the one inside manifest_write), and Manifest::open re-reads waczs.json, runs migrate_flat_finding_aids and parses every collection README. archiveit::import_crawls calls index_location once per crawl and then set_archiveit_provenance_by_id, so an N-crawl import does roughly 3N full manifest loads and 2N full waczs.json rewrites.
- A rebuild holds three copies of the metadata at once: the targets snapshot (alive to the end because the annotations loop reads it), the Vec<Indexed> of everything rebuilt, and the manifest opened inside the closure. Dropping the snapshot after the annotations loop removes a third.

title: Forward-auth refreshes the display cookie on cross-site GETs
description: Found reviewing PR #141 (making /logout a POST). Related class, not closed by it. forward_auth sets/refreshes the display session cookie on EVERY gated request, including GETs. So GET /manage/login is still a state-changing GET, and under the shipped HTTP Basic stopgap (Caddyfile.manage) browsers send cached Basic credentials on cross-origin subresource requests. An on any site therefore passes Caddy basicauth, passes forward_auth, and gets back Set-Cookie: indice_session=... (SameSite=Lax restricts SENDING, not SETTING). Two consequences, both low severity: - a curators 12-hour display session can be refreshed indefinitely by any page they visit, so it never expires while they browse; - a session can be minted for someone who never clicked Log in, making public pages render workroom chrome for them. Evidence::Cookie never admits writes, so neither grants any privilege. It is cosmetic plus a session that will not lapse. But it is the same class as the logout bug ("a GET that changes state"), and PR #141s commit message should not be read as having closed that class generally. Fix direction: only set the cookie when the request is same-site — the same signal same_origin_guard already computes from Origin / Sec-Fetch-Site — rather than on any gated GET. That is a behaviour change to the login path, so it wants its own think: the cookie exists precisely so ungated public pages can render chrome, and the set has to happen on a navigation the browser will follow.

title: Surface status filtering in the UI: a Status facet, and an exclude affordance
description:
From a user report (2026-09-25): "I was wondering if you'd thought of making use of the facets for filtering out 404s. I loaded a WACZ that had a bunch and then I wanted to get them out of the search results."

THE CAPABILITY ALREADY EXISTS. Verified against a real index, not inferred: all three of these work today.

    shared -status:404
    shared NOT status:404
    shared -status:[400 TO 599]        excludes every failed capture

status: is already in EXTRA_FILTERS (search::facets), so once set it renders as an active-filter chip, and FIELD_STATUS is an indexed u64 so ranges work. There is an existing test, search::tests::status_and_modified_year_filters, covering status:200 and status:[400 TO 499].

SO THE GAP IS DISCOVERABILITY, NOT FUNCTION. Nothing in the UI mentions status:, so the only way to find it is to read the source. The user went looking in the sidebar facets, which is exactly where it is not. Ed judged the query syntax sufficient for now (2026-09-25); this bead is the follow-up if it comes up again.

TWO PIECES OF WORK, THE SECOND BIGGER THAN STATUS:

1. Add Status to the sidebar facets. FACET_DIMENSIONS in search/facets.rs has five entries (collection, year, site, type, language) and status is not one. One technical unknown: those five are facet_string() TEXT fields while FIELD_STATUS is add_u64_field(INDEXED | STORED), so check whether the aggregation path handles a numeric field or whether it needs a parallel text field written at index time.

2. Give facets an EXCLUDE affordance. This is what was actually asked for — clicking a facet value filters IN, and the user wanted 404s OUT. A minus control next to a facet value appending -field:value would serve every facet, not just status. More valuable than (1) and not status-specific.

DESIGN QUESTIONS IF PICKED UP:
- Raw codes (200/301/404) or buckets (2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx)? Buckets read better; they hide the difference between 404 and 410, which matters to an archivist.
- Should search DEFAULT to hiding non-2xx? Argued against at the time: a 404 capture is evidence, and a reading room that silently drops captures is doing the wrong thing. An explicit exclude control is the honest version.

AND A TRAP FOR WHOEVER BUILDS THIS. Two status numbers exist and they disagree by design:
- Wacz.status_counts is tallied from the CDX and counts EVERY capture, including the bodyless 4xx/5xx that never become search documents (see the comment on CrawlStats::status_counts). This is what capture_quality renders on the crawl and collection pages, e.g. "1,234 captures, 78% ok - 404x210".
- The search status field exists only on captures that became documents.

So a status facet in SEARCH will undercount 404s relative to the crawl page whenever the failures are bodyless, which is the common case. Two correct numbers that look like a bug. Label the facet as being about indexed pages, or drive it from the CDX tally instead. This user's 404s evidently had bodies, since they were showing up in search results at all.

title: 32-bit x86 (i686): builds cleanly, but untested at runtime and mmap-limited
description:
Probed 2026-09-25 and recorded so it is not re-derived. A user (Ed) has a Debian 13 machine, `metis`, running a 32-bit kernel: `Linux 6.1.0-35-686-pae ... i686 GNU/Linux`, glibc 2.41. Our x86_64 release artifact gives `exec format error` there, and no i686 target is published.

IT BUILDS. A temporary CI probe on ubuntu-22.04 (apt gcc-multilib, rustup target add i686-unknown-linux-gnu, cargo build --release --locked --bin indice --target i686-unknown-linux-gnu) succeeded first try and produced:

    ELF 32-bit LSB pie executable, Intel 80386, version 1 (SYSV),
    dynamically linked, interpreter /lib/ld-linux.so.2, for GNU/Linux 3.2.0

Artifact: https://github.com/edsu/indice/actions/runs/36167452414 (gh run download 36167452414 -n indice-i686-unknown-linux-gnu). Default retention 90 days. The probe workflow lived on branch i686-probe, now deleted; recreate from this description if needed.

gcc-multilib is the only extra step. cc-rs drives `gcc -m32` for i686 on an x86_64 host, which is what ring and zstd-sys need — those two are the C-compiling dependencies and both were the local blocker (cross-compiling from an arm64 Mac fails for want of i686-linux-gnu-gcc).

BUT BUILDING IS NOT THE SAME AS WORKING, AND THIS IS UNTESTED AT RUNTIME. Two reasons not to add it to the release matrix on the strength of a successful compile:

1. TANTIVY MEMORY-MAPS THE INDEX. search::SearchIndex uses Index::open_in_dir, i.e. tantivy's MmapDirectory. A 32-bit process gets roughly 3GB of virtual address space regardless of RAM — PAE extends physical addressing, not per-process virtual. A small archive will be fine; a real one hits that as a wall, and the failure will surface as an obscure mmap error rather than anything a curator can act on. Nobody has measured where the ceiling actually falls.

2. i686-unknown-linux-gnu is Rust Tier 2: std exists, but it is far less exercised, and we have no way to run the test suite on it in CI without an emulator.

IF THIS IS PICKED UP, the work is: (a) run the test suite under qemu-user or a 32-bit container to see whether anything actually breaks; (b) find the practical index-size ceiling; (c) only then decide whether to publish, and if so say plainly in the install docs that it is best-effort with a size limit.

Related: the install docs have no platform-to-asset table at all, which is how "exec format error" became the first experience here. Worth fixing regardless of what happens to i686.
close_reason:
Won't do (Ed's call, 2026-09-27): tantivy is not going to play nice with a 32-bit architecture, so the runtime investigation the bead asks for is not worth doing.

The blocker is the one this bead already recorded: search::SearchIndex opens the index through tantivy's MmapDirectory, and a 32-bit process gets ~3GB of virtual address space no matter how much RAM the box has (PAE extends physical addressing, not per-process virtual). So the ceiling is structural rather than a bug we could fix, it lands on real archives rather than toy ones, and it surfaces as an obscure mmap error a curator cannot act on. Publishing a binary whose failure mode is 'works until your archive gets big, then breaks confusingly' is worse than publishing nothing.

The build itself was never the problem: the i686 probe compiled first try (run 36167452414, ELF 32-bit LSB pie executable, Intel 80386), with gcc-multilib as the only extra step for ring and zstd-sys. That result stays recorded here so nobody re-derives it.

Reopen only if tantivy gains a non-mmap directory we would actually use.

Split out before closing: rustyweb-install-platform-table-47kl, for the missing platform-to-asset table in the install docs. That is what turned this into a confusing first experience, and it is worth fixing whatever happens to i686.

title: Install docs: no platform-to-asset table, so a wrong download fails with 'exec format error'
description:
Split out of rustyweb-w8ip when that was closed (2026-09-27). Independent of the i686 question, and the reason a real user's first experience of indice was a confusing failure.

The install guide lists no mapping from platform to release asset. A user on a 32-bit Debian box (`metis`, `Linux 6.1.0-35-686-pae ... i686`) downloaded the x86_64 artifact and got:

    zsh: exec format error: ./indice

That message says nothing about architecture, so there is no way to self-diagnose from it. The same trap exists for anyone on arm64 Linux, or on an Intel Mac picking up the Apple Silicon build.

The fix is a table in the install docs: platform (uname -sm output) -> which asset to download, plus one line on how to check (`uname -m`, and `file ./indice` to confirm what you got). Worth also naming the platforms we do NOT publish for, so absence is legible rather than looking like an oversight: 32-bit x86 is not published (see the closed rustyweb-w8ip for why), and neither is 32-bit ARM.

Docs live at site/src/content/docs/docs/ (install page); see also the release workflow for the authoritative list of published targets, which is what the table must stay in sync with.

title: reconcile: report a WACZ on disk that neither the index nor the manifest knows about
description:
Found in review of PR #149 (rustyweb-9lxf). `indice reconcile` covers two of the three states the two stores can be in; this is the third.

An ingest files the WACZ into `archive/<slug>/` (acquire::place_local_wacz) BEFORE it opens the search index, indexes anything, commits, or saves the manifest. So the crash window for 'file on disk that nothing references' is much wider than the commit-to-manifest-save window reconcile was built for.
