A crash anywhere in it leaves a stray WACZ consuming disk that neither store mentions, and today reconcile reports 'index and manifest agree'.

The data is already there: `wacz_ids_on_disk` computes exactly the map needed, so this is (ids on disk) minus (manifest) minus (index). Cheap to add.

WHY IT WAS NOT DONE IN #149, and the question to settle first: a stray WACZ is not obviously damage. A curator can legitimately park files under `archive/` before indexing them, or keep a staging area there, and reporting those as findings would be noise that teaches people to ignore the command. The two states reconcile handles now are unambiguous, which is what makes its output trustworthy.

So this needs a decision rather than an implementation:
- report strays as a distinct, non-confirmed category (does not affect the exit code), or
- only report a stray when something corroborates that an ingest was interrupted, or
- leave it out and document that `archive/` may hold unindexed files.

Note the disk scan currently runs only when something is orphaned (a deliberate cost choice on a healthy archive), so reporting strays unconditionally would mean scanning every run. That is the other trade to weigh.

title: Public demo instance at app.indice.page
description:
Stand up a public demo instance of indice at app.indice.page: GitHub sign-in, WACZ bytes in an S3-compatible bucket (UpCloud Managed Object Storage) that the browser range-reads directly, manually approved curators, demo-specific site text, an upload size cap, and a daily reset that preserves a seeded corpus.

Supersedes the hosted-demo framing that died with rustyweb-prod-deploy-mhx (closed stale 2026-08-23). Delivers the ARCHIVE half of rustyweb-object-storage-home-7li7; that bead's INDEX half (Tantivy over a custom Directory) stays out of scope. Overlaps rustyweb-deploy-wo6l.12 (deploy on a container cloud platform) - link or fold, don't run both.

Design decisions made with Ed up front:
(a) Bytes live in the bucket and the browser reads them directly. Upload streams through indice, which PUTs to the bucket and records the crawl as Source::Url(...). serve_file already 302s Url sources and viewer_source hands the raw URL to the viewer, so replay needs no change - but bucket CORS must expose Content-Range/Accept-Ranges or replay breaks silently.
(b) A compose.demo.yaml overlay on the existing compose.yaml + compose.sso.yaml, plus a written runbook. No Terraform, no CI push-to-deploy.
(c) users.yaml stays the source of truth for privilege; make it hot-reloadable and let any GitHub login authenticate as a Reader.
(e) A real 'indice reset' driven by a keep-list in config.yaml, built on the existing delete primitives - not snapshot/restore.

Full plan: ~/.claude/plans/so-we-ve-made-a-magical-honey.md

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
2026-10-03 SCOPE CHANGE: object storage is OUT. Ed's reasoning, which holds up: content is deleted daily, uploads are size-capped, and only manually approved people can upload, so disk use on the UpCloud VM is bounded and block storage is enough. Requirement (a) is also already half-satisfied by code on main - POST /api/archives and the accession desk's path/URL tab accept an http(s) URL, Ingest stream-indexes it over HTTP ranges, and replay reads it straight from that URL - so anyone who wants bucket-hosted WACZs can host them and point indice at them today. The only missing piece was 'indice puts your uploaded bytes in a bucket for you', which is not what a demo needs.

.1/.2/.3 closed not-doing; the design work is preserved on rustyweb-object-storage-home-7li7. Two new children replace what the bucket was implicitly providing: .11 (cap TOTAL archive size from the manifest's file_size sum, since 'the bucket absorbs it' is no longer true) and .12 (harden AddArchiveRequest.path - arbitrary server-side filesystem path, plus blind SSRF via the URL branch - before approved-but-not-fully-trusted people get it).

What this buys: the whole bucket-CORS failure mode disappears (/files/{id} already serves ranges same-origin with the right expose-headers), 'indice verify' actually fixity-checks the demo corpus, and the epic drops from 10 children to 9 with the largest and riskiest one gone.

Revised blocking graph: .7 <- .5,.6 ; .9 <- .6 ; .11 <- .4 ; .10 <- everything. Ready now: .4, .5, .6, .8, .12.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
2026-10-04 PARKED behind rustyweb-open-web-hardening-u9y6. Ed's call after reviewing the risks: 'what this is telling me is that we have work to do before the app can go out on the web. the demo can wait.'

Five children moved to the hardening epic because they were product debt rather than demo tax: .4 + .11 -> u9y6.3 (merged), .6 -> u9y6.2, .12 -> u9y6.4, .13 -> u9y6.7 (broadened to AI scrapers). Earlier, .1/.2/.3 closed not-doing when object storage was dropped.

What remains here is genuinely demo-only: .5 (site text saying it is a demo), .7 (request-access affordance), .8 (the daily reset), .9 (compose overlay + runbook), .10 (provision and launch).

STILL UNDECIDED when work resumes — the shape question. Read-only instance versus a write surface for approved strangers. Read-only needs only .5, .9, .10 plus u9y6.7 (bots), mounts no write surface at all, has fixed storage, and matches DESIGN's 'nothing sent to a hosted service' pitch. The write surface additionally needs .7, .8 and all of u9y6. The one risk that does not transfer to an institution is personal accountability for strangers' uploads, which is a policy question rather than an engineering one. Also unresolved: whether .8 should split into the command and the scheduler, since it had grown to carry the annotation rule, the refuse-without-config guard, the dry-run default and the scheduler.

title: S3 object-storage client and storage: config section
description:
New crates/indice-lib/src/s3.rs: a small S3 client (put_object, head_object, delete_object, list_objects_v2) over the existing ureq 3 agent, with AWS SigV4 signing. ~350 lines + ~200 of tests.

Step zero is a no-behavior-change commit: server/auth.rs::hmac_sha256 is pub(super) and collections.rs::bytes_to_hex is private, so both move to a new pub(crate) crates/indice-lib/src/crypto.rs alongside sha256_hex, carrying the RFC 4231 known-answer test; auth.rs rewires to it.

Why hand-rolled, not a crate: cargo tree -i hyper-rustls shows reqwest enters this workspace ONLY via thirtyfour, a dev-dependency. object_store or aws-sdk-s3 would put hyper+reqwest into the shipped binary for the first time alongside ureq - two HTTP stacks in a project whose ethos is one self-contained binary. aws-sdk-s3 also defaults to aws-lc-sys (cmake + C compiler). rust-s3 is lighter but less maintained.

Risk-shrinking choices to document in the module doc:
- single-shot signing with known Content-Length and a precomputed payload hash. collections.rs::file_sha256 already returns lowercase hex sha256, which is exactly x-amz-content-sha256, and ingest computes it anyway for fixity.
- minimal SignedHeaders: host;x-amz-content-sha256;x-amz-date. Never sign content-length or content-type.
- constrain keys to [A-Za-z0-9._-/] via index::paths::safe_component so URI-encoding edge cases cannot arise.
- path-style URLs by default (keeps CanonicalURI trivial; UpCloud/Ceph RGW supports it).
- redirects OFF on the S3 agent - a followed 307 silently invalidates the signature. Turn 301 PermanentRedirect into a readable wrong-endpoint error.

Unit-test against the published AWS SigV4 vectors (get-vanilla, get-header-value-trim, get-utf8) and the documented PUT Object known-answer with AKIDEXAMPLE - not only our own mock.

config.yaml gains:
  storage:
    endpoint / region / bucket / key_prefix / public_base_url
    # path_style: true (default)
    # legacy_public_base_urls: []  - keeps old objects deletable after a move

Two deliberate departures from config.rs's 'every field optional and defaulted' rule, to argue for in its module doc: the section is Option<StorageConfig> (absence is real information, not a missing knob), and its inner fields are required Strings (a half-configured bucket should be a load error).

Credentials from INDICE_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID / INDICE_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY ONLY - the home directory is committable, so no secret may enter config.yaml. Read them in indice-bin (matching EnvBrowsertrix at main.rs:2762 and connect_archiveit at main.rs:2794); indice-lib reads no credentials from the environment today and shouldn't start. New object_store(cfg) -> Result<Option<Bucket>> errors at startup when storage: is set but credentials are not. 'indice config' prints the resolved section plus credentials: found/missing, never the secret.

If CodeQL flags hand-rolled signing, raise it rather than dismiss it; object_store is the fallback.
close_reason: Not doing: the demo uses block storage on the UpCloud VM instead. Ed's call 2026-10-03 — with content reset daily, uploads size-capped, and only approved people able to upload, disk use is bounded, so an S3 client is complexity the demo does not need. And indice can already index + replay a WACZ from an http(s) URL, so anyone wanting bucket-hosted content can host it and point indice at it today. The full design (use rusty-s3 sans-IO rather than hand-rolled SigV4 or an SDK; the acquire::open seam; content-addressed keys; the resumability and verify regressions; the CORS expose-headers trap) is preserved as a comment on rustyweb-object-storage-home-7li7, which owns the archive-in-a-bucket idea.

title: Ingest writes WACZ bytes to the bucket; indice storage check
description:
Make ingest offload WACZ bytes to the bucket and record Source::Url, and ship the preflight that proves the bucket is actually replay-capable.

THE SEAM ALREADY EXISTS: acquire::open returns (effective_source, access) as two separate things. --download uses it to turn a Source::Url into a Source::File read locally; object storage is the exact inverse - record a Source::Url, read a WaczAccess::Local. Nothing downstream branches on that combination.

HARD CONSTRAINT: wacz_id(&effective_source) is computed in index_one right after open (index/ingest/mod.rs:408) and stamped onto every Tantivy document by pages::index, plus the thumbs path. The source must be settled BEFORE indexing. Rewriting it in record::upsert would change the id after documents were tagged - reject that shape explicitly.

Changes:
- Ingest gains one field + one setter, store: Option<&'a s3::Bucket> (the struct's doc comment names this as the extension point).
- resolve_sources takes &Ingest and, when a store is configured, SKIPS place_local_wacz and returns the unplaced Source::File. Without this you both copy to disk and upload.
- New first arm in open, guarded on Source::File: hash, PUT, return (Source::Url(public_url), WaczAccess::Local). Guarding on File means a reindex of an existing Source::Url takes the streaming arm and is never re-uploaded.
- WaczAccess::Local gains sha: Option<String>; WaczAccess::fixity prefers it, else a multi-GB WACZ is hashed twice.
- PUT before indexing: a 2 GB upload that fails on credentials or quota should fail before ten minutes of indexing ('a bad path errors before we touch the index'). Cost is an orphan object on a later indexing failure - that is what list_objects_v2 is for.

KEY NAMING IS CONTENT-ADDRESSED: <key_prefix><slug>/<sha256[..12]>-<safe-name>.wacz. This replaces pick_archive_dest's -2/-3 disambiguation rather than porting it: you can't cheaply compare bucket contents (ETag is MD5, md5 isn't in the tree), and content-addressing makes a re-PUT idempotent and the URL predictable before uploading.

RESUMABILITY REGRESSES without a helper: the skip-already-indexed guard (mod.rs:313-325) hashes the pre-effective Source::File, whose id won't match the recorded Source::Url - the same wart DESIGN documents for --download. Moot for browser uploads (unique temp path) but a real regression for 'indice index' over a local corpus with a store configured. Add acquire::stored_source(cx, path, slug) deriving the URL WITHOUT uploading, and have the guard check both ids.

indice storage check [--origin URL] [--keep] (default origin from INDICE_SITE_URL, already read at main.rs:1123). Assertions in indice-lib (testable against an axum mock), printing in indice-bin. PUT a 1 KiB probe under <key_prefix>.indice-preflight/, then:
1. signed PUT 2xx; explain 403 as wrong secret / >15min clock skew / path-style mismatch; report the endpoint on 301/307.
2. signed HEAD -> Content-Length: 1024.
3. ANONYMOUS GET of the public URL -> 200 (a different host than step 1 under virtual-host addressing, which is the point).
4. anonymous ranged GET (Range: bytes=100-199, Origin: <origin>) -> 206 NOT 200, exact Content-Range: bytes 100-199/1024, the correct 100 bytes, Accept-Ranges: bytes, matching Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and Access-Control-Expose-Headers containing BOTH Content-Range and Accept-Ranges. That last one is the silent killer this subcommand exists for: without it the browser gets the bytes but fetch() hides the headers, so wabac.js never learns the total length and replay breaks with nothing in the console.
5. OPTIONS preflight with Access-Control-Request-Headers: range -> 2xx, GET in Allow-Methods, range in Allow-Headers. Report Access-Control-Max-Age as informational: absent/0 means a preflight per range request.
6. anonymous HEAD of the public URL - some policies allow GET but not HEAD and wabac.js issues both. WARN, don't fail.
7. signed DELETE of the probe, attempted even after a failed assertion so the check doesn't litter (--keep to inspect).
Print a paste-ready CORS policy on failure; non-zero exit on any hard failure.

DOWNSTREAM CONSEQUENCES of every demo crawl becoming is_remote():
- verify REGRESSES SILENTLY and this is not merely a known gap. run_verify (main.rs:1924) skips Source::Url as 'not re-fetched', which was honest when a URL source had an empty fixity(). A bucket crawl has a NON-EMPTY recorded sha256, so it will look verified and never be checked. At minimum branch on !col.sha256.is_empty() and print REMOTE (sha recorded, not re-hashed), or do a head_object existence+size check. Related: rustyweb-streamed-wacz-fixity-zle5.
- viewer_source (server/util.rs:38), not serve_file, is the load-bearing replay path: it hands the raw bucket URL to the viewer, so /files/{id}'s 302 is never exercised. Bucket CORS is mandatory, not a nicety.
- reindex.rs:139 re-reads bytes over the network instead of off disk - correct, slower, and dependent on the object staying publicly range-readable.
- server/imports.rs:324-340 and archiveit.rs:619 are a second producer of local WACZs: they'll flow through the new arm and get offloaded, but leave the downloaded copy under archive/. Follow-up, not v1.
- reconcile.rs:239 wacz_ids_on_disk only scans <home>/archive, so it can never match a bucket crawl to an orphan object. The bucket equivalent (list_objects_v2 vs manifest) is a follow-up.
- views/mod.rs::source_badge will label every crawl 'Hosted remotely - indice streams this at replay time and doesn't keep a local copy' (fed by server/pages.rs:59-60). True but misleading when indice put it there. Reword under the site-chrome task.
close_reason: Not doing: the demo uses block storage on the UpCloud VM instead. Ed's call 2026-10-03 — with content reset daily, uploads size-capped, and only approved people able to upload, disk use is bounded, so an S3 client is complexity the demo does not need. And indice can already index + replay a WACZ from an http(s) URL, so anyone wanting bucket-hosted content can host it and point indice at it today. The full design (use rusty-s3 sans-IO rather than hand-rolled SigV4 or an SDK; the acquire::open seam; content-addressed keys; the resumability and verify regressions; the CORS expose-headers trap) is preserved as a comment on rustyweb-object-storage-home-7li7, which owns the archive-in-a-bucket idea.

title: Delete and deaccession remove the bucket object
description:
index/delete.rs::local_wacz_to_remove (line 33) only understands Source::File. Add bucket_object_to_remove mirroring it - INCLUDING its 'referenced by another manifest entry with the same source' guard - on top of Bucket::key_for_url.

key_for_url strips the normalized public_base_url and requires the remainder to start with key_prefix AT A / BOUNDARY, so a base of .../bucket cannot match .../bucketX/... . Unit-test the negatives: different host, scheme mismatch, prefix-not-at-boundary, .. in the remainder.

NO Source::S3 variant: Source round-trips through location()/parse() into waczs.json, so a new variant means a manifest migration plus edits to viewer_source, serve_file and reindex - all to express something a URL already expresses.

Thread Option<&Bucket> through delete_crawl and plan_crawl_deletion. Only five call sites (main.rs:1381,1422,1438 and server/manage.rs:614,699), so an explicit parameter beats an Ingest-style builder. delete_collection gets it free - it loops delete_crawl (delete.rs:196). Add object: Option<String> to CrawlDeletion so the confirmation can say what else will go.

ORDERING: put the bucket DELETE in step 2, beside std::fs::remove_file, keeping the existing index-docs -> bytes -> manifest-entry-LAST discipline that delete.rs:76-80 already justifies. The manifest entry is the record of WHAT to clean up, so leaving it last makes a crashed delete safely re-runnable with 'indice crawl delete <id>'.

FAILURE POLICY: best-effort but loud. Add object_delete_failed: Option<String> to CrawlDeletion, surfaced by the CLI and the SSE/flash path as 'index documents and manifest entry removed; bucket object <key> could not be deleted (<err>) - re-run indice crawl delete <id> or remove it manually.' Do NOT abort: refusing to remove the manifest entry because the bucket is briefly unreachable leaves a crawl listed with its documents already gone, which is strictly worse than an orphan object.

Document the migration hazard: if the operator later changes public_base_url or key_prefix, previously recorded URLs stop matching and their objects become undeletable through indice. legacy_public_base_urls (from .1) is the cheap insurance.
close_reason: Not doing: the demo uses block storage on the UpCloud VM instead. Ed's call 2026-10-03 — with content reset daily, uploads size-capped, and only approved people able to upload, disk use is bounded, so an S3 client is complexity the demo does not need. And indice can already index + replay a WACZ from an http(s) URL, so anyone wanting bucket-hosted content can host it and point indice at it today. The full design (use rusty-s3 sans-IO rather than hand-rolled SigV4 or an SDK; the acquire::open seam; content-addressed keys; the resumability and verify regressions; the CORS expose-headers trap) is preserved as a comment on rustyweb-object-storage-home-7li7, which owns the archive-in-a-bucket idea.

title: Cap the size of an uploaded WACZ
description:
server/mod.rs:292 is the only DefaultBodyLimit in the repo and it is DefaultBodyLimit::disable(), so POST /api/archives/upload currently accepts an unbounded body. Every other route keeps axum's 2 MB default.

Add to config.yaml:
  uploads:
    max_mb: 200

When set, layer DefaultBodyLimit::max(n) on the upload route instead of disabling it. Unset keeps today's behavior so existing deployments don't change.

Enforce it a SECOND time inside stream_field_to_file with a running byte counter, so a chunked body with no Content-Length can't slip past the layer, and so the error names the limit instead of being a bare 413.

Show the limit in the accession desk (views/manage.rs) before someone starts a doomed multi-gigabyte upload.

Note this is not only a demo-policy knob once object storage lands: a signed single-shot PUT is valid to 5 GiB, so .1's signing approach needs a server-side cap below that regardless of what the demo chooses.

Tests in tests/manage.rs: over-limit upload is rejected 413, both with and without a Content-Length header.
close_reason: Moved to rustyweb-open-web-hardening-u9y6.3, which merges them: the per-upload cap and the total-archive cap share a config section, two handlers and their tests, and neither is much use alone. Not demo-specific — any operator exposing serve --manage inherits an unbounded upload route and no disk guard.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: 2026-10-03: the '5 GiB single-PUT ceiling' rationale is gone with the bucket (.1-.3 closed not-doing). The cap now stands on its own as demo policy, and gains a companion in .11, which caps TOTAL archive size from the manifest's file_size sum - that is what replaces 'the bucket absorbs it' now that bytes only live on the VM's block storage.

title: Operator-configurable site text (name, tagline, banner)
description:
There is no instance name, banner or about text anywhere today: the wordmark 'indice' is hardcoded in views/mod.rs::layout and the hero string in views/home.rs:50. A demo instance has to be able to say it is one.

config.yaml gains:
  site:
    name / tagline / banner (Markdown) / request_access

banner renders through the existing markdown::render() (markdown.rs), which already escapes raw HTML, drops images to alt text and restricts link destinations to http/https/mailto/relative/anchor - the same safe subset the finding aids use. Do not invent a second renderer.

AppState gains the resolved site chrome. Note the deliberate asymmetry with .1: the BUCKET reaches the server as Providers.store: Option<Arc<s3::Bucket>> -> AppState.store, not as a Config. Providers (server/mod.rs:168) exists precisely so the constructors don't grow a parameter per collaborator, and AppState already follows 'resolve once at startup, keep request handling free of file I/O' (the users field at mod.rs:144). A Bucket is the resolved form of its config; the site text has no resolved form beyond itself.

layout() takes six positional arguments today and this would make it eight. Fold manage/signed_in/can_login plus the site text into one Chrome struct instead - cheaper to read, and it keeps clippy quiet honestly rather than by suppression. This is the bulk of the diff: nine call sites across views/ (home, manage x2, search, crawl, collection x2) plus three in server/tests.rs, and the same three values are threaded through the page functions above them. Do it as its own commit so the config change stays legible.

Also reword views/mod.rs::source_badge's remote tooltip here: with object storage every crawl reads 'Hosted remotely - indice streams this at replay time and doesn't keep a local copy', which is misleading when indice is what put it in the bucket.

title: Hot-reload users.yaml, and refuse to be accidentally open
description:
server/mod.rs:228 reads the roster once at startup (the field's own comment says 'Read once at startup'), so approving someone currently means restarting the instance. That is the single thing standing between 'edit a YAML file' and 'manual approval is painful'.

Make AppState.users reloadable: stat users.yaml on resolution and re-read when its mtime changes, mirroring the existing RwLock<Arc<SearchIndex>> swap pattern. One stat per authenticated request is negligible; a notify watcher would be a new dependency for no gain.

Two properties, a test each:

1. A MALFORMED users.yaml must keep the last good roster and log an error. Users::load already refuses to parse a broken permissions file rather than silently defaulting - preserve that intent across reloads.

2. With NO users.yaml at all, Users::resolve makes every authenticated user an Admin (identity.rs, documented as byte-identical to pre-roles behavior). That is right for a laptop and a loaded gun for a public instance, and it becomes live the moment the demo's oauth2-proxy stops allow-listing a single login (see .9). With --manage AND forward-auth AND no roster, raise the current tracing::info! to a prominent warning naming the risk.

Files: crates/indice-lib/src/{server/mod.rs, server/auth.rs, identity.rs}, tests/authz.rs.
close_reason: Moved to rustyweb-open-web-hardening-u9y6.2. Both halves (the no-roster-means-admin footgun, and the roster needing a restart) apply to every operator who configures forward-auth, not just a demo.

title: Request-access affordance for signed-in Readers
description:
A visitor who signs in with GitHub but isn't on the roster resolves to Role::Reader: they see the public site with no indication that anything more exists or how to get it, and any management route answers a bare 403 with no WWW-Authenticate.

Show them their identity and the site.request_access text (from .5) in the appbar, and on the 403 from a management route.

Small, but it is the entire visible surface of 'manually approve individuals' - without it, requirement (c) has a working back end and no front door.

Depends on .5 for the configurable text and .6 for the roster semantics.

Files: crates/indice-lib/src/views/mod.rs, crates/indice-lib/src/server/auth.rs.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: 2026-10-04 REVIEW: dropped the .10 blocking edge. This was P2 while blocking a P1 launch, which is contradictory — the instance can go live without it (an unapproved visitor just sees nothing inviting them to ask). Keeping it P2 and non-blocking makes that honest. Still worth doing early, since it is the only visible surface of requirement (c).

title: indice reset: daily demo reset preserving a seeded corpus
description:
ONE RULE, stated once: reset keeps the collections you listed, minus anything a visitor added.

config.yaml:
  demo:
    keep: [apod, sucho]
    reset_at: "07:00"   # UTC; omit to disable the in-server schedule

Concretely:
- a collection not in keep is deleted entirely (delete_collection);
- within a kept collection, a crawl is deleted when Wacz.added_by.is_some().

That second test is EXACT, not a heuristic. Ingest defaults actor: None (index/ingest/mod.rs:177) and only server/manage.rs:229 sets it, so added_by is Some precisely when the crawl came in over the web. Seed the demo from the CLI and the seed is, by construction, what survives. (Caveat to document: in loopback --manage mode the local operator also sets an actor; the demo runs forward-auth only.)

One library function, two callers:
- indice reset [--home] [--dry-run]. The dry run prints every collection and crawl it would remove and what it keeps, so the keep-list can be checked before it bites.
- An in-server tokio task when demo.reset_at is set. Running it INSIDE the server is what makes the staleness problem disappear: it takes the same acquire_write_lock() and swaps the read-only searcher exactly as an upload job does. An external cron calling the CLI would mutate the index under a server still holding a stale Arc<SearchIndex>. (It also sidesteps the distroless image having no shell.)

Bucket objects for deleted crawls go through .3.

Tombstones: Tantivy accumulates deletes. index/optimize.rs::optimize_if_fragmented already exists for exactly this, and search/tests.rs::optimize_expunges_deletes_at_default_target pins the behavior - have the reset task call it after a pass. Measure with indice stats before doing anything more.

Audit: reuse the existing Action::CollectionDelete / Action::CrawlDelete variants (events.rs:45) with the local-operator actor rather than minting a reset-specific one.

Tests (new tests/reset.rs): seed via the library with actor: None, add a crawl with an actor, reset, assert exactly the visitor's crawl and the unlisted collections are gone; --dry-run changes nothing.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: 2026-10-03: no longer blocked on .3 (bucket delete, closed not-doing). Reset now only has to remove local files, which delete_crawl/delete_collection already do via local_wacz_to_remove. The rule and the in-server scheduling are unchanged.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
2026-10-04 REVIEW — three gaps found re-reading this against the code:

1. ANNOTATIONS SURVIVE THE RESET, so the one-sentence rule is currently a lie. A signed-in Curator can write page annotations (api.rs:143 gates on Role::can_annotate, which is >= Curator), stored at collections/<slug>/annotations.jsonl. delete_collection DOES take them (it collects ann_ids and remove_dir_all's the dir, delete.rs ~205), so annotations on an UNLISTED collection go away with it. But delete_crawl does NOT: annotations are pinned to URL+timestamp and carry no crawl_id, which delete.rs says explicitly. So a visitor who annotates the SEED corpus leaves notes that outlive every reset, accumulating indefinitely on the kept collections.
   Fix keeps the rule intact rather than adding an exception: apply the same author test to notes as to crawls — in a kept collection, delete annotations whose creator is a remote identity. annotations::delete (annotations.rs:314) is the primitive; the search index also carries doc_type:"annotation" docs keyed by annotation_id that must go with them. The sentence then becomes true as written: 'keeps the collections you listed, minus anything a visitor added', where anything means crawls AND notes.

2. SAFETY: 'indice reset' with no demo: section in config.yaml must REFUSE, not delete everything. As specced, an absent keep-list reads as 'keep nothing', so running reset in a real archive home would deaccession the whole thing. That is a one-line guard and a test, and it is the single most dangerous thing in this epic. Consider also requiring --yes for the non-dry-run form, or making --dry-run the default and --commit the opt-in.

3. SCHEDULER FAILURE MUST BE VISIBLE. If the in-server reset task panics or errors, the disk quietly fills until .11's cap starts refusing uploads, and nobody knows why. Log loudly, and surface last-reset time plus outcome somewhere an operator sees it (/health is the obvious place, or the workroom chrome). A silent scheduler is worse than no scheduler.

title: compose.demo.yaml overlay and the deployment runbook
description:
A third overlay beside compose.manage.yaml / compose.sso.yaml, layered on both base files:
  docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.sso.yaml -f compose.demo.yaml up -d

It differs from compose.sso.yaml in four ways that matter:

1. DROP OAUTH2_PROXY_GITHUB_USER. Today it allow-lists one login (default edsu), so nobody else can even sign in - and with no one able to sign in there is nowhere to show a 'request access' message. Removing it lets any GitHub account authenticate and land as a Reader; users.yaml then decides who can write. This is the single change that turns requirement (c) from 'edit env and restart the proxy' into 'add a line to a file'. It ONLY works together with .6's guard: an open proxy with no users.yaml makes every visitor an Admin.
2. OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_SECURE=true, OAUTH2_PROXY_REDIRECT_URL=https://app.indice.page/oauth2/callback, SITE_ADDRESS=app.indice.page, INDICE_SITE_URL=https://app.indice.page.
3. The S3 credential env vars from .1.
4. No volume for archive/ - only index/ and collections/ are local now.

Runbook as a new site/src/content/docs/docs/guides/demo.md, with a pointer from guides/deploy.md:
- UpCloud server + Managed Object Storage bucket (S3-compatible, supports bucket policies and CORS, anonymous HTTPS access).
- The bucket CORS policy spelled out: AllowedOrigins https://app.indice.page, AllowedMethods GET+HEAD, AllowedHeaders range, ExposeHeaders Content-Range + Accept-Ranges + Content-Length + ETag, a non-zero MaxAgeSeconds.
- app.indice.page A/AAAA records - DISTINCT from the apex, which points at GitHub Pages for the landing site.
- A GitHub OAuth App whose callback is https://app.indice.page/oauth2/callback.
- 'indice storage check' as the gate before announcing.
- Say plainly that the demo home must NOT be pushed to a public repo: index/waczs.json holds SubjectIds derived from login addresses, and so does <home>/events/.

Worth stating rather than leaving to be rediscovered: the existing Caddyfile deliberately omits 'encode' so range responses aren't gzipped - and with the bucket serving bytes directly, Caddy is out of the byte path entirely.

Files: compose.demo.yaml (new), site/src/content/docs/docs/guides/demo.md (new), guides/deploy.md, site/astro.config.mjs (sidebar is hand-listed).

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
2026-10-03: drop the S3 sections. No bucket env vars, no bucket CORS policy, and no 'indice storage check' gate - .1-.3 are closed not-doing and the demo keeps WACZ bytes on the VM's block storage.

Two consequences for the overlay and the guide:
- The archive/ volume comes BACK. The earlier draft said 'no volume for archive/'; with block storage the existing indice-data volume carries archive/ + index/ + collections/ as compose.yaml already does. Size it in the runbook: seed corpus + uploads.max_total_gb (.11) + roughly 10-20% for the Tantivy index + merge scratch.
- Caddy is back IN the byte path, so the existing Caddyfile's deliberate omission of 'encode' (so range responses aren't gzipped, verified under rustyweb-deploy-wo6l.5) is load-bearing again rather than moot. Say so in the guide.

Also document the add-by-URL path in the demo guide as the answer for anyone wanting to host large WACZs elsewhere: indice stream-indexes an http(s) URL and replays straight from it, which is requirement (a) satisfied without indice owning a bucket. Note it interacts with .12.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: 2026-10-04 REVIEW: add robots.txt / noindex (see .13) to the demo config and the runbook. Also worth stating in the guide that this instance needs no backup story at all, which is unusual and is a direct consequence of the daily reset: the seed corpus lives in the repo or in the runbook, everything else is disposable by design.

title: Provision and launch app.indice.page
description:
The ops pass, once the code is in. Depends on every other child.

- Provision the UpCloud server and Managed Object Storage bucket; apply the CORS policy from .9.
- Point app.indice.page A/AAAA at the server (apex stays on GitHub Pages).
- Create the GitHub OAuth App with the /oauth2/callback URL.
- Write users.yaml with Ed as admin. Do this BEFORE first exposing the instance - with no roster every authenticated user is an Admin (see .6).
- Seed the demo corpus from the CLI so added_by stays None and the seed survives reset (see .8): apod.wacz plus one or two richer crawls.
- Set demo.keep, demo.reset_at, uploads.max_mb, and the site: text.
- Run 'indice storage check'.
- Verify replay in a REAL browser, not headless - per the ReplayWeb.page capture finding, headless cannot screenshot an indice /replay/viewer. Confirm in the network panel that range requests go to the bucket host, not to app.indice.page.
- Let one reset cycle run; confirm the seed survived and a test upload did not.

End-to-end checks to walk through:
1. storage check passes.
2. Sign in with a GitHub account NOT on the roster -> Reader, sees the demo banner and the request-access text, and POST /api/archives/upload returns 403.
3. Add that account to users.yaml as curator WITHOUT restarting -> upload now works.
4. Upload a WACZ; replay renders and the ranges come from the bucket.
5. Upload over the cap -> 413 naming the limit.
6. Reset; seed survives, the uploaded crawl is gone from search, replay and the manifest, and its object is gone from the bucket.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
2026-10-03: no bucket to provision. Drop the Managed Object Storage instance, the CORS policy and 'indice storage check' from the launch checklist; add sizing the block-storage volume and setting uploads.max_total_gb (.11). The end-to-end check 'range requests go to the bucket host' becomes 'range requests to /files/{id} return 206 with Content-Range through Caddy, un-gzipped'.

One thing that gets BETTER: the demo corpus is now local, so 'indice verify' actually fixity-checks it. The silent verify regression that bucket-backed Source::Url crawls would have introduced does not exist.

title: Bucket orphan sweep: reconcile list_objects_v2 against the manifest
description:
index/reconcile.rs:239 wacz_ids_on_disk only scans <home>/archive, so with object storage (rustyweb-demo-instance-5b9k) it can never match a bucket crawl to an orphan object. Two ways objects leak: ingest PUTs before indexing, so a later indexing failure strands the object; and a bucket DELETE that fails is logged but not retried (5b9k.3's deliberate best-effort policy).

Add a bucket arm to reconcile: list_objects_v2 over <key_prefix>, diff against the manifest's Source::Url entries, report (and optionally --fix) objects with no manifest entry. list_objects_v2 is already in the client surface for exactly this.
close_reason: Moot: the demo stays on block storage (see rustyweb-demo-instance-5b9k.1-.3, closed not-doing). Both of these only exist once ingest offloads bytes to a bucket. Re-file from rustyweb-object-storage-home-7li7 if that ever lands.

title: Importers leave a local copy under archive/ when object storage is configured
description:
server/imports.rs:324-340 and archiveit.rs:619 download a WACZ into archive_dir and then index the local path. With a store configured (rustyweb-demo-instance-5b9k.2) that local path flows through the new Source::File arm and the bytes get offloaded to the bucket correctly - but the downloaded copy stays on disk, so a hosted instance quietly fills its container volume anyway.

Either download to a temp dir when a store is configured, or remove the archive/ copy once the PUT succeeds. Deliberately left out of 5b9k.2 to keep that change reviewable.
close_reason: Moot: the demo stays on block storage (see rustyweb-demo-instance-5b9k.1-.3, closed not-doing). Both of these only exist once ingest offloads bytes to a bucket. Re-file from rustyweb-object-storage-home-7li7 if that ever lands.

title: Per-principal upload quota for a public instance
description:
There is no rate limiting anywhere in indice: no tower-governor, no ConcurrencyLimitLayer, no TimeoutLayer. rustyweb-demo-instance-5b9k.4 caps the size of ONE upload; it does nothing about a day of them.

On app.indice.page manual approval via users.yaml is the only throttle, which is acceptable with a known roster but is not a quota. If the demo ever widens its roster, an approved curator can upload until the object-storage bill says otherwise.

Shape to consider: a per-principal byte budget per window, checked in the Curator extractor path before the body is read, with the budget in config.yaml alongside uploads.max_mb. The audit log (<home>/events/) already records CrawlUpload per actor, so the accounting source exists.

title: Disk headroom guard: cap total archive size, not just one upload
description:
Dropping object storage (see .1-.3, closed not-doing) means the UpCloud VM's block storage is the only place WACZ bytes live, so the thing that used to be 'the bucket absorbs it' now has to be an explicit guard. uploads.max_mb (.4) bounds ONE request; it says nothing about a burst between daily resets.

Add a second knob beside it:

  uploads:
    max_mb: 200
    max_total_gb: 20

Checked before a job starts, in both add_archive and upload_archive. The accounting is free and needs no new dependency: Wacz.file_size is already recorded per crawl in index/waczs.json, so summing the manifest's local (Source::File) entries gives current usage without touching the filesystem or reaching for statvfs/libc. Refuse with 507 Insufficient Storage (or 413 with a clear message) naming current usage and the cap.

Deliberately NOT a real free-space check: that needs statvfs and so a libc/nix/sysinfo dependency, and it would measure the wrong thing anyway (the volume also holds index/ and Tantivy's merge scratch). A manifest-derived cap is the number an operator can reason about and set.

Why it matters more than it looks: running the volume to ENOSPC is worse than a bucket bill. fsio::write_atomic means a partial manifest write can't corrupt waczs.json, but a Tantivy commit failing mid-merge is a worse day than a rejected upload. Fail early and loudly.

Surface the current usage and the cap in the accession desk next to max_mb, so a curator sees the budget before starting.

Tests in tests/manage.rs: an upload that would cross max_total_gb is refused with the numbers in the message; the sum ignores remote (Source::Url) crawls, which cost no local disk.
close_reason: Moved to rustyweb-open-web-hardening-u9y6.3, which merges them: the per-upload cap and the total-archive cap share a config section, two handlers and their tests, and neither is much use alone. Not demo-specific — any operator exposing serve --manage inherits an unbounded upload route and no disk guard.

title: Harden the add-by-location field before exposing it publicly
description:
POST /api/archives takes AddArchiveRequest.path, an arbitrary string handed to Source::parse: an http(s) prefix makes it a URL, ANYTHING ELSE IS A FILESYSTEM PATH, unconstrained apart from index_location's .wacz extension check. The accession desk exposes it as the 'path or URL' tab. Both branches are gated on Curator and nothing more.

That has been fine while the only curator was Ed on a laptop. app.indice.page is the first time people who are approved but not fully trusted get it, so it should be looked at before launch rather than after:

1. ARBITRARY LOCAL PATH. A curator can make the server read any .wacz it can reach and copy it into archive/. Blast radius in the distroless container is small (only /data is mounted, no shell), but the field has no business accepting a server-side path at all when indice is reached over the network. Suggested: when forward-auth is configured, reject non-URL locations from this endpoint and let the upload endpoint cover local files. The CLI keeps the path form.

2. SSRF. A URL location makes the server fetch an attacker-chosen URL with range requests - http_range::HttpFetch probes it, and remote_warcs_streamable failing just falls back to download_to_temp fetching the whole thing. On UpCloud the cloud metadata service lives at 169.254.169.254, and any internal service on the host network is reachable. The response has to parse as a zip to get anywhere, so this is a blind-SSRF primitive rather than a data-exfiltration one, but it is still a curator turning the server into a request proxy. Suggested minimum: refuse loopback, link-local (169.254.0.0/16, fe80::/10) and private ranges after DNS resolution, with an opt-out for operators who legitimately fetch from an internal host.

Decide and document the position either way - 'curators are trusted with this' is a defensible answer, but it should be a decision in DESIGN rather than an accident. Relates to rustyweb-authz-roles-odc6's witness-type model: this is authorization that exists but is coarser than the act it guards.
close_reason: Moved to rustyweb-open-web-hardening-u9y6.4. The SSRF is arguably worse for an institution than for a demo, since an internal network has more to reach than a bare VM.

title: Decide what search engines may crawl on a public replay instance
description:
There is no robots.txt route and no noindex anywhere in the server (grep for robots/noindex finds only crawl.rs:122, which DISPLAYS a crawl's own robots policy from its warcinfo). app.indice.page is the first indice instance on the open web, so this becomes a decision rather than a default.

Two distinct questions, and they deserve different answers:

1. THE REPLAYED CONTENT. /replay/* and /files/{id} serve third-party pages captured by someone else. Letting Google index them puts other people's content under our hostname and can outrank the live site. Web archives generally keep replay out of search indexes for exactly this reason. Recommend: disallow /replay/, /files/, and the viewer in robots.txt, and consider X-Robots-Tag: noindex on those responses since robots.txt is advisory.

2. INDICE'S OWN PAGES (/, /search, /collection/{id}, /crawl/{id}). For a DEMO that is reset daily, indexing is actively unhelpful: search results would point at collections that no longer exist. Recommend noindex for this instance specifically, driven from config rather than hardcoded, so a real institutional deployment can and should be indexed.

Shape: a site.robots or site.noindex setting in the same config section as .5's site text, plus a GET /robots.txt route. Default should match today's behavior for existing deployments (no robots.txt, indexable), with the demo opting into noindex.

Also note /search is an unauthenticated, uncached, arbitrary-query endpoint. A crawler walking facet links can generate a lot of Tantivy queries. qw5.5 measured faceted search under 100ms at 1M docs so it is not alarming, but it is another argument for keeping bots off this instance.
close_reason: Moved to rustyweb-open-web-hardening-u9y6.7, broadened to cover AI scrapers per Ed's question. Every operator on the open web has the same crawlers pointed at the same infinite replay URL space.

title: indice on the open web: hardening before a public deployment
description:
Everything that has to be true before an indice instance can sit on the public internet, whether that is app.indice.page or an institution's own server.

WHY THIS EXISTS AS ITS OWN EPIC. These started out as children of the demo epic (rustyweb-demo-instance-5b9k), filed as 'risks of letting strangers upload'. Ed pushed back: wouldn't anyone hosting indice have these problems? He was right. Almost all of it is product debt that every operator inherits the moment they expose serve --manage, and several items are WORSE for an institution than for a hobby demo (an internal network has more interesting things for an SSRF to reach than a bare VM does). The demo was simply going to be the first deployment on the open web, which is why the gaps all surfaced while reviewing it.

Evidence that these are genuinely untracked rather than known-and-deferred: before this epic the tracker held five auth/security items, all P3 polish, and three of those turned out to be already done and stale-open (logout-csrf-3k8o, files-cors-pin-3m2s, audit-log-dnon — all closed 2026-10-04). Nothing covered rate limiting, SSRF, the no-roster-means-admin footgun, upload size, disk headroom, error-message leakage, response headers, or bots.

WHAT THIS IS NOT. Not an audit of the authorization model, which was designed deliberately and shipped (authz-roles-odc6, closed): typed Curator/Admin witness extractors, Evidence so a display cookie provably cannot authorize a write, a server-wide same-origin CSRF guard, and an append-only audit log. The model is sound. What is missing is everything around it that assumes a friendly caller.

ORDERING. .1 (bound anonymous work) and .2 (refuse to be accidentally open) are the two that genuinely gate going public, because they are the ones where the failure mode is 'the instance falls over' or 'every visitor is an admin'. The rest are real but survivable.

The demo epic rustyweb-demo-instance-5b9k is parked behind this.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: 2026-10-04: added .9, the threat model in DESIGN, as this epic's ACCEPTANCE CRITERION rather than a ninth finding. .1-.8 fix what this round found; .9 is the only item that reduces the cost of the next review. Rationale, from Ed asking why the September security pass missed all of this: every prior review ran under an unstated premise, and under that premise none of .1-.8 are defects. Tooling was clean (zero open CodeQL alerts, 43 dismissed and all dismissals correct) and the tracker was clean (five auth items, all P3, three already done). The gaps were invisible because nothing recorded which threat model was in force. Write .9 while .1/.2 are fresh, not after.

title: Bound the work one anonymous request can cause
description:
There is NO backpressure of any kind in the server. Greps for TimeoutLayer, ConcurrencyLimitLayer, RequestBodyLimit, load_shed and tower-governor all come back empty; the only timeout in the whole codebase is the 5s client timeout in 'indice health' (main.rs:1904). A single hostile or merely clumsy client is bounded by nothing but Tantivy's speed.

Two things make this worse here than on a typical site:

1. REPLAY IS AN INFINITE URL SPACE. Every archived URL times every capture timestamp is a distinct path under /replay/. That is a textbook crawler trap, and anything that finds it walks it forever.
2. /api/search AND /search ARE UNAUTHENTICATED, UNCACHED AND ARBITRARY. SearchParams.q is an unbounded String (api.rs:21) handed straight to QueryParser::parse_query_lenient. limit IS clamped (.min(200), api.rs:29) and the collector is bounded by CANDIDATE_CAP = 1000 (search/query.rs:25), so the result side is fine; the input side is not. Facet links also generate fresh query combinations on every page, so a crawler manufactures distinct work rather than hitting a cache.

WORK:
- A TimeoutLayer, so no request can occupy a thread indefinitely. Pick the bound off the slowest legitimate route; note /files/{id} streams large bodies and SSE at /api/archives/{id}/events is long-lived by design, so a blanket timeout will break both — they need exemption or a much longer budget. That interaction is the main design question in this ticket.
- A global concurrency limit with load shedding, so saturation answers 503 fast instead of queueing until memory runs out.
- Per-IP rate limiting. tower-governor is the obvious candidate; weigh it against doing it at the proxy. NOTE Caddy's rate limiter is a third-party module and not in the standard caddy:2 image, so the proxy route means a custom build. VERIFY THAT before choosing. Doing it in the binary also benefits every self-hoster, which is the whole premise of this epic.
- Cap the search query length explicitly (a few KB). Today the only thing stopping a megabyte of q is hyper's URI limit, which is an accident rather than a decision.
- Behind a reverse proxy the peer address is the proxy, so per-IP anything needs X-Forwarded-For handling, and that header is client-supplied unless the proxy overwrites it. Get this right or the limiter is trivially evaded: trust XFF only from a configured proxy, the same shape as the existing forward-auth secret.

Relates to rustyweb-stream-fetch-timeouts-v3su (the OUTBOUND half: the ureq agent has no timeouts either, so one slow record stalls a fetch tail).

Tests: a request exceeding the timeout gets a timeout status rather than hanging; over the concurrency limit sheds with 503; an over-length q is refused; XFF is ignored from an untrusted peer.

title: Refuse to be accidentally open, and make approval not need a restart
description:
Two halves of the same problem: the roster is the only thing standing between 'authenticated' and 'can delete the archive', and it is both easy to forget and awkward to change.

HALF ONE — THE FOOTGUN. With no users.yaml at all, Users::resolve makes every authenticated user an ADMIN (identity.rs, documented as byte-identical to pre-roles behavior so upgrading changed nothing). That is right for a laptop and a loaded gun on the open web. There IS a guard for the adjacent mistake — serve_on_listener refuses to start if --manage is bound to a non-loopback address without forward-auth — but NOT for this one: configure forward-auth, forget the roster, and the first stranger your IdP admits can remove_dir_all a collection. All that stands there today is Users::summary() at tracing::info (server/mod.rs:230), which scrolls past during startup.

Decide between: (a) refuse to start when --manage + forward-auth + no users.yaml, requiring an explicit opt-out flag for someone who really means 'everyone who can log in is an admin'; or (b) start but warn prominently and degrade unlisted users to Reader. (a) matches the existing precedent of refusing the non-loopback bind, and a refusal that names the fix is friendlier than an archive someone deleted. Recommend (a).

HALF TWO — APPROVAL SHOULDN'T NEED A RESTART. server/mod.rs:228 reads the roster once at startup; the field comment says so plainly. Approving somebody therefore means restarting the instance, which is the difference between 'manual approval is a YAML edit' and 'manual approval is an ops task'. Make AppState.users reloadable: stat users.yaml during resolution and re-read on mtime change, mirroring the existing RwLock<Arc<SearchIndex>> hot-swap pattern. One stat per authenticated request is nothing; a notify watcher would be a dependency for no gain.

CRITICAL PROPERTY: a malformed users.yaml must keep the LAST GOOD roster and log an error. Users::load already refuses to parse a broken permissions file rather than silently defaulting — and given half one, falling back to the default on a parse error would promote every visitor to admin. That is the single most important test in this ticket.

Tests: forward-auth + no roster refuses to start (or warns and degrades, per the decision); a roster edit takes effect without a restart; a roster that becomes malformed keeps the previous one and does not promote anybody.

title: Bound what an authenticated writer can consume: upload size and total archive size
description:
Merges what were rustyweb-demo-instance-5b9k.4 and .11 — they share a config section, the same two handlers and the same tests, and neither is much use without the other.

TODAY: server/mod.rs:292 is the ONLY DefaultBodyLimit in the repo and it is DefaultBodyLimit::disable(), on POST /api/archives/upload. Every other route keeps axum's 2 MB default. There is no disk check anywhere. So one curator can post an unbounded body, and any number of curators can fill the volume.

  uploads:
    max_mb: 200        # one request
    max_total_gb: 20   # the whole archive

PER-REQUEST: layer DefaultBodyLimit::max(n) instead of disabling, when configured. Enforce AGAIN inside stream_field_to_file with a running byte counter, because a chunked body with no Content-Length slips past a declared-length check, and because the second check can name the limit instead of returning a bare 413. Unset keeps today's behavior so existing deployments do not change under them.

TOTAL: check before a job starts, in both add_archive and upload_archive. The accounting is free and needs no dependency — Wacz.file_size is already recorded per crawl in index/waczs.json, so summing the manifest's local (Source::File) entries gives current usage without touching the filesystem. Remote (Source::Url) crawls cost no local disk and must be excluded. Refuse with the numbers in the message.

DELIBERATELY NOT a real free-space check: that needs statvfs and therefore libc/nix/sysinfo, and it measures the wrong thing anyway because the volume also carries index/ and Tantivy's merge scratch. A manifest-derived cap is a number an operator can choose and reason about.

Why the total matters more than it looks: running to ENOSPC is worse than a rejected upload. fsio::write_atomic means a partial manifest write cannot corrupt waczs.json, but a Tantivy commit failing mid-merge is a much worse day. Fail early and loudly.

Surface both numbers in the accession desk (views/manage.rs) so a curator sees the budget before starting a doomed upload.

Relates to rustyweb-upload-quota-hryt (P3): both caps here are archive-wide, so one curator can still consume everyone's share. Per-principal quota is that ticket.

Tests: over max_mb -> 413 naming the limit, with AND without a Content-Length; an upload that would cross max_total_gb is refused with current usage and the cap; the total ignores Source::Url crawls.

title: Add-by-location: SSRF and server-side filesystem paths
description:
AddArchiveRequest.path (server/manage.rs:125) is an arbitrary string handed to Source::parse: an http(s) prefix makes it a URL, ANYTHING ELSE IS A FILESYSTEM PATH, unconstrained apart from index_location's .wacz extension check. The accession desk exposes it as the 'path or URL' tab. Both branches are gated on Curator and nothing more. This is a DECISION ticket as much as a code one.

1. ARBITRARY LOCAL PATH. A curator can make the server read any .wacz it can reach and file it into archive/. The capability is deliberate and legitimate for staff pointing at a NAS mount, which is exactly why removing it is wrong. The question is whether it should be reachable OVER THE NETWORK. Suggested: when forward-auth is configured, reject non-URL locations from this endpoint and let the upload endpoint cover local files; the CLI keeps the path form unchanged. An institution that genuinely wants network-triggered local reads can opt in.

2. SSRF, AND IT IS WORSE FOR AN INSTITUTION THAN FOR A HOBBY DEMO. A URL makes the server fetch an attacker-chosen address with range requests: http_range::HttpFetch probes it, and remote_warcs_streamable failing just falls through to download_to_temp fetching the whole thing. A VM has little to find; a university network has plenty, and cloud metadata sits at 169.254.169.254 on most providers. The response must parse as a zip to get anywhere, so this is a blind-SSRF/request-proxy primitive rather than direct exfiltration, which lowers the severity without making it fine.
   Suggested minimum: after DNS resolution, refuse loopback, link-local (169.254.0.0/16, fe80::/10) and RFC1918 ranges, with an operator opt-out for sites that legitimately fetch from an internal host. Resolve-then-check has a TOCTOU window against DNS rebinding; note it rather than solving it, unless pinning the resolved address through the fetch is cheap with ureq.
   Same guard belongs on the Browsertrix/Archive-It import hosts, which are also operator- or curator-supplied.

Whatever is decided, write it into DESIGN. 'Curators are trusted with a filesystem path and an outbound fetch' is a defensible position; it should be a recorded decision rather than an accident. Relates to authz-roles-odc6's witness-type model: this is authorization that exists but is coarser than the act it guards.

Tests: with forward-auth configured a non-URL location is rejected; a URL resolving to loopback or link-local is refused; the opt-out re-permits it.

title: Stop returning server internals in error responses
description:
server/util.rs:98:

  pub(super) fn error_response(e: anyhow::Error) -> Response {
      tracing::error!("{e:#}");
      (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, e.to_string()).into_response()
  }

The error text goes to the CLIENT. This codebase's house style is with_context(|| format!("reading {}", path.display())), so anyhow messages here routinely CARRY ABSOLUTE FILESYSTEM PATHS, and error_response is reached from 19 call sites on PUBLIC, UNAUTHENTICATED routes (pages.rs, collection.rs, crawl.rs, api.rs, assets.rs). The homepage alone hits it when Manifest::open fails (pages.rs:30), so a broken or unreadable waczs.json hands an anonymous visitor the server's home path.

It is e.to_string() rather than {e:#}, so only the outermost context escapes, not the whole chain. That limits it without fixing it, because the outermost context is usually the one naming the file.

Low severity on its own — it is reconnaissance, not access — but it is the kind of thing that only matters once you are on the open web, and the fix is cheap:
- return a generic message plus a correlation id to the client, and keep {e:#} in the log where it belongs. The TraceLayer span already exists to hang an id off.
- keep the detailed form for authenticated management routes, where the operator IS the audience and a useful message saves a support round-trip. That split is the actual design decision here.

Tests: a public route forced into its error path returns no absolute path and no home-directory name; the log still contains the full chain.

title: Response hardening headers, with a replay-shaped exception
description:
The server sets no security headers at all: greps for content-security-policy, x-content-type-options, x-frame-options, strict-transport-security, referrer-policy and permissions-policy come back empty in both the Rust and the Caddyfiles. The only deliberate header work is the CORS pair on /files/{id} (assets.rs:117-118), which replay needs.

CHEAP AND UNCONTROVERSIAL:
- X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. This one matters here specifically: /files/{id} serves application/octet-stream and is directly fetchable, and replay serves archived third-party bytes. MIME sniffing is how a stored text file becomes executable HTML on our origin.
- Referrer-Policy. Today a click from a replayed page or a search result can leak the search query, or the archived URL being viewed, in the Referer to a third party. For an archive this is a reader-privacy question, not just a hygiene one.
- HSTS: decide whether indice sets it or the proxy does. Caddy terminates TLS, so the proxy is the natural place; just make it a decision instead of nobody's job.

THE DELICATE ONE — CSP. Replay deliberately runs archived JavaScript in a SAME-ORIGIN frame, mediated by the wabac service worker. That is inherent to how ReplayWeb.page works and it is the whole reason replay is useful. A blanket CSP will break it. So this needs a per-route policy: a reasonably tight one on indice's own pages (homepage, search, collection, crawl, the workroom forms), and an explicitly loose, commented one on the replay routes — with the comment explaining WHY, so nobody tightens it later and breaks replay without understanding the trade.

Frame policy is the same shape: /replay/viewer must be frameable by us, so a blanket X-Frame-Options: DENY is wrong. frame-ancestors scoped to our own origin is the better tool.

Tests: nosniff and Referrer-Policy present on an ordinary page; the replay routes keep their documented looser policy; a browser replay test still passes (cargo test -p indice-lib --test browser -- --ignored) since this is exactly the change that silently breaks replay.

title: Crawler and AI-scraper policy: robots.txt, noindex, and what to block
description:
There is no robots.txt route and no noindex anywhere. (crawl.rs:122 is unrelated — it DISPLAYS a crawl's own robots policy from its warcinfo.) On the open web this stops being tidiness and becomes an availability question, because of the crawl traps described in .1: /replay/ is an infinite URL space (every archived URL x every timestamp) and /search manufactures fresh work per facet combination.

TWO QUESTIONS, DIFFERENT ANSWERS:

1. THE REPLAYED CONTENT (/replay/*, /files/{id}, the viewer). These serve third-party pages someone else captured. Indexing them puts other people's content under the operator's hostname and can outrank the live site; web archives generally keep replay out of search indexes for exactly this reason. Disallow in robots.txt AND send X-Robots-Tag: noindex, since robots.txt is advisory and not every fetcher reads it.
2. INDICE'S OWN PAGES (/, /search, /collection/{id}, /crawl/{id}, the annotations index). An institutional archive probably WANTS these indexed — discoverability is the point of a finding aid. A daily-reset demo does not, because results would point at collections that no longer exist. So this must be CONFIGURABLE, not hardcoded, and the default must match today's behavior (indexable, no robots.txt) so nobody's deployment changes under them.

AI SCRAPERS specifically. Ed raised this and it is the live version of the problem: GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot, Bytespider, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended, meta-externalagent and friends. Layers, in increasing order of actually working:
- robots.txt user-agent denylist — advisory, stops only the ones that behave. A text file.
- X-Robots-Tag — also advisory, but covers fetchers that skip robots.txt.
- user-agent blocking at the proxy — enforced, trivially spoofed, still catches the honest-but-aggressive majority. A few Caddyfile lines.
- rate limiting (.1) — the only layer that works against something lying about its identity. Which is why .1 is the ticket that actually matters and this one is defence in depth.
Keep the denylist operator-editable rather than compiled in; that list changes monthly and nobody should need a new indice release to add a name.

Shape: a setting in the same config section as the site text, plus GET /robots.txt. Worth doing for every operator, not just a demo — an institutional archive has the same scrapers pointed at it.

Tests: robots.txt renders from config; replay routes carry noindex; defaults leave an existing deployment byte-identical.

title: Request-log privacy: client IP and full query strings
Write indice's threat model into DESIGN, per deployment shape
description:
DESIGN describes indice's deployment shapes in prose but never says WHICH GUARANTEES HOLD IN EACH. That omission is why this epic exists: every prior security pass ran under an unstated premise (a laptop, or a trusted institution behind SSO), and under that premise none of .1-.8 are defects. 'No users.yaml means every authenticated user is an Admin' is the DOCUMENTED default and the code comment argues FOR it as upgrade safety. An arbitrary local filesystem path is a FEATURE for staff with a NAS mount. An error message containing a path is HELPFUL when the reader is the operator. All of them flip sign only when the premise becomes 'strangers on the open web', and nothing in the repo recorded which premise was in force.

So this is the epic's ACCEPTANCE CRITERION rather than a documentation chore. .1-.8 fix this round's findings; this is the item that makes the NEXT review cheap, and it has to be written while the context is fresh or it will not be written at all.

A new DESIGN section naming the shapes and, for each, the principals, what is trusted, which guarantees hold, and which guards are load-bearing:

1. LAPTOP / LOOPBACK. Caller is the operator; trust total. Load-bearing: serve_on_listener refuses a non-loopback bind without forward-auth; CsrfPolicy requires a loopback authority in local mode (DNS-rebinding defence).
2. INSTITUTION BEHIND SSO. Curators are staff or affiliates under an acceptable-use policy; readers may be internal or public. Load-bearing: the forward-auth shared secret, users.yaml, the typed Curator/Admin extractors, Evidence (a display cookie provably cannot authorize a write).
3. PUBLIC READ-ONLY. No write surface mounted at all. Materially the smallest surface and worth naming separately, because it is the demo shape under consideration: .3 and .4 simply do not apply, while .1 and .7 still do.
4. PUBLIC WITH A WRITE SURFACE. Readers anonymous and hostile-capable; curators are approved strangers rather than colleagues. Everything in this epic applies.

THE FORMAT THAT MAKES IT MAINTAINABLE: state each guarantee with the TEST THAT PINS IT. Several already exist — tests/authz.rs has a route-by-route privilege matrix and the display-cookie-cannot-write case, the /files credentialed-CORS pin is at authz.rs:916, the loopback refusal has a test. Writing 'guarantee X, pinned by test Y' makes an UNPINNED guarantee visible as a gap, which is the difference between a document that rots and one that fails CI when it stops being true.

Also record a short assumption -> what-breaks-if-false -> which-bead table, so a future premise change (a PaaS, a multi-tenant host, federation per shwl) can be checked against it in minutes instead of re-derived.

QUESTIONS THE DOCUMENT MUST ANSWER, not dodge:
- IS A CURATOR-SUPPLIED WACZ TRUSTED INPUT? This is unexamined today and it has a concrete edge. Zip entries are read by name or index and never extracted to a path from the archive (wacz.rs:111,151,213,274,309...), so zip-slip is structurally impossible — good. But datapackage.json, pages/pages.jsonl and the CDX are read_to_end with NO SIZE CAP (e.g. wacz.rs:396), so a small WACZ whose pages.jsonl inflates to many GB is a decompression bomb that OOMs the indexer. Under shape 2 'curators are trusted' is a fine answer. Under shape 4 it probably is not. Either way, decide it here rather than discovering it.
- Which populations exist, now that annotations created a second one (contributors) alongside administrators. identity.rs:160 already notes where an annotate-only role would slot in.
- What indice deliberately does NOT defend, so it stops being re-litigated: it authenticates nobody (so credential stuffing, password policy and MFA belong to the proxy); replay runs archived third-party JavaScript SAME-ORIGIN by design via the wabac service worker, which is inherent to ReplayWeb.page and not a defect; /files/{id} sends access-control-allow-origin: * on purpose.

EVIDENCE WORTH CITING in the section, because it shows the failure mode this prevents: before this epic the tracker held five auth/security items, all P3, and three were already done and stale-open. CodeQL had zero open and 43 dismissed alerts, all dismissals correct — 36 rust/path-injection, every one of them on paths that ARE guarded by fsio::ensure_within (collections.rs, assets.rs, fsio.rs, events.rs, annotations.rs), and NONE on server/manage.rs or the index_location flow, so it never traced AddArchiveRequest.path to a sink and never emitted an SSRF or information-exposure alert at all. Clean tooling, clean tracker, and eight real gaps, because nobody had written down which threat model was in force. Separately: rustyweb-stream-fetch-timeouts-v3su found 'the HTTP agent has no timeouts' OUTBOUND on 2026-09-07 from an observed stalled progress bar, and nobody asked whether the inbound side had the same gap. It does (.1). A threat model is what turns one symptom into that question.
